Histologic Features of Non-Hodgkins Lymphomas Involving Bone Marrow

Type of Lymphoma

Incidence of Involvement (%)

Pattern of Involvement*

Cytology

Comments

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL)

85 (SLL)

100 (CLL)

Interstitial, nodular, mixed, or diffuse involvement

Small, mature lymphocytes; proliferation centers may be present

Paratrabecular infiltrates indicate lymphoma of non-CLL/SLL type; LEF1 positivity distinguishes CLL/SLL from other small B-cell lymphomas

Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma

80-100

Nodular, diffuse interstitial infiltrate, sometimes paratrabecular aggregates

Spectrum of cells from small lymphocytes to plasma cells; immunoblasts may be present; Dutcher bodies are often present; increased mast cells

Paratrabecular infiltrates may be present; majority of cases have MYD88L265P mutation

Mantle cell lymphoma

60-90

Usually mixed paratrabecular and nonparatrabecular

 

Small lymphocytes with irregular nuclei; may be blastoid; rare cells with prominent nucleoli

Cases with paratrabecular only may be confused with follicular lymphoma; circulating lymphoma cells are common; BCL1 and SOX11 are positive

Follicular lymphoma

Grade 1-2: 50-70

Grade 3: 15-25

Paratrabecular

Small cleaved lymphocytes usually predominate; large cleaved or non-cleaved cells may be present

Distinct paratrabecular infiltrates are common; neoplastic follicles may be present; CD10 and BCL6 positivity in the lymphoma cells is lower in the bone marrow than in the lymph node; large B-cell lymphoma may have discordant, low-grade follicular lymphoma in the bone marrow

Hairy cell leukemia

 

Interstitial or patchy with preservation of fat and hematopoietic elements

 

 

Splenic marginal zone lymphoma

100

Nodular interstitial infiltrate, intrasinusoidal lymphoma cells

Small lymphocytes with slightly irregular nuclei, condensed chromatin, and moderate amounts of cytoplasm

Intrasinusoidal infiltration is common; reactive germinal centers may be present; villous lymphocytes may be present in the blood smears

Low-grade extranodal marginal zone lymphoma

5-44

Mixed, focal nonparatrabecular, intrasinusoidal, diffuse

Small cells with condensed chromatin and scant to moderate amounts of cytoplasm; occasional scattered large cells may be present

Extent of bone marrow infiltration usually minimal; overt blood involvement is uncommon

Nodal marginal zone lymphoma

30-50

Interstitial or nodular with intertrabecular or paratrabecular distribution, intrasinusoidal infiltration may be seen

Small cells with condensed chromatin and scant to moderate amounts of cytoplasm

 

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Common type: 10-30

Double-hit: 40-90

Diffuse, nodular, other interstitial rarely intrasinusoidal

Large cells with irregular nuclei, distinct or prominent nucleoli; may have discordant histology subtype in the bone marrow such as a low-grade B-cell lymphoma

Lymphomatous infiltrates can be heterogeneous with prominent T cells (T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma); immunohistochemistry for B-cell antigens is essential in identifying the large B-cell component; rare cases of large cell lymphoma are intravascular

Burkitts lymphoma

30-60

Interstitial, diffuse interstitial

Medium-sized cells with reticular chromatin, multiple small nucleoli, and basophilic cytoplasm; cytoplasmic vacuoles are common

MYC gene rearrangement positive; starry sky pattern may be present; frequent mitoses and necrosis are common

Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified

20-40

Including interstitial, intrasinusoidal, diffuse, or nodular distribution patterns

Polymorphous lymphoid population; nuclei are often hyperchromatic and irregular; large cells with nucleoli may be present; prominent reactive cell component often intermixed with lymphoma cells

Vascularity and reticulin fibrosis are often prominent; infiltrate is less well demarcated than most B-cell lymphomas

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma

10-30

Nodular

Interstitial with scattered cells

Diffuse

Large cells with horseshoe-shaped nuclei and abundant cytoplasm (hallmark cells)

Detection rate is higher with immunostaining for CD30 or ALK1

Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma

100

Distinct intrasinusoidal pattern of infiltrate

Variable; often medium-sized lymphocytes with cytologic atypia; may have dispersed chromatin resembling blasts

Lymphomatous infiltrates may be subtle, and immunostaining for CD3 and cytotoxic proteins is helpful; typically, TCR γδ+/CD4−/CD8−isochromosome 7q is common

Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma

50-80

Polymorphous infiltrate

Polymorphous infiltrates; neoplastic cells with clear cytoplasm are uncommon

Positivity for CD10 and CXCR13 in the lymphoma cells is less common in the bone marrow; primary diagnosis based on the bone marrow findings alone is challenging

Aggressive NK-cell leukemia

Highly variable

Infiltrates typically patchy & interstitial; sinusoidal infiltrates reported in some cases

Highly variable cytologic features, bland to pleomorphic

Bone marrow necrosis may be present

High association with secondary hemophagocytosis

Hemophagocytosis may mask ANKL

Overview of B Cell Development

Stage

Location

Key Events

Features and Markers

Hematopoietic Stem Cells (HSC)

Fetal liver / Bone marrow

Differentiation into common lymphoid progenitors (CLPs)

CD34+ (HSC marker)

Lymphoid Progenitors (CLP)

Bone marrow

Commitment to B cell lineage through signaling and transcription factors

Expresses FLT3, IL-7Rα

Pro-B Cell

Bone marrow

D-J rearrangement of heavy chain (IGH locus); transcription factors EBF1, E2A, and PAX5 guide B cell fate

CD19+, CD10+, CD43+ (early markers)

Pre-B Cell

Bone marrow

V-DJ rearrangement completes heavy chain; formation of the pre-B cell receptor (pre-BCR); allelic exclusion ensures only one heavy chain is expressed

Pre-BCR (μ heavy chain with surrogate light chain); CD20+

Immature B Cell

Bone marrow

Light chain V-J rearrangement (kappa or lambda), forming the complete BCR; negative selection against self-reactive BCRs

Expresses IgM on the cell surface

Transitional B Cell

Blood / Spleen

BCR is tested for tolerance; cells undergo further selection in peripheral lymphoid tissues

IgM+, transitional marker CD24high, CD38+

Mature Naïve B Cell

Peripheral tissues (spleen, lymph nodes)

Co-expression of IgM and IgD; cells circulate in search of antigen

IgM+ IgD+, CD23+

Activated B Cell

Peripheral tissues (secondary lymphoid organs)

Upon encountering antigen and T cell help, activation occurs; proliferation and formation of short-lived plasma cells or entry into germinal center

Expresses activation markers CD80, CD86, MHC class II

Germinal Center (GC) B Cell

Germinal center (lymph nodes)

Undergoes somatic hypermutation (SHM) and class switch recombination (CSR) to refine antibody affinity and function

Divided into dark zone (centroblasts) and light zone (centrocytes)

Memory B Cell

Peripheral tissues

Long-lived, resting cells that quickly respond upon re-exposure to antigen; expresses high-affinity, class-switched BCR

Expresses high-affinity IgG, IgA, or IgE (depends on CSR)

Plasma Cell

Bone marrow / Mucosal sites

Differentiates to produce and secrete large quantities of antibodies

High levels of Ig secretion, CD138+ (plasma cell marker)

Additional Notes on Key Processes

  • V(D)J Recombination: Occurs in early stages (pro-B and pre-B) to generate diverse B cell receptors.
  • Negative Selection: Eliminates self-reactive immature B cells, preventing autoimmunity.
  • Somatic Hypermutation (SHM) and Class Switch Recombination (CSR): Occur in GC B cells, enhancing affinity for specific antigens and changing antibody isotypes for varied immune functions.
  • Memory and Plasma Cells: Final differentiation stages that provide long-term immunity and immediate antibody production, respectively.

Preneoplastic and neoplastic small lymphocytic proliferations

*CLL/SLL and MBL

WHO 2022 definition of CLL/SLL

·       Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL) is a B-cell lymphoma comprising monomorphic small mature B-cells that frequently co-express CD5 and CD23.

·       A peripheral blood diagnosis of CLL requires a B-cell count >5×109/L, with the characteristic morphology and immunophenotype.

·       A tissue-based diagnosis of SLL requires organ enlargement (e.g., lymphadenopathy >15 mm) and its infiltration by the above neoplastic B-cells.

·       Although CLL and SLL represent the same disease, the name SLL is used for cases with <5×109/L circulating B cells and nodal, splenic, or other extramedullary involvement.


Typical CLL lymphocyte morphology?

●      "Soccer ball"

●      "Snickerdoodle cookie"

●      Small rim of cytoplasm

●      Nucleus with prominent chromatin clumping

●      No discernible nucleoli

 

WHO 2022 definition of CLL/SLL  

·       a B-cell lymphoma comprising monomorphic small mature B cells that frequently coexpress CD5 and CD23.

·       A peripheral blood diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) requires a B-cell count of ≥ 5 × 109/L, with the characteristic morphology and immunophenotype.

·       A tissue-based diagnosis of small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) requires organ enlargement (e.g. lymphadenopathy > 15 mm) and its infiltration by the above neoplastic B cells.

·       Although CLL and SLL represent the same disease, the latter term is used for cases with < 5 × 109/L circulating B cells and nodal, splenic, or other extramedullary involvement.

 

What are the RAI(4) and BINET(3) classifications for CLL?

 

 

CLL/SLL cells usually coexpress CD__? and CD__?          

●      CD5 and CD23, 19+

●      (CD 5 = aberrant expression of T lineage marker)

To Dx CLL, lymphocytosis be present for at least _____ months?          

●      3 months

●      (IWCLL requirement, not mentioned in WHO)

What exception allows Dx of CLL with lymphocyte count <5x109/L?          

●      Cytopenias or disease-related symptoms

●      IWCLL

In CLL, cytopenias may be the result of what 2 processes?          

●      BM involvement/infiltration

●      Immune related

What criteria are used to differentiate between CLL & monoclonal B lymphocytosis (MBL)?          

●      CLL = must be a monoclonal B-cell count ≥ 5 x 10^9/L, with the characteristic morphology and phenotype of CLL in the peripheral blood.

●      MBL = clonal CLL-like cell count < 5 x 10^9/L AND without lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, or other extramedullary disease (note: when signing out flow you may not have this info, so cannot outright diagnose MBL vs SLL → leave this to clinician)

The term SLL is used for cases with what features?          

●      Non-leukemic cases with the tissue morphology and immunophenotype of CLL

●      Cases with < 5 × 109/L circulating B cells and nodal, splenic, or other extramedullary involvement.

IWCLL definition of SLL? 3 criteria          

●      1) < 5 x 10^9/L PB B-cells

●      2) Lymphadenopathy

●      3) No cytopenias due to BM infiltration by CLL/SLL (which will be qualified to be CLL)

 

CLL mean age at diagnosis          

·       The median age at diagnosis in fair-skinned populations (≥ 70 years) is higher than in Asian and African people (5862 years).

 

In which countries is CLL very rare?          

●      Far eastern countries.

●      With the low incidence maintained in emigrant populations

 

What findings support the concept of a limited set of (auto-) antigenic elements promoting division of precursor cells and clonal evolution in CLL?

●      B-cell receptors (BCR) of CLL cells demonstrate highly selected immunoglobulin heavy chain variable (IGHV) gene usage or even very similar entire antigen-binding sites, coded by both heavy and light chain genes (so called stereotypes) → thus CLL cells differ from the B-cell receptors of much broader diversity found in normal B lymphocytes
       

Is aleukaemic tissue involvement common?           

●      No. Rarely, patients with CLL/SLL present with aleukaemic tissue involvement, but usually develop BM and PB involvement during the evolution of the disease.

Typical Sites of CLL involvement?          

●      Peripheral blood and BM are usually involved.

●      Secondary lymphoid tissues such as the → spleen, lymph nodes, and Waldeyer ring

●      Extranodal involvement in small subset

○      e.g. of the skin, gastrointestinal tract, or CNS

 

% of SLL that evolves into frank CLL          

●      SLL is diagnosed in 10 - 20% of cases, and as many as 20% evolve into frank CLL


Typical clinical features of CLL?          

Clinical features are very variable including presentation, course and outcome.

●      Asymptomatic → most patients are asymptomatic

●      Symptomatic → some present with fatigue, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, infections (most frequently pulmonary), splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy or extranodal infiltrates.

●      A small M-component may be found in some patients.

●      Most cases of CLL in western countries are diagnosed on the basis of routine blood analysis in asymptomatic subjects = incidentally in an asymptomatic patient

Egs of autoimmune cytopenias that may occur in CLL          

●      Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, immune thrombocytopenia, autoimmune agranulocytosis or erythroblastopenia/PRCA

○      Dont forget CLL on your PRCA DDx with T-LGL & thymoma

A small paraprotein, usually of lg ___ type, can be observed in approximately ___% of the patients          

●      IgM - 10%

 

Healthy individuals may show monoclonal or oligoclonal B-cell expansions with the characteristic phenotype of CLL in about ___ % of tested subjects >___ years old          

●      3.5% of tested subjects

●      >40 years old

The frequency of hypogammaglobulinaemia is about ____ % at diagnosis and increases over time, to as much as ___% among patients with advanced disease          

●      30% at diagnosis

●      60% in advanced disease

Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis with a non-CLL phenotype (CD5-) may correspond to?          

●      Similar phenomena in other B-cell neoplasms

●      early or indolent forms of B-cell neoplasms such as marginal zone lymphoma, follicular lymphoma, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, hairy cell leukemia, or splenic B-cell lymphoma.

 

Characteristic morphology of lymph nodes involved by CLL?          

●      Enlarged lymph nodes in patients with CLL/SLL show effacement of the architecture by a proliferation of small lymphocytes with variably prominent scattered paler proliferation centres

○      So-called pseudofollicular pattern

●      In some cases, there is a vaguely nodular appearance.

●      Involvement may be limited to interfollicular areas.

 

What sized cells are contained in proliferation centres?          

●      A continuum of small, medium and large cells.

 

What are the scores for diagnosis of CLL by immunophenotype?

Describe classic CLL morphology of the 3 types of cells present in proliferation centers





●      Mixture of small lymphocytes with scant cytoplasm and clumped chromatin

●      Slightly larger prolymphocytes with more dispersed chromatin and small nucleoli

●      Single paraimmunoblasts (arrows), which are larger cells with round to oval nuclei, dispersed chromatin and a central nucleolus.

Describe the predominant cell seen in CLL infiltration of a tissue (classic CLL cell)          

●      A small lymphocyte, which may be slightly larger than a normal lymphocyte, with clumped chromatin, usually a round nucleus, and occasionally a small nucleolus.

Is there a high mitotic rate in CLL?          

●      No. Mitotic activity is usually very low.

●      Finding of > 40% is adverse prognosis

Prolymphocyte histologic appearance?          

●      Small to medium-sized cells with relatively clumped chromatin and small nucleoli

Paraimmunoblasts histologic appearance?          

●      Larger than prolymphocytes, with round to oval nuclei, dispersed chromatin, central eosinophilic nucleoli and slightly basophilic cytoplasm.



What region of the spleen may be involved?          

●      Prominent white pulp involvement

●      But the red pulp is also involved

Carlos slide

Are proliferation centres seen in the spleen?          

●      Yes.

●      They may be seen but are less conspicuous than in lymph nodes

 

In some cases, the small lymphoid cells show moderate nuclear irregularity, which can lead to a differential diagnosis of          

●      Mantle cell lymphoma

 

Some CLL cases may show ______________ differentiation          

●      Plasmacytoid differentiation

 
Describe CLL cell appearance on BM & PB          

●      Small lymphocytes with clumped chromatin and scanty/small rim of cytoplasm

●      No discernible nucleoli

●      Smudge or basket cells are typically seen in peripheral blood smears.

 


   
What are smudge or basket cells?          

●      Disrupted cells



Accelerated CLL/SLL

What is Histologically aggressive CLL/SLL?

●      Large/confluent proliferation centres (broader than a 20x objective lens and 10x ocular lens)

●      Or with high proliferation index (> 2.4 mitoses per PC or > 40% Ki-67+ cells in PCs, whereby traditionally PC size is not defined)

 

The proportion of prolymphocytes in PB films is usually <___ % of the lymphoid cells          

●      Usually <15%

●      Prolymph morph: cells with irregular nuclear contours, larger cells with more dispersed chromatin and more abundant cytoplasm

 

What is the term for cases with >15% prolymphocytes, but < 55%?          

●      If the total proportion of prolymphocytes (medium-sized cells with basophilic cytoplasm and a prominent nucleolus) is > 15% in peripheral blood, prolymphocytic progression is established

●      Typically, prolymphocytes are <15% in CLL

 

More than 55% of prolymphocytes would favor the diagnosis of?          

·       It should be noted that cases with > 55% prolymphocytes, that have otherwise immunophenotypic features of CLL and that were classified as B-prolymphocytic leukaemia in the previous edition of the WHO classification of haematolymphoid tumours, are now classified as prolymphocytic progression of CLL/SLL (not as B-prolymphocytic leukaemia).

·       A blastoid variant of mantle cell lymphoma should be excluded in these cases.

 

How frequent is histologically aggressive CLL/SLL or prolymphocytic progression and what does it imply?

·       5%

·       TP53 and clinical outcome between typical CLL/SLL and RT

 

Differentiating morphologic features of atypical CLL in PB          

●      Less condensed nuclear chromatin and nuclear irregularities in PB lymphocytes

 

Atypical CLL immunophenotypic and genetic associations/characteristics?          

●      Trisomy 12

●      Strong positivity for surface immunoglobulin, CD20, and FMC7

 

CLL - 3 possible patterns of BM involvement?          

●      Interstitial, nodular and/or diffuse

●      NEVER paratrabecular: if present, rethink the diagnosis

●      Nodular pattern

●      Interstitial pattern

●      Proliferation centres can be observed, although they are not as prominent as in lymph nodes, and follicular dendritic cells may be present

●      Most cases have > 30% CLL cells in the bone marrow aspirate

What infiltration pattern is usually associated with more advanced disease          

●      Diffuse
     

What is the definition of minimal BM involvement required to diagnose CLL/SLL in the absence of other defining features?          

●      This definition is not established, although the IWCLL describes >30% lymphoid cells as "characteristically" present

Typical CLL immunophenotype using flow cytometry

·       typically monotypic surface IgM dim+, IgD+/− (IgG+ in ~10% of cases),

·       CD19+, CD5+, CD23+, CD43+, CD200+, CD20 dim+, CD11c variable,

·       CD10−, CD79b−, FMC7−, CD25−, and CD103−,

·       along with showing light chain restriction (dim expression).

 

Name 3 negative immunophenotypic markers helpful in evaluating the DDx          

●      CD10 is negative

●      FMC7 and CD79b are usually negative or weakly expressed in typical CLL.

●      The immunophenotype of PB lymphocytes has been integrated into a scoring system that helps in the differential diagnosis between CLL and other B-cell leukaemias

Strong expression of _ and _ and an absence of _ expression characterize CLL.

·       CD200 and ROR1

·       CD81

 

Expression of _ and _ is associated with a worse prognosis.

·       CD38

·       CD49d

 

New IHC marker for CLL (Jaffe discusses)          

●      LEF1: nuclear stain

What does LEF1 stain in addition to CLL?

●      Caution: also Pos in normal T cells

●      LEF1 is useful to identify CLL/SLL infiltration in tissues, because it is aberrantly expressed in almost all CLL/SLL, whereas normal mature B lymphocytes and virtually all other small B-cell lymphomas are negative

 

Give at least 5 examples of ATYPICAL CLL immunophenotypic findings          

●      CD5- or CD23-

●      FMC7+ or CD11c+

●      strong sIg

●      CD79b+

In a case of true CLL, where may you see positive Cyclin D1 staining          

●      Cyclin D1 is not expressed, but some positive cells can be seen in proliferation centres in about 30% of cases.

●      These cells are SOX11-negative and do not carry chromosomal translocations affecting the CCND1 gene

●      Note: CD20 and CD23 expression is usually stronger in cells of the proliferation centres than inthe diffuse areas

MYC and NOTCH1 proteins may also be expressed in proliferation centres independently of gene alterations

CLL postulated normal counterpart          

●      An antigen-experienced mature CD5+ B cell with mutated or unmutated IGHV genes

The overall risk is ___-___ times increased in first degree relatives of CLL patients          

●      2-7 times increased

Family members of patients with CLL show an increased incidence of?          

●      CLL-phenotype monoclonal B- cell lymphocytosis (MBL) at all ages, but especially in those <40 years old

Describe    

    

●      Plot 1 shows selection of lymphocyte subpopulations according to phenotype (T-cells in dark blue, NK-cells in light blue, CLL cells in orange and residual normal B-cells in grey).
Of note, CLL cells are CD5+, CD19+

●      Plot 2 shows a CLL with no ZAP70 expression (2% positive CLL cells)
Residual B-cells (grey) show no expression of ZAP70

●      Plot 3 shows a CLL with high ZAP70 expression (65% positive CLL cells)
CLL cases with > 20% ZAP70 expression are usually considered as positive.
Residual B-cells (grey) show no expression of ZAP70

 

Two genetic subtypes of CLL based on antigen receptor genes          

●      Antigen receptor genes = IG genes (B cell antigen receptor = surface Ig)

●      1) Unmutated IG gene rearrangements

○      >98% homology with germline

●      2) Somatic hypermutation IG genes rearrangements

○      < 98% identity with the germline

●      These two sub-types differ in many other biological and clinical parameters.

What % of CLL have unmutated vs somatic hypermutation of their IG genes?          

●      30-50% of cases are unmutated

●      50-70% showing somatic hypermutation

Microenvironment

What is 'BCR stereotypy' in CLL          

●      Different patients can have very similar, if not identical, immunoglobulin sequences, a phenomenon that is present in 30% of all CLL cases and termed 'BCR stereotypy'

BCR signaling is more active in CLL with mutated or unmutated IGHV genes?

●      Unmutated IGHV genes, whereas other cases, in particular those with mutated IGHV genes, have a response resembling anergy (absence of the normal immune response to a particular antigen or allergen)

 

What is "autonomous signaling" in CLL?          

●      CLL B-cell receptors have been shown to recognize both foreign and self antigens, including the possibility of the monoclonal immunoglobulin recognizing itself on the same or an adjacent cell (so-called autonomous signalling)

 

New WHO 2022 about BCR signalling, impact on disease aggressiveness, therapy targeting

●      The BCR and its downstream molecules are pivotal for CLL/SLL cell growth.

●      BCR signaling is antigen-driven, relying on microbial antigens, autoantigens, or homotypic interactions.

●      Skewed immunoglobulin gene (IG) usage leads to BCR stereotypy, present in 41% of patients, offering a selective advantage.

●      IGHV gene mutation status (SHM) correlates with clinical outcomes:

○      IGHV-unmutated CLL/SLL (few/no SHMs) → Aggressive disease.

○      IGHV-mutated CLL/SLL (high SHM) → Less aggressive disease.

●      Kinase inhibitors targeting BCR-related kinases (Syk, BTK, PI3K) are effective.

●      BTK inhibitors have shown the highest therapeutic efficacy.

Genetics

CLL has no specific genetic markers - what are the most common cytogenetic alterations and what underlying genes are affected in each?         

·       del(13q) (5060% of patients):

    • Removes the DLEU2-miR-15-16 cluster.
    • Impacts the regulation of anti-apoptotic and cell-cycle proteins.

·       del(11q) (1020% of patients):

    • Results in the loss of ATM, a gene involved in DNA repair.

·       del(17p) (510% of patients):

    • Leads to the loss of TP53, a critical tumor suppressor gene.

·       Trisomy 12 (1520% of patients):

    • Involves an unknown set of genes.

Chromosomal translocations in CLL are uncommon, but one well known translocation from another disease can rarely be found in 2% of cases, usually with mutated IGHV          

●      t(14;18)(q32;q21), resulting in IGH/BCL2, can be found, most likely as a secondary change CLL.

What are the 5 most commonly mutated genes in CLL?          

  1. NOTCH1 10-15%
  2. SF3B1 10%
  3. TP53 5-10%
  4. ATM 10-15%
  5. BIRC3 5%
  6. They are newer risk stratification parameters

Mutated and unmutated CLL show a single distinctive signature, although there is a group of genes that distinguishes these two genetic subtypes - Give 1 example gene          

●      The tyrosine kinase ZAP70

●      More common in unmutated and more aggressive

 

In what % of cases are the mutational status of ZAP70 expression discordant?          

●      In up to 20% of the cases

Molecular path

 

What % of cases have CG abnormalities detected by FISH?          

●      80%

●      del(11q), del(13q), del(17p), and trisomy 12

Unlike other B-cell malignancies, CLL/SLL rarely exhibits IG gene locus translocations, except:

  • t(14;18)(q32;q21)/IGH::BCL2 (~2% of cases).
  • t(14;19)(q32;q13)/IGH::BCL3 (rare).


Distribution of CG abnormalities in CLL varies based on?          

●      Mutational status

What recurrent CG aberration is more common in mutated CLL?          

●      Del 13q (65% vs 48%)

●      Isolated 13q deletion (50 vs 26%)

What 2 recurrent CG aberrations are more common in unmutated CLL?          

●      del 11q (27% vs 4%) → ATM

●      del 17p (10% vs 3%) → TP53

 

Epigenetics

DNA Methylation Subtypes:

  • Memory-like CLL (m-CLL):
    • DNA methylation pattern resembles germinal centerexperienced B cells.
    • Strongly correlates with IGHV-mutated CLL/SLL, associated with a more favorable prognosis.
  • Naïve-like CLL (n-CLL):
    • Resembles germinal centerinexperienced B cells.
    • Corresponds to IGHV-unmutated CLL/SLL, linked to a poorer prognosis.
  • Intermediate Methylation Profile:
    • Associated with an intermediate prognosis.
    • Enriched for cases with:
      • Stereotyped subset #2 (IGHV3-21/IGLV3-21).
      • IGLV3-21R110, both linked to aggressive disease.
    • Other cases typically align with IGHV-mutated CLL/SLL and exhibit a more indolent course.

Naive-like CLLs have mainly mutated or unmutated IGHV genes?          

●      unmutated IGHV genes

Proposed specific micro-RNA expression signature to distinguish between mutated and unmutated CLL and ZAP70 negative versus positive CLL          

●      A specific micro-RNA expression signature that includes miR-16-1 and miR-15a

Why is FISH more appropriate than conventional karyotyping?          

●      Mature lymphocytes are difficult to culture due to low mitotic rate which means CG studies (which require metaphase cells) will have low sensitivity

3 markers (not CG abnormalities) associated with an adverse prognosis in CLL          

●      Expression of ZAP70, CD38, or CD49d > 30%, are associated with an adverse prognosis

What is the prognostic association of the 3 epigenetic subtypes of CLL          

●      Naive-like cases have the worst prognosis

●      Memory-like cases the best

The presence of what mutation is predictive of lack of response to fludarabine-containing regimes          

●      TP53 abnormalities (i.e. deletion in 17p13 and TP53 mutations)

Is the presence of the VH3-21 B cell receptor a good or adverse prognostic marker?          

●      The presence of a stereotyped B cell receptor utilizing the IGHV3-21 gene (so-called subset #2) is an adverse prognostic marker independent of IGHV mutation status

What is Beta-2 microglobulin a marker for?          

●      Beta-2 microglobulin levels rise with increased cell turnover

The presence of what mutations is associated with a poor outcome in CLL?          

●      Mutations in TP53, ATM, NOTCH1, SF3B1, and BIRC3, among others, are associated with a poor outcome

Prognostic factors in WHO 2022

del(17p) and/or TP53 Mutation

  • Prognostic: Poor PFS/OS with CIT; less adverse with BTK/BCL2 inhibitors.
  • Predictive: Poor response to CIT; better outcomes with targeted therapy.
  • Frequency: 48% (early-stage), 4050% (relapsed/refractory).

Complex Karyotype (≥3 or ≥5 Aberrations)

  • Prognostic: Negative, especially with ≥5 aberrations.
  • Predictive: Limited evidence.
  • Frequency: 15%.

IGHV Mutation Status (Unmutated ≥98% vs. Mutated <98%)

  • Prognostic: Worse PFS/OS for unmutated (U-IGHV).
  • Predictive: Poorer response to CIT; better outcomes with targeted therapy.
  • Frequency: ~30% unmutated in early-stage, 5075% in advanced.

BTK Mutations

  • Predictive: Progression on BTK inhibitors within 318 months.
  • Frequency: None in naïve; 2357% in relapsed after ibrutinib.

PLCG2 Mutations

  • Predictive: Resistance to BTK inhibitors.
  • Frequency: 13% after 3 years on ibrutinib.

BCL2 Mutations

  • Predictive: Resistance to venetoclax.
  • Frequency: 4547% in venetoclax-resistant CLL.

Serum β2-Microglobulin (B2M)

  • Prognostic: Independent negative factor.
  • Frequency: Elevated in 34% of cases.

Large Proliferation Centres

  • Prognostic: Poor prognosis (associated with accelerated CLL).
  • Frequency: ~23% in advanced stages.

 

How common is progression and transformation of CLL to high grade lymphoma? What lymphomas? Incidence?          

●       2-8% of patients with CLL develop diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)

●      <1% develop classical Hodgkin lymphoma (HL)

 

What is the median survival of patients with Richter's syndrome?          

●      The median survival for patients with DLBCL (Richter's syndrome) is less than one year

Are the majority of DLBCL seen in transformed CLL
1) Clonally related or unrelated to the previous CLL
2) Mutated or unmutated?          

●      DLBCL type Richter syndrome are clonally related to the previous CLL, and are IGHV-unmutated

●      Whereas clonally unrelated cases usually occur in IGHV-mutated CLL

●      The former are associated with a median survival time of < 1 year, whereas the prognosis of the latter is identical to that of a de novo DLBCL

DLBCL transformation is associated with what mutations - mention 3?          

●      TP53 and NOTCH1 mutations, CDKN2A [QZ1] [QZ2] deletions, and MYC translocations

The vast majority of HL cases occur in mutated or unmutated CLL?  Are they related to the CLL clone?

●      Mutated CLL

●      EBV-positive

●      Unrelated to the CLL clone


Some CLL cases show scattered EBV positive or sometimes negative Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of CLL.  Should these cases be diagnosed as CHL?          

●      No

●      The diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma in the setting of CLL requires classic Reed- Sternberg cells in an appropriate background

In CLL, what lymphoproliferative disorders may occur after fludarabine therapy?          

●      EBV-associated lymphoproliferative disorders, including Hodgkin lymphoma- type proliferations, may occur in patients with CLL following immunosuppressive therapy

Causes of thrombocytopenia in CLL?         

  1. immune phenomena
  2. progression of the underlying disease.

MBL

Define Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis          

●      Monoclonal B-cell count <5 x 10^9/L in the peripheral blood

●      No associated lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, other extramedullary involvement, or any other feature of a B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder

○      This means NO features of SLL

○      Caution when signing out flow

 

MBL is classified into three categories on the basis of phenotype:

3 subtypes of MBL:          

●      (1) low-count: clonal B-cell <0.5x109/L

●      (2) CLL/SLL type: monoclonal >= 0.5 and total <5x109/L

●      (3) Non-CLL/SLL type: any monoclonal & no symptoms  MZ origin

ICC

●      Tissue-based MBL: incidental nodal infiltrate w/o lymphadenopathy + MBL in PB

●      Differentiation between accelerated CLL and diffuse large B-cell (Richter)

●       WHO-HAEM5 recognizes three subtypes of monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (MBL):

●       a. Low-count MBL or clonal B-cell expansion: clonal CLL/SLL phenotype B-cell count below 0.5 x 109/L with no other features diagnostic of B-lymphoproliferative disorder. The arbitrary threshold is based on the distribution of clonal B-cell counts in population studies compared to clinical cohorts [29].

●       b. CLL/SLL-type MBL: monoclonal CLL/SLL-phenotype B-cell count ≥0.5 x 109/L and total B-cell count less than 5 x 109/L with no other features diagnostic of CLL/SLL [30]. The threshold of less than 5 x 109/L is arbitrary but identifies a group with a very low likelihood of requiring treatment compared to individuals with B-cell counts between 510 x 109/L [31].

●       c. non-CLL/SLL-type MBL: ANY monoclonal non-CLL/SLL phenotype B-cell expansion with no symptoms or features diagnostic of another mature B-cell neoplasm. The majority of cases have features consistent with a marginal zone (MZ) origin [32].

 

What is tissue-based Monoclonal B-cell Lymphocytosis?

●      LN < 1.5 cm in size with CLL phenotype, but no proliferation centres

●      Clonal CLL-like cells can be detected in up to 0.4% of prostatic tissues at the time of prostatectomy and in 1.9% of liver biopsy specimens in the absence of meeting any other diagnostic criteria for CLL and SLL.

●      Progression to first therapy has been only rarely reported in these cases, suggesting the concept of tissue MBL.

○      Whether the coexistence of such a clone influences the outcome of the primary malignancy, as has been observed in CLL, is currently unknown.

○      The extent of infiltration in such cases is also likely important, where extensive tissue replacement or infiltration is more consistent with a diagnosis of SLL.

●      Blood 2015 126:454-462; doi: https://doi.org/10.1182/blood-2015-02-585059

 

Immunophenotype of "chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL)-type" MBL?          

●      Coexpression of CD19, CD5, CD23, and CD20 (dim)

●      B cells show light chain class restriction or ≥ 25% lack surface Ig (surface null)

 

Estimated frequency of CLL-type MBL in the general population?          

●      Depends on the sensitivity of the method used for detection

○      Ranging from 3.5% to 12% among healthy individuals

●      Frequency increases with age

○      Negligible among individuals aged < 40 years

○      50-75% among 90-year-old individuals

 

Are all CLLs are preceded by MBL?          

●      Yes

●      It has been reported that virtually all CLLs are preceded by MBL, although not all MBL progresses to CLL

 

CLL-type MBL must be further classified on the basis of the size of the monoclonal
population, as?          

●      1) Low-count (< 0.5 x 109/L) MBL

●      2) High-count (≥0.5 x 109/L) MBL

 

Why bother categorizing MBL as low vs high count?          

●      Low count MBL has some biological differences from high-count MBL and CLL

○      Does not seem to progress

●      High-count MBL has biological features identical to those of low-stage (Rai stage 0) CLL

○      Progresses to frank leukemia requiring therapy at an annual rate of 1-2%

●      The higher the MBL count, the more likely there will be progression

 

Do MBL cases usually have mutated IGHV genes          

●      Yes; present in 75-90% of cases and may carry the same chromosomal abnormalities and somatic mutations as CLL

○      NOTCH1, SF3B1, ATM, and TP53 aberrations, although at lower frequencies

 

List all poor prognostic features/risk factors for aggressive CLL biologic type          

●      IGVH unmutated/germline CLL genotype 

●      Usage of VH3-21 independent of VH mutation status is an adverse prognostic marker

●      CD49d (+) expressed on > 30% of leukemia cells

○      Most predictive flow cytometry marker of outcome

●      CD38 (+) expressed on > 30% of leukemia cells

●      ZAP70 (+) expressed on > 30% of leukemia cells

●      Unfavorable cytogenetics:

○      Especially del(11q), del(17p), plus del(6q) & complex abnormalities

○      Note: Isolated del 13q14.3 is associated with a more favourable clinical course

●      Rapid lymphocyte doubling time in the PB (<12 months)

●      Elevated serum markers of rapid cell turnover:

○      Elevated thymidine kinase, sCD23 and β-2 microglobulin

●      A high degree of bone marrow effacement by CLL is unusual and is often linked to other poor prognostic features such as ZAP70 positivity

●      Histological features

○      Broader than a 20x field or becoming confluent.

○      Ki-67 proliferation index is > 40% or

○      > 2.4 mitoses in the proliferation centres

 

FISH/CG in CLL and risk (with treatment strategy)

B-PLL -> now splenic B lymphoma

WHO5 -> no longer recognized due to heterogeneous nature

** variant of MCL

** prolymphocytic progression of CLL (>15%)

** NEW  splenic B-cell lymphoma with prominent nucleoli

 

What is B-cell prolymphocytic leukaemia (B-PLL)           

●        A neoplasm of B-cell prolymphocytes affecting the peripheral blood, bone marrow, and spleen.

●        Prolymphocytes must constitute >55% of lymphoid cells in peripheral blood


2 other disease entities that should be excluded when making a diagnosis of B-PLL           

1) CLL with increased prolymphocytes
2) Lymphoid proliferations with relatively similar morphology but with a t(11 ;14)(IGH/CCND1)
translocation or SOX11 expression; MCL with leukaemic expression.

B-PLL clinical features           

Most patients present with B symptoms, massive splenomegaly with absent or minimal peripheral lymphadenopathy, and a rapidly increasing lymphocyte count, usually > 100x109/L.

Anaemia and thrombocytopenia are seen in 50% of cases


Describe the typical morphology of B-PLL in the PB           

The majority (> 55% and usually > 90%) of the circulating cells are prolymphocytes.

Medium-sized lymphoid cells (twice the size of a normal lymphocyte) with a round nucleus, moderately condensed nuclear chromatin, a prominent central nucleolus, and a relatively small amount of faintly basophilic cytoplasm

Although the nucleus is typically round, in some cases it can be indented.


B-PLL BM infiltration pattern

Interstitial or nodular intertrabecular infiltration of lymphoid cells similar to those found in blood.

Histological findings in spleen infiltrated by B-PLL           

Expanded white pulp nodules and red pulp infiltration by intermediate to large cells with abundant cytoplasm and irregular or round nuclei with a central eosinophilic nucleolus


Histological findings in LN infiltrated by B-PLL           

Lymph nodes display diffuse or vaguely nodular infiltration by similar-looking cells. Proliferation centres (pseudofollicles) are not seen.

When considering a Dx of B-PLL what other conditions need to be considered and excluded?           

-          Distinguishing B-PLL from pleomorphic mantle cell lymphoma, splenic marginal zone lymphoma, and CLL with an increased number of prolymphocytes can be difficult on morphological grounds.

-          The diagnosis of B-PLL cannot be made without excluding other conditions, because there are no specific markers for B-PLL.


B-PLL immunophenotype?           

B-PLL cells strongly express surface lgM/lgD, as well as B-cell antigens (CD19, CD20, CD22, CD79a, CD79b, and FMC7).

CD5 and CD23 are only positive in 20- 30% and 10-20% of cases, respectively, and CD200 is weakly positive or negative


ZAP70 and CD38 expression in B-PLL?           

ZAP70 and CD38 are expressed in approximately 50% of cases. ZAP70 expression does not correlate with IGHV mutation status

Does B-PLL have t(11;14)?           

No
Initial studies demonstrated t(11;14) (IGH/CCN01) in as many as 20% of B-PLLs
However, these cases are now considered to be leukaemic variants of mantle cell lymphoma

CG abnormalities seen in B-PLL?           

Complex karyotypes are common
Deletion in 17p13 is detected in 50% of the cases and is associated with TP53 mutations
FISH analysis detects deletions at 13q14 in 27% of the cases
Aberrations of MYC, including gains, amplifications, and translocations with the IGH, IGK, or IGL loci, have been reported


What genetic abnormality likely underlies the progressive course and relative treatment
resistance of B-PLL           

TP53 mutations

General prognosis for B-PLL           

B-PLL responds poorly to therapies for CLL, with a median survival of 30-50 months

What therapies may be of benefit for B-PLL           

Splenectomy may improve symptoms.
Responses have been recorded with the CHOP chemotherapy regimen, fludarabine, and cladribine
A combination of chemotherapy and rituximab may be a reasonable treatment approach
In selected cases, allogeneic bone marrow transplantation should be considered.

What is the correlation between survival and ZAP70 expression and IGHV mutation status in B PLL          

There is no correlation between survival and ZAP70 expression, CD38 positivity, deletion in 17p, or
IGHV mutation status

Splenic B-cell lymphomas and leukemias

Hairy cell leukemia

Hairy cell leukaemia (HCL) is an indolent mature B-cell neoplasm composed of neoplastic cells with abundant cytoplasm and characteristic hairy projections that usually involve the bone marrow, peripheral blood, and spleen and bear the BRAF p.V600E somatic mutation in ≥ 95% of cases.

 

What is HCL?          

●        It is a cytologically and immunophenotypically distinct, indolent neoplasm of small mature lymphoid cells with oval nuclei and abundant cytoplasm with so-called hairy projections involving peripheral blood and diffusely infiltrating the bone marrow and splenic red pulp.

What is the percentage of HCL from all lymphoid leukemias?           

●        2%


HCL is more common in males or females          

●        M:F = 4:1


What is the median age of HCL?          

●        58

●        Predominantly middle-aged to elderly adults

What is the disease-defining genetic event in HCL?          

●        BRAF V600E mutation in virtually 100% of cases.


What is BRAF?          

●        A gene that encodes for a protein B-RAF.

●        It is involved in signaling pathway which involving → cell proliferation.

●        It is proto-oncogene that leads to → constitutive activation of MAPK upon mutation.


What are the main sites of involvement by HCL?          

●        Spleen, bone marrow.

●        May infiltrate the liver and LNs


What are the most common presenting symptoms in HCL          

●        Weakness and fatigue

●        Left upper quadrant pain

●        Fever, and bleeding

●        Most patients present with splenomegaly and pancytopenia with few circulating neoplastic cells

What is the main characteristic finding in PB in HCL?          

●        Monocytopenia

●        +/- pancytopenia


What are some of distinctive clinical manifestations in HCL?          

●        Hepatomegaly

●        Recurrent opportunistic infections

●        Less common unique findings include vasculitis, bleeding disorders, neurological disorders, skeletal involvement, and other immune dysfunction

What are the macroscopic findings in HCL in spleen          

●        Diffuse expansion of the red pulp with variably sized blood lakes in markedly enlarged spleen


What are morphological characteristics of hairy cells?          

●        Size: small to medium

●        Nucleus: an oval or indented (reniform/kidney-shaped) nucleus

●        Chromatin: homogeneous, spongy, ground-glass chromatin that is slightly less clumped than that of a normal lymphocyte.

●        Nucleoli : absent or inconspicuous.

●        Cytoplasm: abundant and pale blue, with circumferential so-called hairy projections on smears.

●        Occasionally, the cytoplasm contains discrete vacuoles or rod-shaped inclusions that represent the ribosome lamellar complexes that have been identified by electron microscopy

What are the patterns of HCL infiltrate in BM?          

●        Interstitial or patchy with some preservation of fat and hematopoietic elements.

What are the morphological characteristics of HCL in BM?          

●        The infiltrate: widely spaced lymphoid cells with oval or indented nuclei, in contrast to the closely packed nuclei of most other indolent lymphoid neoplasms involving the bone marrow

●        Cytoplasm: is abundant

●        Prominent cell borders may produce a so-called fried-egg appearance

●        The obvious discrete aggregates that usually characteristics of bone marrow infiltrates of many
other chronic LPDs are not a feature of HCL.


Are mitotic figures high or low in HCL in BM ?          

●        Virtually absent

What is the reason for dry tap in HCL?          

●        Due to increase in reticulin fibrosis is associated with all hairy cell infiltrates in bone marrow and other sites

In some cases HCL can be misdiagnosed as aplastic anemia. Why?          

●        Due to hypocellular bone marrow in some cases mainly in granulocytic component.

●        CD20 stain is essential for the identification of an abnormal B-cell infiltrate, prompting the use of immunohistochemical stains more specific for HCL.


What are the morphological findings of HCL in spleen?          

●        HCL infiltrates are found in the red pulp.

●        The white pulp is typically atrophic.

 

 

Predominantly white pulp involvement

Predominantly red pulp involvement

Blood cell lakes:

●        The cells characteristically fill the red pulp cords.

●        Red blood cell lakes, collections of pooled erythrocytes surrounded by elongated hairy cells, are the presumed consequence of disruption of normal blood flow in the red pulp → infiltrating hairy cells clog up the blood vessels


HCL infiltrates in liver and LNs          

●        Liver: infiltrates predominantly in the sinusoids

●        Lymph node infiltration: with advanced disease variably interfollicular/paracortical, with sparing of follicles and intact sinuses.

What is the cytochemical stain used for HCL?          

●        TRAP: tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase
the pattern: strong, granular cytoplasmic TRAP positivity; weak staining is of no diagnostic utility.

●        Technically difficult and it has been replaced by IHC and flow

What is the immunophenotype of HCL          

●        Classic immunophenotypic profile:

●        Bright monotypic sIg.

●        Bright coexpression of CD20, CD22, and CD11c

●        Expression of CD103, CD25, CD123, TBX21 (also called TBET), annexin A1, FMC7, CD200, and cyclin D1

●        Lack both CD5 and CD10, but CD10 expression is reported in about 10-20% of cases and
CD5 expression in about 0-2%


What is the most specific marker in HCL?          

●        Annexin A1

●        It is not expressed in any B-cell lymphoma other than HCL = specific

●        Annexin-1 is a protein that serves a complex role in the inflammatory response, one of several proteins uniquely up-regulated in HCL.

Apart from lymphoma cells, do other cells (myeloid and T-cell ) express Annexin A1?          

●        Yes.

●        Staining for annexin A1 must always be compared with staining for a B-cell antigen (e.g. CD20), because annexin A1 is also expressed by myeloid cells and a proportion of T cells.

Is Annexin A1 a good maker for monitoring MRD in HCL?          

●        No  - because it can be expressed by myeloid cells and a proportion of T cells.

What is the best method to monitor MRD in HCL          

●        Multicolour flow cytometry

●        Targeting the distinctive HCL profile or immunostaining for TBX21.

What is TBX21          

●        T-box transcription factor TBX21 gene encodes for a transcription factor T-bet.
Studies showed it is highly expressed in HCL.

●        T-bet is the master regulator of the T-helper (Th)1 cell response regulating interferon gamma (IFN-gamma) production and also plays a central role in the T-cell independent Th1-like B-cell response.

Is there IHC for BRAF?          

●        Yes

●        lmmunohistochemical staining for V600E-mutant BRAF protein can also be helpful and may be useful for recognizing residual disease

●        IHC co-expression of CyclinD1, Annexin A1 and BRAF are quite useful for the diagnosis.

Does HCL have t(11;14)?

●        No

●        The cyclin D1 positivity is not due to the t(11;14)(q13;q32); CCND1-IGH fusion (like in mantle cell lymphoma and some cases of myeloma).

What is the postulated normal counterpart for HCL?          

●        The postulated normal counterpart is a late, activated memory B cell

Does HCL have somatic hypermutation in IGHV - what does this indicate?          

●        Yes

●        >85% of cases

●        Indicates a post-germinal centre stage of maturation (cell of origin = late, activated memory B cell)

●        A unique feature of HCL is the common co-expression of multiple clonally related immunoglobulin isotypes, suggesting arrest at some point during isotype switching

Is there any specific cytogenetic abnormality in HCL?          

●        No

●        Numerical abnormalities of chromosomes 5 and 7 have been rarely described.

●        Translocations are distinctly uncommon

What is the most frequent mutated gene in HCL          

●        BRAF V600E

Name 3 treatments for HCL?          

●        Interferon alfa

●        Nucleosides (purine analogues such as pentostatin and cladribine)

●        Vemurafenib → BRAF inhibitor

50% of cases may relapse → what are the treatment option for refractory or relapsed cases - give 3 egs?           

Salvage therapeutic options include:

●        Chemotherapy combined with rituximab

●        Anti-CD22 immunotoxin therapy → eg  Inotumumab or Moxetumomab

●        BRAF inhibitors (more recently developed agents) → eg Vemurafenib

What is the inclusion in hairy cell on Electron microscopy?

●        Ribosome lamellar complex




Pathogenesis of HCL (blue table) reference

 

 
Diagnostic features of HCL (Jaffe)     

   
Useful markers in HCL (Jaffe)     

   
What is the DDX of HCL (Jaffe)     

HCL, vHCL, SMZL, SDRPL, CLL, LGL

 

What 2 other normal cells in the BM can express Annexin A 1?

●        T cells

●        Granulocytes

●        Therefore not useful for MRD

HCL EM finding

●        Ribosome lamellar complexes

What are 4 other neoplasms express BRAF V600E?

●        Melanoma

●        Langerhans

●        Erdheim chester disease

●        Juvenile xanthogranuloma

BRAF inhibitor?

●        Vemurafenib

 

*Splenic Marginal Zone Lymphoma

Splenic marginal zone lymphoma (SMZL) is an indolent mature B-cell neoplasm primarily presenting in the spleen, preferentially involving the white pulp, often with villous lymphocytes in the peripheral blood, with or without involvement of splenic hilar lymph nodes.

 

What is SMZL?           

●        A B-cell neoplasm composed of small lymphocytes that:

○        1. Surround and replace the splenic white pulp germinal centers

○        2. Efface the follicle mantle, and merge with a peripheral (marginal) zone of larger cells, including scattered transformed blasts; both small and larger cells infiltrate the red pulp.

Describe the normal architecture of a lymphoid follicle found in the spleen? How does it differ from a lymph node follicle?          

 

 

●        Image = B-lymphoid follicle around an eccentrically placed arteriole (big arrow) is shown (the central arteriole is the difference between splenic vs nodal follicles)

●        Denser inner collection of concentric lymphoid tissue = the mantle zone

●        Paler outer collection of concentric lymphoid tissue = the marginal zone

●        The terminal/penicillar branch of an arteriole (shown with an arrowhead on the right) gives rise to capillaries in or around the marginal zone of the follicle

●        This 'perifollicular zone' is the boundary between white and red pulp and serves as the area where macrophages are abundant supported by a dense reticulin meshwork. The macrophages serve as the 'custom officers' for the newly entered red and white blood cells and particulate material.

 

SMZL involves ......... (multiple sites) and doesn't typically involve ........ (single site)            

●        Spleen

●        Splenic hilar LNs

●        BM

●        PB

●        Liver may be involved

●        Peripheral lymph nodes are not typically involved

 

SMZL has been associated with what virus?           

●        Hep C virus

 

What are the main clinical manifestations of SMZL           

●        Splenomegaly

●        Sometimes accompanied by autoimmune thrombocytopenia or anemia

●        A variable presence of peripheral blood villous lymphocytes


●        Bone marrow is regularly involved

●        Peripheral lymphadenopathy and extra nodal infiltration are extremely uncommon


Can you see paraproteinemia in SMZL?           

●        Yes: a small paraprotein can be detected in 1/3 of cases.

●        Hyperviscosity and hypergammaglobulinemia are uncommon

 

PB film findings in SMZL           

●        Lymphocytes are characterized by short polar villi.

●        Some may appear plasmacytoid


What are the macroscopic spleen findings in SMZL?           

●        Marked expansion of the white pulp and infiltration of the red pulp.

What are the microscopic findings in the splenic white pulp in SMZL?          

●        A central zone of small round lymphocytes surrounds or, more commonly, replaces reactive germinal centres

●        Effacement of the normal follicle mantle

●        This zone merges with a peripheral zone of small to medium-sized cells with more dispersed chromatin and abundant pale cytoplasm, which resemble marginal zone cells, and interspersed transformed blasts.



What are the microscopic findings in the red pulp of spleen in SMZL?          

●        Infiltrated, with small nodules of the larger cells and sheets of the small lymphocytes, which often invade sinuses.

●        Epithelioid histiocytes may be present in the lymphoid aggregates.

●        Some cases have a markedly predominant population of the larger marginal zone-like cells

Can plasmacytic differentiation present in SMZL?          

●        Yes.

●        In rare cases clusters of plasma cells are present in the centres of the white pulp nodules

What are the microscopic findings in splenic hilar LNs involved by SMZL?           

●        Sinuses: dilated

●        Lymphoma surrounds and replaces germinal centres, but the two cell types, small lymphocytes and marginal zone cells, are often more intimately admixed, without the formation of a distinct so-called marginal zone


What are the morphological findings in BM in SMZL?           

●        A nodular interstitial infiltrate cytologically similar to that in the lymph nodes.

●        Occasionally, neoplastic cells surround reactive follicles.

●        lntrasinusoidal lymphoma cells, which are more apparent after CD20 immunostaining, are a helpful feature, although they are sometimes observed in other lymphomas





What is the immunophenotype of SMZL? What Ig do they typically express?           

●        Express lgM and usually lgD

●        Bright CD19, CD20, CD79a, CD22, FMC7

●        LEF1, cyclin-D1, SOX11, CD43, annexin A1, BRAF, CD10, CD23, CD25, BCL(-); often DBA.44(-)[KNOW WHAT IS NEGATIVE IN MZL]

●        CD5 usually negative but can weakly express in 25% cases

 

What are the scores for diagnosis of HCL by immunophenotype?



CD 103 and cyclin D1 are ..... (+ or -) in SMZL     

●        CD103 usually negative (dont assume HCLv if it is positive)

●        Cyclin D1 is absent


ki 67 in SMZL has a distinctive pattern. What is it?           

●        Distinctive targetoid pattern due to an increased growth fraction in both the germinal centre, if present, and the marginal zone.

IHC: In SMZL, the absence of ...... and ....... is useful in excluding mantle cell lymphoma and CLL, respectively.           

●        1. Cyclin D1 exclude MCL

●        2. LEF1 to exclude CLL

○        LEF1 is a useful marker in the differential diagnosis of CLL in difficult cases. It shows a high specificity (92%) and a reasonable sensitivity (70%) for this entity.

○        LEF1 stands for lymphocyte enhancer-binding factor 1

In SMZL , the absence of ...... excludes HCL           

●        Annexin A1

 

In SMZL, lack of .... and .... exclude FL (IHC)           

●        GC markers CD10 and BCL6

Can SMZL be CD5+?           

●        Yes

●        A group of CD5+ SMZL cases has been described


What is the difference between CD5-ve and CD5+ve SMZL? (Hint: 1 CBC & 1 histological feature)   

●        CD5+ SMZL has a higher lymphocytosis and diffuse BM infiltration

What is the postulated normal counterpart for SMZL?           

●        A marginal-zone B cell that may or may not demonstrate evidence of antigen exposure

Does SMZL have recurrent chromosomal translocation.           

●        No.

●        However there is a small number that carry a recurrent t(2;7) (p12;q21) translocation, which activates the CDK6 gene through juxtaposition with the IGK locus (chr 2)

Apart from t(2;7), what other CG abnormalities can be present in SMZL?           

●        30-40% show a heterozygous deletion in 7q, which is rarely found in other lymphoma subtypes.

●        Can FISH for this abnormality

●        Gain of 3q is present in a considerable subset of cases

Is MYD88 commonly mutated in SMZL?           

●        No.

●        MYD88 is helpful to differentiate LPL from MZL that have evidence of plasmacytic differentiation and difficult to diagnose.

Mention 2 mutations that can be seen in SMZL           

●        NOTCH2: one of the most common mutated genes. 10-25%. NOT specific for this lymphoma.

●        KLF2: mutated in 10-40%, not specific

●        Both these genes are involved in proliferation and commitment of mature B-cells to the marginal zone

●        Both these mutations are associated with SMZL that have → deletion in 7q.

●        SMZL has an expression signature characterized by up regulation of genes belonging to the marginal zone differentiation program.

The clinical course of SMZL is .... (aggressive or indolent)?           

●        Indolent

●        10-year survival probability from 67-95%

In SMZL, what is the percentage that may transform into DLBCL?           

●        10-15%


Does SMZL respond well to conventional chemotherapy typically effective in other lymphomas?           

●        No - the response is poor.

What is the treatment of SMZL?          

●        1.Splenectomy

●        2.Rituximab

What is the treatment for SMZL that is associated with Hep C?           

●        Some cases respond to antiviral medication using interferon gamma with or without ribavirin

What are 3 genes that confer adverse outcome in SMZL?           

●        NOTCH2

●        KLF2

●        TP53


DDx of SMZL (Jaffe)            

 

●        SMZL

●        HCL

●        vHCL

●        Splenic Diffuse Red Pulp Lymphoma

●        LPL

●        HCLv: 2s are neg (CD25, CD123), 1s are pos (CD11c, CD103)

What does reniform mean?         

●        Kidney shaped/like = HCL nuclear shape

Splenic diffuse red pulp small B-cell lymphoma

Splenic diffuse red pulp small B-cell lymphoma (SDRPL) is a small B-cell lymphoma involving the spleen, bone marrow, and peripheral blood, characterized by diffuse infiltration of the splenic red pulp by a monomorphic lymphoid population associated with circulating tumour cells bearing cytoplasmic projections.

 

What is splenic diffuse red pulp small B-cell lymphoma(SDRPL)

●        An uncommon lymphoma with a diffuse pattern of involvement of the splenic red pulp by small monomorphous B lymphocytes.

Does SDRPL involve BM or PB?

●        Yes

●        It involves bone marrow sinusoids and peripheral blood, commonly with a villous cytology

What should you exclude prior to diagnose SDRPL?

●        Care should be taken in diagnosing cases with lymphoma growing diffusely in the spleen

●        DDx: CLL, HCL, LPL and B-cell PLL should all be excluded

 

Patients with SDRPL is diagnosed in early or late stage?

●        Advanced stage

Are LNs involved in SDRPL?

●        Very rarely reported.


What are the clinical features of SDRPL?       

●        A relatively low lymphocytosis.

●        Almost all patients have splenomegaly (frequently massive).

●        Thrombocytopenia and leukopenia are frequently present.

 

Is anemia common in SDRPL?       

●        No, rare

are B symptoms common in SDRPL? 

●        B symptoms are infrequent.


Is a paraprotein a feature of SDRPL? -         

●        No

●        The presence of a paraprotein has not been reported .

What are the morphological findings on the PB of SDRPL? -         

●        Villous lymphocytes similar to the ones seen in SMZL.

 

Can isolated lymphocytosis be a presenting feature of SDRPL?    

●        Yes

●        Some of these cases fulfil the criteria for non-CLL MBL.

●        Clonal B cell expansion with immunophenotype of MZL may be an early stage of either splenic B cell leukemia/lymphoma unclassifiable or SMZL.

 

What is the most prominent feature of BM involvement by SDRPL?   

●        Intrasinusoidal infiltration occasionally as a sole finding.

●        Interstitial and nodular infiltration can be seen.

●        Lymphoid follicles, as seen in SMZL, have not been reported.


What are the morphological findings of SDRPL in spleen? -         

●        Red pulp: diffuse pattern with both cord and sinusoid infiltration.

●        Characteristic blood lakes lined by tumoural cells may be seen.

●        White pulp: involvement is absent (unlike in SMZL)

●        Residual lymphoid nodules may be present.


Describe the characteristics of the infiltrate including cells' size, nucleus and cytoplasm   

●        The infiltrate: a monomorphic population of small to medium-sized lymphocytes.

●        Nuclei: round and regular, compact chromatin, and occasional distinct small nucleoli, with scattered nucleolated blast cells.

●        Cytoplasm: pale cytoplasm and plasmacytoid features but lack phenotypic features of plasmacytic differentiation such as cytoplasmic immunoglobulin and CD38 expression.

●        Some cases show focal plasmacytic differentiation.

 

Is TRAP positive or negative in SDRPL?  

●        Negative

 

What are the immunophenotypic features of SDRPL?

  • Immunohistochemistry
    • Pan-B-cell antigens (+), DBA.44(+), CD11c(+)
    • p53(+) in ~ 30%; TRAP(-) by cytochemistry
    • CD3(-), CD4(-), CD5(-), CD10(-), CD23(-), CD25(-), CD38(-), CD123 (-/+)
    • Cyclin-D1 (-), BCL-6(-), annexin-A1 (-/+),
    • CD8 highlights expanded splenic cords
    • Low Ki-67 index
      • Usually < 5-10%
  • Flow Cytometry
    • Characteristic immunophenotype
      • Increased IgM/IgD; IgG(+) > IgD(+), CD20(+), CD11c(+), CD103(+/-)
      • CD103(+), subset of cases IgM(+)
      • CD5(-), CD10(-), CD11c(-), CD25(-), CD123(-)
        • Rare cases CD5(+) or CD123(+)

 

What is the postulated normal counterpart for SDRPL?   

●        A mature B cell of unknown type

 

Is IGHV mutated in SDRPL?   

●        Yes. 70-80% of cases

●        Overrepresentation of IGHV3-23 and IGHV4-34, as is seen in hairy cell leukaemia, has been
reported

 

What are the cytogenetic abnormalities in SDRPL?

  • Complex cytogenetic abnormalities are common
    • del(7q) (~ 25%), trisomy 3q (~ 5%), &/or trisomy 18 (~ 5%) reported
  • > 60% of cases harbor somatic mutations in IGH variable region genes
  • t(9;14)(p13;q32)/PAX5::IGH reported in small subset of cases
  • IGH variable region use similar to that in classic HCL
    • No bias of VH1.2 usage of genes (similar to SMZL)
  • Overrepresentation of VH3-23, VH4-34, and VH1.69

 

What are the genetic(mutation) abnormalities in SDRPL?

●        TP53 mutation in some cases

●        Increased expression of cyclin D3

●        Recurrent mutations in the CCND3 PEST domain in a high proportion of SDRPL cases

●        Infrequent mutations in NOTCH1, MAP2K1, BRAF, and SF3B1

 

What are the prognosis and predictive factors in SDRPL?

●        It is indolent

●        Incurable disease

●        Good responses after splenectomy

●        Some patients do develop progressive disease and have an adverse outcome.

●        Patients with mutations in NOTCH1, MAP2K1, and TP53: shorter progression-free survival.

Hairy cell leukemia variant -> Splenic B-cell lymphoma/leukemia with prominent nucleoli

Splenic B-cell lymphoma/leukaemia with prominent nucleoli (SBLPN) is a splenic B-cell neoplasm with some but not all of the cytomorphological and immunophenotypic features of cells of hairy cell leukaemia (HCL); it lacks BRAF mutation and is resistant to conventional HCL therapy. Characteristically, the cells have a single large nucleolus.

 

Definition of Hairy cell leukemia variant?   

●        Mature small B-cell neoplasm that primarily involves peripheral blood, bone marrow, and spleen

●        It closely resembles classic HCL but exhibits variant cytological and hematological features.


What are the hematological and cytological difference between HCL-v and classical HCL?   

●        HCL-v:

○        1. Leukocytosis → ie proliferative

○        2. Presence of monocytes

○        3. Cells with prominent nucleoli

○        4. Cells with blastic or convoluted nuclei, and/or absence of circumferential shaggy contours

 

What is the immunophenotypic difference between HCL-c and HCL-v   

●        Absence of CD25, CD123

●        Absence of annexin A1

●        Absence of TRAP

●        Difficult to distinguish from SMZL

 

Does HCL-v express BRAF mutation?   

●        NO
