Does HCL-v respond to Conventional HCL-c therapy?   

●        NO.


Are HCL-c and HCL-v biologically related?

●        No. They are biologically different.


HCL-v is known as ......variant of HCL?     

●        Prolymphocytic variant of HCL


How common is HCL-v compared to HCL?          

●        It is about 1/10 as common as HCL.

HCL-v is common in what ethnicity? 

●        Asian, may be more common than HCL.


HCL-v is common in males or females?   

●        Male predominance

●        Affect middle age group to elderly.


Is lymphadenopathy common in HCL-v?       

●        No


What are the most common sites affected by HCL-v?

●        Spleen, BM and PB

●        Hepatomegaly in 1/3 of cases.

●        Solid organ involvement is uncommon


What are the hematological features of HCL-v?

●         Lymphocytosis with WBC of about 30 x 10>9/L.

●        Thrombocytopenia: 50% of cases

●        Anemia: 25% of cases

●        The absolute monocyte count is typically within normal range.


What are the cytological features of HCL-v cells?   

●        The cells commonly exhibit hybrid features of → prolymphocytic leukemia and classic HCL




●        Nucleus: range from condensed chromatin with the prominent central nucleoli of a prolymphocytic cell to dispersed chromatin with highly irregular nuclear contours.

●        Cytoplasm: variable features, although some degree of hairy projections is typically noted

●        Transformation to large cells with convoluted nuclei has been described, and cases of so-called convoluted HCL may be explained by this phenomenon.


Can HCL-v be a dry tap?   

●        No → It is not characteristically associated with a dry tap (unlike classic HCL)

●        No significant reticulin fibrosis.


What are the BM findings in HCL-v?   

●        Interstitial and nodular infiltrate.

●        Intrasinuosoidal infiltrate have been described.

●        The infiltrate may be subtle and very inconspicuous, often requiring immunohistochemical staining to highlight the extent of infiltration


What are the morphological findings in the spleen in HCL-v?         

●        Red pulp: diffusely involved expanded

●        White pulp: almost absent

●        The leukemic cells fill dilated sinusoids, and red blood cell lakes may be noted


What are the morphological findings of HCL-v infiltrate in the liver?     

●        It is characterized by both portal tract and sinusoidal infiltrates.


What is the immunophenotype of HCL-v?         

●        It shares some of HCL features but lack several key features e.g: CD25, Annexin A1, TRAP, CD200 and CD123.

●        Positive: DBA.44 (CD72), pan-B-cell markers, CD11c, bright sIg (IgG most common), CD103, FMC7

What is the postulated normal counterpart for HCL-v?        

●        An activated B cell at a late stage of maturation

 

IGHV is unmutated in ..... HCL-v cases. 

●        1/3 of cases

 

What are the most common copy number alterations in HCL-v?  

●        Gains on chromosome 5 and losses on 7q and 17p.


What mutations can be seen in HCL-v?   

●        Recurrent MAP2K1 mutations have been found in HCL-v and in cases described as classic HCL with IGHV4-34 gene family usage.


What is the treatment for HCL-v?  

●        Ranges from splenectomy to combination chemotherapy with rituximab.

●        Typical HCL agents are not effective → ie single agent cladribine and pentostatin are not effective.

●        However, patients seem to achieve a long-lasting response to the combination of cladribine and rituximab

 

What is the 5-year survival rate in HCL-v?

●        57%

 

What are the significant adverse prognostic factors in HCL-v?

●        Older patient age

●        Greater severity of anemia

●        TP53 mutations

 

What is the DDx for HCL-v?

●        1.HCL-v

●        2.HCL

●        3.SDRPL

●        4.SMZL

●        5.B-PLL


Differential diagnosis of HCL-v? comparison table

 

*Lymphoplasmacytic Lymphoma

Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (LPL) is a neoplasm comprising small B lymphocytes, plasmacytoid lymphocytes, and plasma cells, usually involving the bone marrow and sometimes involving the lymph nodes and spleen. Waldenström macroglobulinaemia (WM) is defined by the combination of LPL in the bone marrow and an IgM monoclonal component in the blood.

 

What is Lymphoplasmacytic Lymphoma?          

●        Neoplasm of small B lymphocytes, plasmacytoid lymphocytes, and plasma cells

●        Usually involving bone marrow +/- lymph nodes and spleen

●        Does not fulfil the criteria for any of the other small B-cell lymphoid neoplasms that can also have plasmacytic differentiation

●        Note: difficult to distinguish LPL from other small B-cell neoplasms (MZLs)

●        Some cases diagnosed as:

○        A small B-cell lymphoid neoplasm with plasmacytic differentiation, with DDx listed eg. LPL vs MZL

What is the mutation in LPL?          

●        MYD88 L265P


How common is the MYD88 L265P mutation in LPL?          

●        >90% of LPLs


Is the MYD88 L265P mutation specific for LPL?          

●        No!


Is Waldenstrom's Macroglobulinemia synonymous with LPL?          

●        NO!

●        It is found in a substantial subset

What is Waldenstrom's Macroglobulinemia?           

●        LPL with BM involvement and IgM Monoclonal gammopathy of any concentration

 

What is Bing Neel syndrome?

●        WM with CNS involvement

What is the relationship between LPL and Hep C?          

●        Some Hep C virus-associated Lymphoplasmacytic proliferations are monotypic BUT are not necessarily neoplastic

○        Can consider them like MBL

●        Treatment with antiviral agents may lead to → regression of Lymphoplasmacytic proliferations

What is the localization of LPL?          

●        Bone Marrow

●        Some with LN and Extranodal sites

●        PB involvement possible

●        15-30% of WM patients have splenomegaly, hepatomegaly and/or adenopathy

 

What are the possible clinical features of the IgM paraprotein may be seen with WM?          

●        Autoantibody or cryoglobulin (type 2) activity in 20% of WM (Note IgG possible)

●        30% have hyperviscosity

●        Neuropathies → from IgM reactivity with myelin-sheath antigens

●        Coagulopathies → from IgM binding to clotting factors, platelets, fibrin → bleeding

●        Cold agglutinins may be present

●        B symptoms

What is the morphology of LPL in the Bone marrow?          

●        Pattern:

○        Nodular, diffuse, and/or interstitial infiltrate

○        Sometimes paratrabecular aggregates

●        Cells:

○        Small lymphocytes

○        Variable plasma cells (may form separate clusters from the lymphoid cells)

○        Variable plasmacytoid lymphs

○        Increased mast cells → prominent in the squash preparation


What is the morphology of LPL in the LN?          

●        Mostly Retention of normal architecture

●        Dilated sinuses with PAS-positive material (Other cases have greater destruction)

●        Monotonous proliferation of small lymphs, plasma cells, lymphoplasmacytic lymphocytes

●        Other typical features:

○        Dutcher bodies, increased mast cells, hemosiderin

●        Proliferation centres like in CLL must be absent


What is the immunophenotype of lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma?          

●        Light-chain restricted plasma cells

●        Usually IgM, sometimes IgG or IgA

●        B-cell antigen positivity:

●        CD19, CD20, CD22, CD79a

●        Frequent expression

○        CD25, CD38

●        Negative for:

○        CD10, CD103, CD23

●        Possible CD5 expression

Note: when evaluating flow → on kappa/lambda plot, always look for a clonal B cell population in the background behind clonal plasma cells


What is the genetic profile of LPL?          

●        Ig gene rearrangement

●        Somatic hypermutation

●        >90% with MYD88 L265P mutation

●        30% have truncating CXCR4 mutations

●        17% ARIDA1A mutations

●        Other:

○        KMT2D (MLL2)

○        MYBBP1A

Is MYD88 L265P specific for LPL?          

●        No

●        Other small B cell lymphomas:

○        Non-GC DLBCL

○        Primary cutaneous DLBCL

What are some chromosomal abnormalities in LPL?           

●        del 6q in Bone marrow cases

●        Trisomy 4 in 20% WM

●        t(9;14) (IGH/PAX5) but rare


Is there a genetic susceptibility to Waldenstrom's Macroglobulinemia?          

●        20% of patients have familial predisposition

●        Diagnosed at younger age, with greater BM involvement

What is the typical course for LPL?          

●        Indolent

●        Median survival: 5-10 years

●        Poor prognosis:

○        Increased age, poor performance status, high Beta 2 microglobulin

○        CXCR4 mutation → yes, important

○       Higher tumor burden, extramedullary involvement. Resistance to Ibrutinib, idelalisib, everolimus

○        ? Increased number of transformed cells

●        ? Prognostic implication of MYD88

Marginal zone lymphoma

*Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma)

Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (EMZL) is an indolent primary extranodal B-cell lymphoma with cytological and architectural features reminiscent of Peyer patch lymphoid tissue, the prototypical mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT). EMZL typically arises from marginal zone B cells of acquired MALT and is often associated with an underlying chronic inflammatory disorder.

 

What is Extranodal Marginal Zone B-cell Lymphoma (MALT Lymphoma)

●        An extranodal lymphoma composed of morphologically heterogeneous small B cells including:

●        1) Marginal zone (centrocyte-like) cells

●        2) Monocytoid cells

●        3) Small lymphocytes

●        4) Scattered immunoblasts and centroblast-like cells

●        There is plasmacytic differentiation in some cases


What locations can MALT lymphoma be found?

 

●        GI  stomach; intestine

●        Salivary glands

●        Respiratory tract  lung, pharynx, trachea

●        Ocular adnexa  conjunctiva, lacrimal gland, orbit

●        Skin

●        Thyroid

●        GU  bladder, prostate, kidney

●        Breast

●        Thymus

●        Rare sites


In what part of lymphoid tissue are the neoplastic cells of MALT lymphoma found

●        The neoplastic cells reside in the marginal zones of reactive B-cell follicles and extend into the interfollicular region as well as into the follicles (follicular colonization)


In epithelial tissues where are the neoplastic cells of MALT lymphoma found

●        The neoplastic cells typically infiltrate the epithelium → forming lymphoepithelial lesions



MALT lymphomas variably recapitulate what type of lymphoid tissue?

 

●        Peyer's patch-type lymphoid tissue → the prototypical normal mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT)

●        Peyer's patches

○        Small masses of lymphatic tissue found throughout the ileum of small intestine.

○        Also known as aggregated lymphoid nodules

○        Form an important part of the immune system by monitoring intestinal bacteria and preventing the growth of pathogenic bacteria in the intestines

 



4 infectious organisms implicated in the pathogenesis of MALT Lymphoma AND the specific site at which each causes MALT lymphoma

 

  1. Helicobacter pylori: Stomach
  2. Campylobacter jejuni: Intestine
  3. Chlamydia psittaci: Ocular adnexa
  4. Borrelia burgdorferi: Skin


Name 2 autoimmune diseases implicated in the pathogenesis of MALT lymphoma AND the specific site at which each causes lymphoma

 

  1. Sjögren syndrome: Salivary glands and lung
  2. Hashimoto thyroiditis: Thyroid gland

 

MALT lymphomas share what common microscopic features?

 

  1. Marginal zone pattern surrounding reactive follicles
  2. Heterogeneous cell population
  3. ± lymphoepithelial lesions

Marginal zone pattern surrounding the reactive follicles

Lymphoepithelial lesion

 

What is indicated by top arrow? Bottom arrow?

 




●        The lymphoma cells are small with centrocyte-like irregular nuclei and admixed with plasma cells and plasmacytoid lymphocytes.

●        This image shows benign acini (arrow on top right) and a cluster of lymphoma cells invading into the parenchyma (lower left long arrow)



What lesion is shown in this MZL?

 




●        Lymphoepithelial lesion

●        In glandular tissues → epithelium is often invaded and destroyed by discrete aggregates of lymphoma cells resulting in the so-called → lymphoepithelial lesions


Specific definition of Lymphoepithelial lesion in extranodal MZL?

●        Aggregates of 3 or more marginal zone cells with distortion or destruction of the epithelium, often together with eosinophilic degeneration of epithelial cells


Most common lymphoma in the parotid gland?

 

●        Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma)


Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma). What is shown?

 




●        Lymphoepithelial lesion

●        Aggregates of 3 or more marginal zone cells with distortion or destruction of the epithelium, often together with eosinophilic degeneration of epithelial cells.


What is shown? Most likely lymphoma?



●        Lymphocytes infiltrating within the glandular epithelium (lymphoepithelial lesion)

●        Dx: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma)

●        Some of the cells also demonstrate plasmacytic differentiation, as evidenced by the numerous Russell bodies in some of the cells, resembling Mott cells (bottom right)


MALT lymphoma: 3 Ancillary Tests

●        Immunophenotype by IHC

●        Cytogenetics

●        FISH or PCR for common translocations


Is MALT BCL2 pos?

●        Yes

Is MALT IgD pos?

●        No

●        IgD(-) but demonstrates intact follicular IgD(+) mantle zones


What do you expect to see with CD21 staining in MALT?

●        CD21 highlights follicular dendritic cell meshworks in follicles

●        Meshworks are disrupted by follicular colonization


Utility of CK stain in MALT w/u?

●        MALT is Cytokeratin (-)

●        Useful for highlighting lymphoepithelial lesions

 

Typical MALT lymphoma immunophenotype?

●        Pan B cell markers(+)

○        CD19(+), CD20(+), CD22(+)

○        CD79-a(+), pax-5(+)

●        IgM (+) > IgA (+) > IgG (+)

●        Monotypic Ig light chain (+); best seen in plasmacytoid cells

●        Bcl-2 (+), CD43 (+/-), Bcl-10 (+/-)

●        Ki-67 (MIB-1) → low; high in residual reactive germinal centers

●        IgD(-) → but demonstrates intact follicular IgD(+) mantle zones (explain: IgM+, IgD+ → mantle zone cells; IgM+, IgD- → MALT lymphoma cells)

●        CD21 highlights follicular dendritic cell meshworks in follicles → meshworks are disrupted by follicular colonization

●        Cytokeratin (-); useful for highlighting lymphoepithelial lesions

●        CD10(-), Bcl-6(-), cyclin-D1 (-)

●        CD2(-), CD3(-), CD7(-), EBV-LMP1(-)

●        CD5 usually (-)

●        ∼ 5% of cases are CD5(+); correlates with dissemination


Recurrent translocations are identified in what % of MALT lymphomas?

●        30-40%

Chromosomal translocations are identified in 30-40% of MALT lymphomas → they result in ________ pathway activation

 

●        Result in NF-κB pathway activation → enhanced cell survival, proliferation, and impaired apoptosis

●        NF-κB pathway activation is shared feature of many MALT lymphomas

4 common translocations in MALT lymphoma?

●        BIRC3-MALT1/t(11;18)(q21;q21)

●        IGH-MALT1/t(14;18)(q32;q21)

●        FOXP1-IGH/t(3;14)(p14.1;q32)

●        BCL10-IGH/t(1;14)(p22;q32)

●        Note: MALT1 is on chr 18


MALT lymphoma Top Differential Diagnoses

●        Reactive inflammatory diseases or Reactive hyperplasia

●        Mantle cell lymphoma

●        Follicular lymphoma

●        Plasmacytoma


T vs F Ki-67 highlights malignant cells in MALTOMA?

●        F

●        Ki-67 highlights the pre-existent germinal center similar to the BCL6 stain, indicating that the proliferative activity is high in the germinal center cells, but low in lymphoma cells


3 B cell LPD pos for CD43

●        SLL

●        MCL

●        1/3 or MZL, but not LPL (therefore may be helpful differentiating the 2)


Do marginal zone B cells normally express BCL2?


●        Yes

 

Primary cutaneous marginal zone lymphoma

*Nodal Marginal Zone B-cell Lymphoma

Nodal marginal zone lymphoma (NMZL) is a primary nodal lymphoma of small, mature B cells derived from marginal zone B cells, without involvement of extranodal sites or the spleen.

 


Define Nodal Marginal Zone B-cell Lymphoma (NMZL)

 

●        A primary nodal B-cell neoplasm that morphologically resembles lymph nodes involved by marginal zone lymphoma (MZL) of the extranodal or splenic types, but without evidence of extranodal or splenic disease

●        aka Monocytoid B-cell lymphoma

●        There can be NO evidence of extranodal (MALT) or splenic disease (SMZL)

 

 

What do you call NMZL when it occurs in children?

●        This lymphoma can also occur in children, and is then separately designated as pediatric
NMZL

To call it "Nodal Marginal Zone B-cell Lymphoma (NMZL)" there must be no evidence of?

  1. Extranodal (MALT) or
  2. Splenic disease (SMZL)

 

B/c it is a primary nodal B-cell lymphoma

A significantly increased incidence of NMZL has been observed among females with what systemic disease?

 

●        Autoimmune disorders

 

A relationship to what infection has been detected in some cases of NMZL

 

●        Hepatitis C virus

 

NMZL sites of involvement

 

●        Peripheral lymph nodes, but can also involve the bone marrow and occasionally the peripheral blood

 

 

●        Bone marrow involvement and a leukemic phase may be present in nodal marginal zone lymphoma

●        This peripheral blood smear shows → centrocyte-like neoplastic lymphocytes.

●        The tumor cells are small to medium-sized with clumped and sometimes irregular nuclear chromatin

●        The cytoplasm is scanty and basophilic with inconspicuous projections (green arrow).

●        The morphological picture is similar to CLL.

 

NMZL can be placed in any of what 3 categories depending on large cell number (Working Formulation [1982])

 

●        1. Small lymphocytic plasmacytoid

●        2. Diffuse small cleaved cell

●        3. Diffuse mixed small and large cell

 

 

●        Bone marrow involvement and a leukaemic phase may be present in nodal marginal zone lymphoma.

●        Plasmacytoid morphological features are frequent in the disease.

●        Peripheral blood smear (above) shows

○        Neoplastic lymphocytes with plasmacytoid differentiation.

○        The tumour cells have abundant, slightly basophilic cytoplasm and eccentric rounded or oval nuclei with densely clumped chromatin.

○        Sporadically, the nucleolus is prominent (yellow arrow) and perinuclear hof is seen (red arrow).

○        In this case, the distinction from lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma is practically impossible only on the basis of cytology.

 

Clinical features of NMZL?

●        Age: 5th-6th decades

●        Lymphadenopathy, localized or widespread

●        Systemic B symptoms in 1/3 of patients

●        Bone marrow involvement in 30-60% of patients

●        Most patients present with asymptomatic, localized, or generalized peripheral lymphadenopathy

●        The head and neck lymph nodes are more frequently involved

 

Nodal dissemination of a MALT lymphoma is particularly common in which patients

●        Patients with autoimmune disorders → Hashimoto thyroiditis or Sjogren syndrome

NMZL can transform into?

●        DLBCL: diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

●        5-15% of patients


Compare survival between NMZL, MALT and SMZL

●        NMZL = worse survival than MALT lymphoma or splenic MZL

●        > 60% of patients have > 5-year overall survival

 

In MZL, the lymph nodes can be partially or completely effaced by lymphoma → what would you see in each of these situations?

 

●        Marginal zones expanded in cases with partial involvement

●        Neoplasm has diffuse pattern in completely replaced lymph nodes = effacement

 

Typical Microscopic Pathology of NMZL?

 

●        NL shows expanded marginal zones or replacement of lymph node by small cells with scattered large cells

●        Small cells can be centrocyte-like or monocytoid: irregularly-shaped nuclei and moderately
abundant pale cytoplasm

●        Lymphoplasmacytoid or mature-appearing plasma cells can be prominent (plasmacytic differentiation)

●        Residual reactive follicles with hyperplastic germinal centers may be seen

 

 

The cytologically predominant cell type in MZL is?

 

●        Small, with variably irregular nuclear contours

●        Lymphoma cells commonly have abundant pale cytoplasm (so-called monocytoid features)

●        Lymphoid cells with plasmacytoid differentiation or plasma cells common and can be numerous

●        Large cells always present in varying numbers; can be numerous

What do the residual GCs look like in MZL

●        Residual reactive follicles with hyperplastic germinal centers common

○        Germinal centers often have numerous tingible body macrophages

○        Reactive follicles can be colonized by lymphoma (mimicking follicular lymphoma)

○        Germinal centers often surrounded by residual mantle zone


Why is a LN involved by NMZL often pale appearing at low-power magnification?

●        Attributable to many monocytoid cells: irregularly-shaped nuclei and moderately abundant pale cytoplasm

 

NMZL: The tumour is composed of a proliferation of small cells expanding between what 2 areas?

●        A reactive germinal centre and an attenuated mantle cell cuff.

●        Look for residual germinal centers surrounded by mantle zones with expanded layer in between (marginal zone)

NMZL is typically positive for what IHC markers?

●        Positive for monotypic Ig (bright) and pan-B-cell markers

●        CD43(+) in ∼ 50%; CD5(-) or rarely (+, dim)

●        CD10(-), Bcl-6(-)

●        In paraffin sections, only plasmacytoid cells express cytoplasmic Ig


Mutations seen in NMZL?

●        Monoclonal IGH rearrangements

●        KMT2D/MLL2, PTPRD, NOTCH2, and KLF2 mutations


What mutation appears to be unique to NMZL?

●        PTPRD mutations


What is the PTPRD gene?

●        Polymorphism in protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor delta

●        The protein encoded by this gene is a member of the protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) family

●        PTPs are known to be signaling molecules that regulate a variety of cellular processes

○        Cell growth, differentiation, mitotic cycle, and oncogenic transformation

 

NMZL - What does IgD staining show?

●        Weak positivity of the tumour cells that surround the negative germinal centre whereas the residual mantle cells are strongly positive (OUTSIDE LAYER)

 

 

NMZL - What does CD10 staining show?

●        Tumour cells are negative

●        Residual germinal centre is positive

 

 

NMZL - What does BCL2 staining show?

●        Tumour cells are positive

●        Reactive germinal centre is negative

●        Opposite of CD10

 

NMZL Ancillary Tests - Aberrant expression of what T cell marker in ~ 50% of cases?

●        Aberrantly express CD43 (T cell marker) in ~ 50% of cases

●        Usually not expressed in LPL

 

NMZL Ancillary Tests - Usually negative for what markers (think of DDx)?

●        Usually negative for CD5, CD10, and CD23

●        (DDx includes SLL, MCL, FL)

 

NMZL - What may CD21 show?

●        Disruption of follicle architecture by invading MZL after it has expanded to fill the interfollicular areas

●        This may be further evidenced by scattered BCL6 and CD10 positive B cells outside of follicle centres

 

NMZL - Secondary disruption of residual reactive follicles may be evidenced by what 4 stains?

●        1) CD21 showing disruption of follicle architecture by invading MZL

●        2) Scattered BCL6 and CD10 (+) germinal center B cells outside of follicles

●        3) BCL2 (+) neoplastic MZL inside the GCs


NMZL Top Differential Diagnoses?

●        MALT lymphoma draining into/secondarily involving lymph node or SMZL

●        LPL/Waldenström macroglobulinemia - similar immunophenotype

●        Follicular lymphoma

●        Mantle cell lymphoma

●        CLL/SLL with plasmacytoid differentiation

●        Peripheral T-cell lymphoma


Do you expect to see scattered large cells present in MZL?

●        Yes

●        Large cells always present in varying numbers; can be numerous

 

Pediatric nodal marginal zone lymphoma

Follicular lymphoma

In situ follicular B-cell neosplasm

What is in situ follicular neoplasia ISFN?

●        Previously Follicular lymphoma in situ

●        Partial or total colonization of GCs by clonal B cells carrying BCL2 translocation characteristic of FL in otherwise reactive node

How common is ISFN?

●        2% of randomly selected LN biopsies!

●        May be incidental finding

●        Increases as we age


Who is more likely to have ISFN?

●        Patients with environmental risk

●        Herbicides, pesticides

Does ISFN progress to FL? and if so how soon?

●        Some patients progress

●        In situ FL precedes the lymphoma by 23 months to 10 years

 

Can you detect ISFN in H&E sections?

●        Not usually - mostly detected by IHC

●        Uninvolved follicles appear similar to the involved

●        On closer inspection, packed centrocytes may be appreciated

●        Note: Partial involvement by FL will be seen on H&E!


What is the immunophenotype in ISFN?

●        Only detected by IHC

●        BCL2 staining of centrocytes in germinal centres

●        CD10+ cells stronger

What are the genetics of ISFN?

●        t(14;18)

●        Very few other genetic aberrations


What is the risk of FL in patients with only ISFN?

●        Very low <5%

*Follicular Lymphoma

Follicular lymphoma (FL) is a neoplasm of germinal-centre (GC) B cells with varying proportions of centrocytes and centroblasts or large transformed cells and at least a partially follicular growth pattern. In rare cases with an entirely diffuse growth pattern, the neoplastic cells should still show GC B-cell morphology and immunophenotype.



Define Follicular Lymphoma

●        Neoplasm is composed of follicle centre (germinal centre) B cells


What 2 cells is Follicular Lymphoma composed of?

●        Both

○        Centrocytes

○        Centroblasts/large transformed cells

 

 

What are the 3 patterns of follicular lymphoma?

  1. Follicular pattern (>75% follicular area)
  2. Diffuse Pattern (0%)
  3. Both Follicular & Diffuse (25-75%)


After a diagnosis of FL, what is a diffuse lymphoma composed of centroblasts evidence of?

●        Transformation of the disease to DLBCL


Are Primary cutaneous follicular centre lymphomas classified under FL?

●        NO

●        Yes

 

What are the subtypes of FL?

 

Who gets FL?

●        Nearly exclusive to adults

○        Rare in patients < 18

○        Median age 6th decade

●        M:F 1:1.7 → more common in females

●        2-3x more common in white populations

●        Increased risk with agricultural exposures

●        Summary → old North American or European white ladies who live on farms

 

 

 

Where is FL localized in the body?

●        Lymph Nodes, mostly peripheral

●        Spleen, BM, PB

●        Waldeyer Ring → less common

●        Extranodal sites are not as common, and pure extra-nodal presentations uncommon

What percentage of follicular lymphoma has BM involvement?

●        40-70%


What "stage" are most cases at diagnosis

●        Most have wide-spread disease

●        III or IV

●        Only 15-25% have Stage 1-2

Are most patients with FL symptomatic?

●        NO, usually asymptomatic at time of diagnosis


Are B symptoms in FL common?

●        No - Uncommon

●        Usually asymptomatic at time of diagnosis

What imaging modalities are helpful in FL?

●        CT and MRI

●        PET less useful than in aggressive lymphomas, but patients with high FDG-avid disease are at risk for progression

What staging system is used for FL?

●        Lugano classification

○        Modified Ann Arbor

■        Designation of A or B (asymptomatic or B-sx) is not required in Lugano

●        BM biopsy must be done


What is the MACROscopic appearance of FL in an LN?

●        Vaguely nodular pattern macroscopically


What is the predominant histological pattern of FL cases?

●        Follicular pattern

●        Closely packed follicles effacing nodal architecture →  back to back appearance

●        Poorly defined follicles may have → attenuated or absent mantles

●        Centroblasts and centrocytes → not polarized

●        Tingible body macrophages → not usually present


What is the difference in morphology between reactive follicles and Follicular lymphoma → compare the 2?

●        Reactive Follicular hyperplasia

○        BCL2 in GC 

○        GC markers (CD10, BCL6): restricted to GC

○        Ki67: very high, polarized

○        Monoclonal K or L light chain restriction: -

○        Polarized follicles of varying sizes with distinct mantle zones. GC contain mitotic figures and tangible body macrophages.

●        Follicular Lymphoma

○        BCL2 in GC +

○        GC markers (CD10, BCL6): GC and interfollicular zones

○        Ki67: lower

○        Monoclonal K or L light chain restriction: +

○        Atypical follicles are uniform and tightly packed with attenuated poorly defined mantle zones. Follicles may extend into the perinodal fat. Low grade FL show follicles lack tangible body macrophages and mitotic figures are rare.


Can you have interfollicular neoplastic cells in follicular lymphoma?

●        YES → they are usually centrocytes and smaller than those in GCs with less irregular contours

●        Highlighted by BCL2 and CD10


What are the three different patterns of FL, with the % to call each?

●        1. Follicular (> 75% follicular)

●        2. Follicular and diffuse (25-75% follicular)

●        B. Focally follicular/ predominantly diffuse (< 25% follicular)

●        Recommended that the relative proportions of follicular and diffuse areas be noted in the pathology

[FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA]. Follicular lymphoma is the 2nd most common B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma after diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. It comprises up to 20% of lymphoma in adults in the USA and in Western Europe. As the name implies the lymphoma takes a follicular or nodular pattern of growth with or without diffuse areas. This form of lymphoma is almost always a disease of adults with very rare examples documented in the pediatric age group.

[FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA]. A neoplastic follicle is a round to oval structure comprised of follicular center B-cells distributed evenly throughout the follicle with no definition of light or dark zones of a normal lymphoid follicle. This lack of polarity of smaller and larger cells is a helpful morphologic finding in distinguishing a neoplastic follicle from a benign reactive follicle. Also, neoplastic follicles generally either have no mantle zones or reduced, thin, or incomplete mantle zones around follicles.

[FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA]. Generally, neoplastic follicles are regular, back-to-back with similar shapes and sizes but neoplastic follicles can be heterogeneous with small and large follicles next to each other. The nodal architecture is effaced by numerous nodules without an obvious boundary between cortex and medulla. The neoplastic follicles show a monotonous population of cells with no light or dark zones and lack any significant mantle zones.

[FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA]. Note a predominant population of larger cells in this neoplastic follicle without any light or dark zones and lack of any obvious mantle zone around the follicle.

[FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA]. The boundary between the edge of a neoplastic follicle and interfollicular zone is depicted. The larger cells to the right of the arbitrary line are those of a grade 3/3 follicular lymphoma whereas the small lymphocytes to the left of the line are small cells in the interfollicular zone. Note the absence of any mantle zone around the follicle.

[FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA]. The neoplastic follicles consist of a variable mixture of centrocytes and centroblasts. Centrocytes, also known as cleaved cells, are small to large cells with irregular nuclei that often show nuclear clefts, indentations, and grooves without any nucleoli. The cells contain scant cytoplasm and nuclei often appear stretched toffee like and twisted. In contrast, centroblasts (large non-cleaved cells) are larger cells with scant to moderate cytoplasm and round to oval nuclei with open chromatin and small to distinct nucleoli.

[FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA]. Note typical centrocytes with often elongated and irregular nuclei that may show linear clefts and small chromocenters but no nucleoli. Centrocytes can be small or large but all share the same basic individual morphology. Follicular lymphoma is graded based on the number of centroblasts present in neoplastic follicles in 10 high power fields (40x fields). A practical approach of low grade versus high grade is clinically significant but a 3-tier system of grading is allowed. Grade 1 follicles contain up to 5 larger centroblasts in a 40x field whereas in a grade 2 lymphoma up 15 centroblasts are allowed. More than 15 centroblasts in a 40x field are seen in grade 3/3 (high grade) follicular lymphoma.

[FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA]. Low grade lymphomas may be reported as grade 1-2/3 rather than strictly as grade 1/3 or 2/3 since it can be very difficult to count exact number of centroblasts in a neoplastic follicle and in up to 10 such follicles. In this low grade lymphoma centroblasts are highlighted with arrows.

[FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA]. In this grade 3/3 follicular lymphoma most of the cells are centroblasts (arrowhead) both small and large. A small possibly benign lymphocyte is also shown with an arrow. Not only centroblasts are generally bigger but the defining characteristic is the quality of nuclear chromatin which is open and vesicular in appearance.

[FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA]. Note the morphologic difference between the nuclear chromatin of larger centroblasts (arrow) and a possibly benign small lymphocyte (arrowhead). High grade (grade 3/3) follicular lymphoma is generally treated with regimens used for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

[FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA]. In a lymph node both benign and neoplastic follicle center cells show nuclear staining for the transcription factor BCL6. Thus, BCL6 severs as an excellent immunohistochemical marker for follicular center cells, whether benign or malignant. This image shows nuclear staining for BCL-6 in a follicular lymphoma.

[FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA]. Typically, increased numbers of neoplastic follicle center cells are identified outside the neoplastic follicles and can be identified using immunostaining for BCL6 or CD10. The follicular cells in the interfollicular zone are generally small centrocytes but sheets of larger cells can also be seen and constitute the presence of a diffuse large cell lymphoma component in a follicular lymphoma. Note the presence of scattered larger BCL6+ cells outside the follicles. This, however, does not constitute the diffuse large B-cell lymphoma definition. To be qualified as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma it must be composed of a predominant population of larger cells packed together in a sheet-like pattern. The most useful diagnostic value of BCL6 immunostaining is in identification of follicular B-cells whether benign or neoplastic and whether inside or outside of follicles.

[FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA]. Benign lymphoid follicular center cells DO NOT show expression of bcl-2 oncoprotein whereas up to 85-90% of low grade follicular lymphoma and a lesser proportion of high grade follicular lymphoma show coexpression of bcl-2. Thus, expression of bcl-2 by follicular B-cells (arrow) is a feature of lymphoma and not benign follicular center cells. Care must be taken not to mistake for the normal expression of bcl-2 by T-cells present within lymphoid follicles, by mantle zone B-cells, and by T and B-cells in the interfollicular zone (arrowhead). Also, bcl-2 expression is NOT diagnostic of a follicular lymphoma as many other B and T-cell lymphomas express bcl-2 oncoprotein. The most useful diagnostic value of bcl-2 immunostaining is in differentiating benign follicles from neoplastic ones.

[FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA]. This fortuitous image shows the presence of two neoplastic follicles with expression of bcl-2 oncoprotein (two arrowheads) and three non-neoplastic reactive lymphoid follicles without any bcl-2 expression by the follicular center cells (three arrows). This partial nodal involvement by a follicular lymphoma can be missed if neoplastic follicles constitute a smaller proportion of all follicles. The diagnostic morphologic finding is the lack of polarity in neoplastic follicles and the absence of any significant mantle zones around follicles.

[FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA]. This image show bcl-2 coexpression by a grade 3/3 follicular lymphoma. Bcl-2 expression is less common in grade 3 follicular lymphoma.

[FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA]. Immunostaining for the follicular dendritic cell marker CD21 can be very helpful in two situations: in identifying a follicular architecture in an apparent diffuse pattern and in identifying abnormal follicles as neoplastic follicles in early follicular lymphoma sometimes called in-situ follicular lymphoma. In follicular lymphomas the follicular dendritic cell network is commonly disrupted by expansion of neoplastic follicle center cells as seen in this case. In benign reactive follicles, however, a diffuse meshwork of CD21+ follicular dendritic cells is present evenly throughout the follicle.

 


What do we call diffuse areas of Grade 3 Follicular Lymphoma?

●        Diffuse Large B Cell Lymphoma

●        By definition, anything with >15 centroblasts per high power field is called DLBCL

What is the cellular morphology of FL?

●        Two types of B cells

●        Centrocytes:

○        Small to medium cells with angulated, elongated, twisted or cleaved nuclei and inconspicuous nucleoli

○        Scant pale cytoplasm

●        Large Centrocytes:

○        Dispersed chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli

●        Centroblasts:

○        Large cells with round/oval nuclei, vesicular chromatin, 1-3 peripheral nucleoli and a rim of cytoplasm

○        3x the size of lymphocytes usually


What is the typical pattern of involvement of the Marrow in Follicular Lymphoma

●        Paratrabecular region

●        May spread to interstitial areas

●        Rarely follicular growth pattern with FDC meshwork

What is Diffuse follicular lymphoma variant? Common mutation?

●        Novel diffuse FL variant

●        Characterized by diffuse growth pattern and → absence of t(14;18)/IGH::BCL2

●        Can see micro follicles in all cases with → weak to absent BCL2 staining (+/-)

●        Usually CD10 positive, and CD23+, BCL6+

●        Mainly in → inguinal region

●        1p36 deletion

●        STAT6 mut


What are the extranodal FL?

·       Duodenal type FL

·       Ocular adnexal FL

·       Thyroid FL

·       Testicular FL

·       Primary cutaneous FL

 

What is Testicular Follicular lymphoma?

●        Distinctive variant of FL

●        Higher frequency in children (median age 4)

●        Absence of BCL2 translocation t(14;18)

●        Cytologically, they are high-grade (usually 3A) but have good prognosis even without therapy beyond surgical excision

 

What is the immunophenotype of follicular lymphoma?

●        B-Cell antigens

○        CD20, CD19, CD22, CD79a

●        Usually positive for

○        BCL2 (90% Gr 1-2, 50% Gr3), BCL6, CD10

●        Meshworks of CD21+ FDC sparser

●        Usually negative for

○        CD5, CD43

○        CD10 can be negative in Gr 3B

●        Other GC markers

○        LMO2, GCET1, HGAL (GCET2)


Why are some FLs negative for BCL2 by IHC?

●        Apparent absence of protein due to mutations in BCL2 gene that eliminate epitopes recognized by the antibodies

●        E17 clone at BCCA


Is BCL2 useful to distinguish FL from other lymphomas?

●        NO

●        Most Low-grade B cell lymphomas are positive for BCL2, but FL can also be negative


What is the Ki67 proliferation index in FL?

●        Depending on Grade

○        Grade 1-2 have <20%

○        Grade 3 >20%


What is the normal counterpart to FL?

●        Germinal centre B cell

●        t(14;18) cases occur in BL, but fully malignant transformation of these cells occurs during re-entry to GC in 2ndary lymphoid organs


How do we grade Follicular Lymphoma?

●        Estimating the absolute number of centroblasts (large or small) in 10 neoplastic follicles

●        Expressed per high power field (40x)

●        AT LEAST 10 HPFs within different follicles must be evaluated, and representative

●        FL Grades

○        Grade 1: 0-5 Centroblasts per HPF

○        Grade 2: 6-15 Centroblasts per HPF

■        Combination of Gr 1-2 is preferred = low grade

○        Grade 3: >15 centroblasts per HPF

■        Grade 3A - centrocytes present

■        Grade 3B - centroblasts/immunoblasts only, centrocytes absent

 

●        Difference between 3B and DLBCL is presence/absence of underlying FDC meshwork demonstrated by CD21

 

#lymphomafacts - follicular-2

Very elegant pathology

- large, abnormal follicles without formed mantle zone

- CD10+ (i.e. germinal centre derived)

- INTERfollicular CD10+ cells characteristic

- Bcl2+ (reactive follicle is Bcl2-)

- t(14;18) seen in approx 90% cases

#lymsm #MedEd

 

#lymphomafacts - follicular-3

Graded by path:

gd 1: < 5 centroblasts/high power field (hpf)

gd 2: 5-15 / hpf

gd 3: >15 / hpf

     3a - centrocytes still seen

     3b - all centroblasts

- gd3b treated as high grade lymphoma

- gd 1-3a generally treated as low grade
