What do you report if distinct areas of Grade 3 FL are present in a Bx of otherwise Gr 1-2 FL?

●        A separate diagnosis of grade 3 FL should also be made and the approximate percentages of each grade reported

What is the preferred biopsy type for diagnosis of FL and why?

 

●        Excisional biopsy for primary diagnosis for adequate sampling

What percentage of FLs are Gr 1-2?

●        80-90%


How common is pure Grade 3B FL?

●        RARE

●        Biologically related to DLBCL

 

What is the antigen receptor status of FL?

 

●        IgH and IgL genes rearranged

●        IGV extensive somatic hypermutation


Why can there be a high false negative rate on IGH PCR?

●        Due to mutations in the IgH affecting PCR primers


What is the classic cytogenetic abnormality in Follicular Lymphoma?

●        t(14;18)(q32;q21)

○        IGH and BCL2 Gene

●        t(14;18)(q32;q21)/IGH::BCL2 in 80-90% of FL

○        Juxtaposes BCL2 at 18q21 adjacent to IGH on derivative chromosome 14

●        90% of Gr 1-2 FLs

●        Less likely in Grade 3B

●        Negative in Testicular FL

 

What is the preferred diagnostic method for the IGH/BCL2 translocation, and why?

●        FISH (can detect up to 90%); large probes detect multiple breakpoints

●        Cytogenetics cannot distinguish IGH/BCL2 from IGH/MALT1 translocations

●        Both MALT1 and BCL2 are on chr 18


What are other CG abnormalities in FL?

 

●        Additional abnormalities: loss of 1p, 6q, 10q, and 17p and gains of chromosomes 1, 6p, 7, 8, 12q, X, and 18q/dup

Name some gene mutations associated with Follicular Lymphoma?

●        EZH2

●        CREBBP

●        KMT2D

Easy Crazy Krista Marcon


Is there a genetic susceptibility to FL?

●        Yes - genome wide studies identified 5 susceptibility loci outside HLA region

What is the prognosis of FL?

●        Related to extent of disease


What is used to predict the prognosis in FL?

●        FLIPI score → 5 independent predictors of inferior survival

○        Age > 60

○        Hb <120 g/L

○        Increased LDH

○        Stage - Ann Arbour III/IV

○        >4 involved nodal areas

○        Mnemonic: No LASH (No=Node, L=LDH, A=Age, S=Stage (AA), H=Hb)

●        Stratification

○        0-1 = low risk

○        2 - intermediate risk

○        3-5 = high risk

What is the survival for patients with Grade 1-3A FL

●        >12 years


What is the rate of transformation of FL to DLBCL?

●        Progression to DLBCL occurs in 25-35% of patients with FL

●        Could progress to HGBL or Burkitt-like lymphoma with MYC or BCL2

●        Rarely B-Lymphoblastic lymphoma

●        FL can relapse as cHL

 

Pediatric-type Follicular Lymphoma

Paediatric-type follicular lymphoma (PTFL) is a localized, nodal mature B-cell lymphoma occurring predominantly in the paediatric, adolescent, and young adult age group. It is characterized by a clonal proliferation of germinal-centre B cells with a pure follicular growth pattern, altered lymph nodal architecture, a high proliferation index, and an absence of BCL2, BCL6, and IRF4 rearrangements.


What is Pediatric-type Follicular Lymphoma?

●        Nodal Lymphoma occurring in young adults and children

●        Elevated proliferation index and absence of BCL2, BCL6 and IRF4 rearrange

●        Considered a separate entity

 

What is pediatric-type Follicular Lymphoma?

·       Uncommon nodal FL occurring primarily in children and young adults


What lymphomas does pediatric-type Follicular Lymphoma exclude?

·       DLBCL of follicle centre origin, testicular FLs, or Large B-cell lymphomas with IRF4 rearrangement


What is the localization of pediatric-type Follicular Lymphoma?

·       Often involves lymph nodes of the head and neck

·       Usually presents with stage I disease.

 

What age group/gender is pediatric-type Follicular Lymphoma seen in?

●        5-25 years mostly

●        Median age 15-18 years

●        Rare cases >40 years

●        10:1 M:F

What are the clinical features of pediatric-type Follicular Lymphoma?

●        Isolated asymptomatic LN enlargement

●        Occasional more extensive disease

●        Mostly with stage I, single site

●        No BM involvement

●        No B symptoms


What are the diagnostic criteria of pediatric-type Follicular Lymphoma? 

 

·       Essential: 

o   a patient in the paediatric, adolescent, and young adult age group (usually age < 40 years, most 225 years);

o   localized nodal disease; purely follicular growth with marked architectural distortion and germinal-centre marker expression;

o   predominance of intermediate-sized to large blastoid cells and a high proliferation fraction;

o   absence of diffuse proliferation of large cells meeting criteria for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma;

o   evidence of B-cell monoclonality by immunophenotyping or genetics; absence of BCL2, BCL6, and MYC rearrangements;

o   absence of strong, uniform IRF4 (MUM1) protein expression and/or absence of IRF4 rearrangement.

·       Desirable: markedly expansile follicles; mutations in MAP2K1 and TNFRSF14.

 

What is the morphology of pediatric-type Follicular Lymphoma?

- Total or subtotal effacement of LN architecture
- large expansile/serpiginous follicles
- partial involvement possible
- "Starry-sky" pattern of follicles with thin/absent mantle zones
Cells: monotonous
- intermediate in size with usually blastoid appearance without prominent nucleoli
(Grade 3A-like, but grading is not typically used)
- mitotic figures are apparent

What is the immunophenotype of pediatric-type Follicular Lymphoma?

·       Mature B-cell phenotype
CD20, CD79a, Pax5
CD10 strong, BCL6+
BCL2 negative, or weak
Ki67 moderate to high >30% without evidence of follicle polarization
CD21 outlines FDC meshwork
Note: architectural effacement is a key feature that distinguishes PTFL from reactive follicular hyperplasia with clonal B cells

 

What is the status of BCL2, BCL6 and IRF4 mutations in pediatric-type Follicular Lymphoma?

·       ABSENT!!


What are the most common genetic aberrations in pediatric-type Follicular Lymphoma?

·       1p36 and TNFRSF14

○        Note 1p36 is the same as Follicular Lymphoma, diffuse variant (which is also negative for t(14;18)

●        MAP2K1 in 40-50%


What is the prognosis of pediatric-type Follicular Lymphoma?

●        Excellent

●        Localized cases can be surgically excised without need for adjuvant chemo/radiation


Who should we be cautious about making the diagnosis of pediatric-type Follicular Lymphoma in

●        Patients >25 because the DDx includes normal FL of Grade 3A or B

●        May be challenging to distinguish

●        Correlation with clinical features is essential

 

Duodenal type follicular lymphoma

What are the features of duodenal type FL?

●        Localize to duodenum

●        Distinct from other FL of gastrointestinal tract

●        Excellent prognosis

●        Follicular, low-grade, some features overlap with in situ follicular neoplasia and extranodal MZL

 

Where does primary duodenal type FL occur and where does secondary involvement of FL occur?

●        Primary duodenal FL in 2nd portion of duedenum

●        Secondary duodenal FL in mesenteric lymph node

What is duodenal-type follicular Lymphoma?

●        Primary follicular lymphoma of the GI tract

●        Usually in small intestine (duodenum) found as multiple small polyps on endoscopy (incidental)

●        Specific variant of FL


What is the immunophenotype of duodenal FL?

●        Same as nodal FL


Is duodenal FL a diffuse or localized disease?

●        Localized

●        Mostly Stage IE, IIE


Who gets duodenal Follicular Lymphoma?

●        Middle age

●        M=F

●        ? Japanese


What is the morphology of duodenal-type FL?

●        Neoplastic follicles in mucosa/submucosa

●        With infiltration of lamina propria outside of the follicles

●        Centrocytes with infrequent centroblasts (Gr1-2)

 


What is the immunophenotype of duodenal-type FL?

●        Similar to nodal FL

●        CD20+, CD10+, BCL2+, variable BCL6

●        Low Ki67


What are the genetics duodenal-type FL?

●        t(14;18) IGH/BCL2

What is the prognosis of duodenal-type FL?

●        Excellent long term survival

●        Low <10% risk of progression to nodal disease


What is the treatment approach to duodenal-type FL?

●        Watch and wait approach

●        Chemo, ritux and radiation have been tried

 

Cutaneous follicle center lymphoma

Primary cutaneous follicle center lymphoma

Primary cutaneous follicle centre lymphoma (PCFCL) is a tumour of follicle centre cells, including centrocytes and variable numbers of centroblasts, with a follicular, follicular and diffuse, or diffuse growth pattern, that generally occurs in the skin of the head or trunk.


What is Primary Cutaneous Follicle Center Lymphoma?

●        Lymphoma arising in skin composed of follicular center cells

●        Confined to skin for at least 6 months upon staging

●        Mainly centrocytes (small cleaved cells); less frequently centroblasts (large cleaved and noncleaved cells)

●        Follicular or diffuse growth pattern

●        Subset of cases appear to be clinically and genetically distinct from nodal follicular lymphoma


3 PCFCL growth patterns?

●        Follicular

●        Follicular & diffuse

●        Diffuse growth patterns


How does PCFCL differ from nodal FL?

●        Subset of cases appear to be clinically and genetically distinct from nodal FL

●        BCL2 gene rearrangements less frequent than in nodal FL

 

PCFCL typical presentation?

●        Usually solitary, erythematous lesion in → head and neck

●        Recurrences more common in patients with multiple site lesions


PCFCL Rx modalities?

●        Therapy with local radiation or surgical excision

 

PCFCL prognosis?

●        Recurrences more common in patients with multiple site lesions

●        Prognosis favorable, even in patients with multiple skin lesions

●        5-year survival rate is 95%

PCFCL: does prognosis vary according to the number of skin lesions?

·       No

·       Prognosis favorable, even in patients with multiple skin lesions

 

PCFCL histologic findings?

·       Dermal lymphoid follicular infiltrate that → spares epidermis and subdermal (Grenz zone)

·       Perivascular, periadnexal to diffuse dermal infiltrate


Skin biopsy showing perivascular (blue arrow) and periadnexal (hair follicle and sebaceous gland depicted by yellow and red arrow, respectively) lymphocytic infiltration within superficial and deep dermis. There is also diffuse mucin deposition throughout the dermal layer.

 

PCFCL immunophenotype?

·       CD10(+) in cases with follicular pattern (50%)

·       Bcl-6(+);

·       Bcl-2(+/-) in up to 60% of cases

·       PCFCL that is CD10(+), Bcl-2(+) likely carries t(14;18)

 

What % of PCFCL cases have t(14;18) by FISH?

·       PCFCL that is CD10(+), Bcl-2(+) likely carries t(14;18)(q32;q21)

·       ~ 30% of PCFCL cases have t(14;18) by FISH


PCFCL Top Differential Diagnoses?

●        Secondary follicular lymphoma of skin

○        Usually strongly CD10(+) and Bcl-2(+)

○        BCL2 rearrangements in ∼ 80-90% of cases

●        Cutaneous marginal zone B-cell lymphoma

●        Primary cutaneous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PCDLBCL), leg type

●        PCDLBCL, other (non-leg type)

●        Cutaneous follicular hyperplasia


5 useful IHC markers to differentiate PCFCL from secondary FL of Skin, MZL, PCLBCL Leg Type & FH?

●        Bcl-6; Bcl-2; CD10; CD21; Ki-67


Bcl-6, Bcl-2; CD10; CD21; and Ki-67 staining pattern for PCFCL?

●        Bcl-6(+), Bcl-2(dim +/-); CD10(+/-); CD21(+) meshworks; low Ki-67

●        Usually BCL2(-) but positive cases reported, esp with at least partial follicular pattern often weaker than background T cell expression

Bcl-6, Bcl-2; CD10; IRF-4/MUM1, cIgM staining pattern for PCLBCL Leg Type?

●        IRF-4/MUM1(+), cIgM(+), FOXP1(+), Bcl-6(+), Bcl-2(+), CD10(-)

 

Mantle cell lymphoma

In situ mantle cell neoplasm

 

*classic Mantle Cell Lymphoma

Mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) is a mature B-cell neoplasm derived from the mantle zone of lymphoid follicles and typically composed of small to medium-sized monomorphic cells expressing CD5, SOX11, and cyclin D1. It is associated with CCND-family rearrangements, most commonly CCND1.



Characteristic translocation seen in MCL?

●        t(11;14)/CCND1::IgH

●        Break point: (q13;q32)

●        Cyclin D1 aka → BCL-1

 

Define Mantle Cell Lymphoma (MCL)

●        Clinically aggressive B-cell lymphoma

●        Usually composed of monomorphic small to medium-sized cells

●        Associated with t(11;14) & Cyclin-D1 overexpression

○        t(11;14)/CCND1::IgH

 

3 key steps by which the t(11;14) leads to cell cycle progression (from G1 to S phase) in the etiology/pathogenesis of MCL

●        Translocation Juxtaposes CCND1 at 11q13 with IgH at 14q32 resulting in:

○        1) Cyclin-D1 overexpression

○        2) Rb phosphorylation

○        3) Release of E2F transcription factors

●        These steps facilitate/lead to → cell cycle progression from G1 to S phase: ie cell proliferation

 

 

 

What is E2F?

●        A family of transcription factors regulating the expression of a number of genes required for DNA synthesis and cell cycle progression

 

Age group and gender affected by MCL ?

●        Elderly people (6th-7th decades); male predominance

What are the typical sites of involvement of MCL?

●        LNs

●        Spleen,

●        BM +/- PB involvement

●        - Extranodal (GI, waldeyer ring, lungs, pleura)


Most MCL patients present with what disease stage and symptoms?

●        Most patients present with advanced clinical stage III/IV disease, B symptoms, lymphadenopathy, extranodal involvement

●        Most common cause of lymphomatous polyposis of the colon

 



MCL prognosis?

●        Currently considered incurable

●        Median survival of 2-5 years

●        MCL is incurable but variable clinical course and prognosis

●        Prognostic assessment based on symptoms, clinical risk factors, and tumor burden

●        In recent years, approach to therapy is more tailored


3 growth/infiltration patterns of MCL?

●        Nodular

●        Diffuse

●        Mantle zone

 

Describe the typical/classic microscopic cellular features of MCL

-Malignant cells
-Growth patterns
-Other characteristic histological features

●        Monotonous population of small/medium-sized cells with variably irregular nuclear contours, condensed chromatin, scanty cytoplasm

●        LN

○        Architectural effacement by lymphoma with nodular, diffuse, or mantle-zone pattern

○        Hyalinized blood vessels → common

○        Single benign "pink" histiocytes with abundant eosinophilc cytoplasm

●        Bone marrow

○        Involvement is present in most cases of mantle cell lymphoma.

 

●        Image: BM smear shows a massive infiltration by neoplastic lymphocytes resembling centrocytes.

●        The cells are medium-sized with a high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio and a small amount of slightly basophilic cytoplasm.

●        The shape of the nucleus is variable, mostly irregular and indented.

●        Nuclear chromatin is less condensed and some small nucleoli are visible (red arrows).

●        The presence of buttock cells (blue arrows) is a typical finding in the classic morphological variant of mantle cell lymphoma.

4 histologic variants of MCL?

●        classic

●        Aggressive:

○        Blastoid

○        Pleomorphic

●        Other:

○        Small cell

■        Most common variant

○        MZ-like

 



Describe the morphology of Blastoid variant MCL

●        Cells resemble lymphoblasts with dispersed chromatin and a high mitotic rate (usually at least 20-30/ 10 hpf)

●        "Medium sized cells"

 

 

●        Blastoid variant of mantle cell lymphoma is characterized by → larger, young blastoid cells (black arrows) with fine chromatin and visible nucleoli, some with nuclear impressions and abundant cytoplasm.


Describe the morphology of Pleomorphic variant MCL

●        Cells are pleomorphic (variable morph) but many are large with oval to irregular nuclear contours, generally pale cytoplasm and often prominent nucleoli in at least some of the cells

 

 

●        Pleomorphic variant is quite rare and is associated with a more aggressive clinical behaviour of the disease.

●        This bone marrow smear shows a massive infiltration by a mixed pleomorphic population of neoplastic lymphocytes.

●        The size and appearance of tumour cells is not uniform but very variable: large lymphocytes with abundant cytoplasm are present (blue arrows), vacuolation of the cytoplasm is observed (yellow arrow).

●        The shape of the nucleus is often irregular (red arrows) and some fine nucleoli are visible (green arrows).


Describe the morphology of small cell variant MCL

●        Small round lymphocytes with more clumped chromatin, either admixed or predominant, mimicking SLL

 

●        Bone marrow smear shows a predominant infiltration by a uniform population of small neoplastic lymphocytes.

●        Tumour cells have a high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio and a small amount of slightly basophilic cytoplasm.

●        The shape of the nucleus is mostly regular and rounded, nuclear chromatin is clumped and nucleoli are not visible.

●        The morphological picture resembles chronic lymphocytic leukaemia / small lymphocytic lymphoma and the distinction from this disease is practically impossible only on the basis of cytology.


Describe the morphology of MZ-like variant MCL

●        Prominent foci of cells with abundant pale cytoplasm resembling marginal zone or monocytoid B-cells mimicking a marginal zone lymphoma; sometimes these paler foci may also resemble proliferation centres of CLL/SLL

 

●        Marginal-zone like variant is a very rare morphological form of the disease.

●        This bone marrow smear shows a predominant infiltration by neoplastic lymphocytes with plasmacytoid features.

●        The tumour cells are medium-sized with abundant basophilic cytoplasm and eccentric location of nuclei. 

●        Nuclear chromatin is less condensed, sometimes irregular (blue arrow), and small nucleoli are visible (red arrows).

●        The plasmacytoid appearance is seen especially in the lymphocyte on the left (green arrow).


What is the significance of Ki67 in MCL?

●        Prognostic impact of high Ki67 >30% → associated with adverse prognoses

●        Also: >10 mitoses per 15 HPF

 

MCL Ancillary Tests? 4 test types?

 

●        Immunohistochemistry

●        Flow cytometry

●        Cytogenetics/FISH

●        Gene expression profiling (GEP)

 

Key IHC finding in MCL?

 

●        CD5+ B cells

●        Cyclin-D1(+)

●        Check SOX11 if CyclinD1 neg

●        CD10 (-)


Classic MCL immunophenotype?

●        CD19(+), CD20(+), CD5(+), CD10(-), BCL6(-), CD43(+/-), sIgM/IgD, BCL2+, CD23(-) or dim (-/+), CD200(-), Cyclin-D1(+), Sox11(+), FMC-7(+), Ki-67 variable

  • IHC:
    • Positive for CD5, cyclin-D1, BCL2, surface IgM/IgD, SOX11

o   Usually negative for CD200, CD23, BCL6, CD10, LEF1

o   Aberrant immunophenotypes seen in 10-20% of cases

      • CD10 &/or BCL6 positivity seen in up to 16%

 

 

●        PB flow cytometry

○        The analysis of peripheral blood shows neoplastic B lymphocytes (purple), T lymphocytes (blue), all lymphocytes (green), monocytes (yellow) and granulocytes (red).

○        Neoplastic B cells express a high intensity of CD45 and a low intensity of SS (A), and display the characteristic phenotype → CD5+ (B), CD23-, CD62L- (C), CD20+ and CD200- (D).

○        Note the negative expression of CD200 and CD23, useful in the diagnosis of CLL.

 

What proportion of Mantle Cell Lymphomas have Cyclin D1 expression'?

·       >95%

 

What proportion of MCLs have Sox 11 positive?

·       Most sensitive antibody

·       >90% MCLs

-          including Cyclin D1 negative and blastoid cases

 

MCL cytogenetic/FISH abnormalities?

●        t(11;14)(q13;q32) or CCND1::IgH (FISH) in >95%

 

Cases without the CCND1/IGH translocation can have what other genetic abnormalities - give 4 egs?

·       Variant CCND1 with the Ig light chains (chr 2 and 22 for K and L respectively)

·       CCND2 (cyclin D2) or CCND3 (Cyclin D3) with IG partner

 

In Cyclin D1 negative MCL with CCND2 or CCND3 translocation, which stains will be useful?

●        Sox-11

●        Note: Cyclin D2 and D3 are not useful, as they are present in other B cell lymphomas

 

What are other cytogenetic or gene mutations seen in MCLs (along with CCND1/IGH) that dont involve K, L D2 or D3

●        Gains of 3q26, 7p21,

●        8q24 (MYC)

●        ATM- TP53


How may gene expression profiling influence MCL prognosis?

·       MCL has a unique gene expression/proliferation profile

·       Proliferation predicts prognosis

·       Proliferation profile may be used to divide patients into prognostic groups

 

MCL Top Differential Diagnoses (3)

·       CLL/SLL

·       Follicular lymphoma

·       Nodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma

 

What does MCL transform into?

·       Trick question

·       MCL does not transform into typical DLBCL

·       Loss of mantle zone growth pattern, increase in nuclear size and pleomorphism, increase in Ki67 activity → can be seen at relapse

 

What is the prognosis of MCL?

·       Median survival 3-5 years

 

What are the 2 variants of mantle cell lymphoma?

1.       Leukemic non-nodal mantle cell lymphoma

2.       In situ mantle cell neoplasia

 

What is leukemic non-nodal mantle cell lymphoma?

·       MCL with PB and BM (+/- splenic)

·       No adenopathy

·       Usually small cells resembling CLL

 

What are the staining characteristics of leukemic non-nodal mantle cell lymphoma?

·       Usually Sox-11 negative!!

·       CD5 less common

·       More likely to have CD200

·       Note: phenotype overlaps with CLL!

 

What are the CG abnormalities in leukemic non-nodal mantle cell lymphoma?

·       CCND1 translocation

·       Few other CG abnormalities

 

What is the prognosis of leukemic non-nodal mantle cell lymphoma?

·       Better than classic MCL

·       Median survival 79 months

·       More indolent course

·       Therapy may not be required

·       Worse/more aggressive with TP53 mutations

 

What is In situ mantle cell neoplasia?

·       Formerly in situ mantle cell lymphoma

·       The presence of cyclin D1- positive lymphoid cells with CCND1 re- arrangements restricted to the mantle zones of otherwise hyperplastic-appearing lymphoid tissue

 

Does peripheral blood involvement exclude the diagnosis of In situ mantle cell neoplasia?

·       No, but some cases may actually be leukemic non-nodal MCL

 

Where are the Cyclin D1 cells found in In situ mantle cell neoplasia?

·       Usually in the inner mantle zone

-          may be scattered throughout the mantle zone

 

When is the diagnosis of over MCL vs. In situ mantle cell neoplasia made?

·       When the mantle zones are expanded and completely replaced by Cyclin D1 positive cells

 

What is the immunophenotype of In situ mantle cell neoplasia?

●        More likely to be:

○        CD5 negative

○        May be sox-11 positive or negative

○        Cyclin D1 positive

 

What is the expected LEF1 staining in MCL?

●        LEF1 negative (pos in CLL and normal T cells)


What is the clinical course of In situ mantle cell neoplasia?

●        Frequently stable disease without therapy

●        Rare cases may progress to overt MCL

 

What is the name of the MCL clinical prognostic scoring system?

  • MCL International Prognostic Index

 

2 normal BM cell types that are cyclin D1 positive?

●        Endothelial cells

●        Histiocytes

 

Mantle Cell Lymphoma, Blastoid and Pleomorphic Variants



Define Mantle Cell Lymphoma, Blastoid and Pleomorphic Variants

●        Highly aggressive variants of MCL composed of cells that resemble lymphoblasts (classic variant) or are large, atypical, and pleomorphic (pleomorphic variant)

●        High-grade cytologic features

●        Clinically aggressive type of MCL with high-grade cytologic features: 2 major variants: Blastoid and pleomorphic

 

Mantle Cell Lymphoma, Blastoid Variant - Clinical Issues - compared to typical MCL?

 

●        Clinical and biological features are comparable to those of typical MCL

●        Associated with particularly short durations of response after chemotherapy and poorer overall survival

 

Which of the 2 MCL aggressive variants often presents de novo

 

●        Blastoid variant: Often presents de novo

●        Pleomorphic variant: Often history of classic MCL (represents disease progression or evolution)


IHC, CG and molecular w/u results in MCL blastic & pleomorphic variants?

  • Immunophenotype
    • Pan-B cell (+), cyclin-D1 (+), SOX11(+), Ki-67 high
  • Cytogenetic or FISH analysis
    • t(11;14)(q13;q32)/CCND1::IGH in virtually all cases
    • Karyotypes are often complex (≥ 3 abnormalities)
  • Molecular testing
    • Monoclonal IGH and light chain rearrangements
    • t(11;14)(q13;q32) shown by PCR in 30-50% of cases
    • Truncated cyclin-D1 transcripts in ~ 33% MCL
  • Mutations in many genes
    • ATM (~ 40%), TP53 (~ 25%), CDKN2A (TP16) (10-20%)
    • KMT2D (MLL2) (~ 10%), NSD2 (WHSC1) (~ 10%), BIRC3 (~ 5%), NOTCH1/NOTCH2 (~ 5%)
  • Gene expression profile
    • Proliferation signature high

 

Mantle Cell Lymphoma, Blastoid Variant → Top Differential Diagnoses?

  • Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
  • High-grade B-cell lymphoma
  • Lymphoblastic lymphoma
  • Burkitt lymphoma

Cytology of mantle cell lymphoma classical (A), pleomorphic (B), and blastoid (C) MCL (original magnification ×1000, hematoxylin and eosin stain).

 

Large B-cell lymphoma

*Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma NOS

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) NOS is a lymphoma consisting of medium-sized to large B cells with a diffuse growth pattern. This is a morphologically and molecularly heterogeneous entity that does not meet the diagnostic criteria for specific large B-cell lymphoma neoplasms.

 

What is DLBCL, NOS      

●        Neoplasm of medium or large B lymphoid cells

○        Classification as small, medium or large = comparison to macrophage nuclei

○        Nuclei are the same size as, or larger than macrophages, or more than twice the size of those of normal lymphocytes = medium or large

●        Diffuse growth pattern

 

What is the etiology of DLBCL?

●        Unknown

○        Can be de novo

○        Can be transformation from less aggressive lymphoma

■        CLL, FL, MZL, NLPHL

 

What are known risk factors for DLBCL?

●        Immunodeficiencies

●        EBV+

 

Where does DLBCL occur?

●        Nodal  60%

●        Extranodal - 40%

○        GI tract (stomach, Ileocecal region)

○        Bone, testes, spleen, waldeyer ring, salivary glands, thyroid, liver, kidney, adrenal

○        Primary CNS

○        Primary testicular

 

What sites are considered a distinct entity from DLBCL, NOS?    

●        Skin

○        Primary cutaneous follicle centre Lymphoma

○        Primary cutaneous DLBCL, leg type

●        CNS

○        Primary DLBCL of the CNS

●        Other:

○        EBV+ DLBCL, NOS

■        EBV+ leads to separate and specific diagnosis of "EBV positive DLBCL, NOS"

○        DLBCL associated with chronic inflammation

 

Can a bone marrow biopsy substitute for diagnosis in DLBC Lymphoma, why or why not?

●        Not always

○        Bone marrow can be discordant (ie low grade found) in 1-25% of cases

○        Concordant in up to 25% of cases

 

What are the clinical features of DLBCL?

●        Rapidly enlarging mass

●        50% have Stage 1 or 2 disease

●        B symptoms may be present

 

Which infections play a role in pathogenesis of DLBCL

●        Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and HHV-8 involved in specific types of DLBCL

○        Increased risk associated with HIV infection

■        Attributable primarily to immunodeficiency

■        Some data suggest that virus has direct effects

●        Evidence suggests that hepatitis C infection is risk factor

 

What is the common lymph node pattern of DLBCL?

●        Partial or complete architectural effacement

●        Diffuse proliferation of med/lg lymphoid cells

●        Often peri-nodal tissue infiltration

●        Broad/fine sclerotic bands may be present

 

3 histologic variants of DLBCL, NOS?

  1. Centroblastic: 85% of DLBCL, NOS cases
  2. Immunoblastic: ∼ 10% of cases
  3. Anaplastic: ∼ 3% of cases

DLBCL subtypes. (A) DLBCL, centroblastic variant. The cells have vesicular chromatin and often membrane-bound nucleoli. Polylobated centroblasts may be common, as in this case. (B) DLBCL, immunoblastic variant. The cells are round with prominent central nucleoli. (C) PMBL. The cells have clear cytoplasm and fine compartmentalizing fibrosis. (D) B-UNC/BL/DLBCL is composed of monomorphic medium-sized cells without a starry sky pattern. This case had translocations involving both MYC and BCL2, so-called double hit.

 

Key morphologic features of Centroblastic variant DLBCL?

●        Medium to large sized cells (10-14 μm)

●        Round/oval nuclear borders

●        Vesicular chromatin

●        2-4 small nucleoli

●        moderate cytoplasm

●        Most cases have mixture of centroblasts and immunoblasts

 

Key morphologic features of Immunoblastic variant DLBCL?

●        Large Cells 15-20 μm

●        prominent single central nucleolus

●        moderate basophilic cytoplasm

●        few centroblasts (>90% of cells are immunoblasts)

 

Key morphologic features of Anaplastic variant DLBCL?

●        Large and bizarre pleomorphic nuclei

●        Reed-Sternberg-like (+/-)

●        May show sinusoidal or cohesive growth mimicking carcinoma

 

What are rare morphological variants of DLBCL, NOS?

●        Rare cases have myxoid stroma or fibrillary matrix

●        Pseudorosette formation

●        Spindle-shaped cells

●        Signet ring cells

 

Immunophenotype for DLBCL   

●        Usually express pan-B markers: CD19, CD20, CD22, CD79a, PAX5

●        Surface and cytoplasmic IgM > IgG > IgA

●        Ki67 40-90%

●        CD30+ in up to 20%

●        CD5+ in 10%

●        BCL2 and MYC may be expressed

○        Cutoff for positivity is → 50% BCL2 and 40% MYC

○        Double expressor lymphoma: MYC(+) and Bcl-2(+) correlates with poorer prognosis

●        Germinal centre markers, CD10 and Bcl-6, expressed in variable proportion of cases depending on phenotype

○        (also MUM2, GCET, LMO2, FOXP1)

●        EBV+ leads to diagnosis of "EBV positive DLBCL, NOS"

 

What are the two cell of origins in DLBCL?

●        Germinal Centre B-cell (GCB) 60%

●        Activated B cell (ABC) 40%

●        10-15% cannot be included in either of these subtypes

 

Which cell origin type has better prognosis?

●        GCB - better prognosis

 

What is the Hans' algorithm?

Used to determine cell of origin in DLBCL. All markers cutoff 30%.


 

 

What are common chromosomal aberrations in DLBCL?

  • 3q27/BCL6 (~ 30%); t(14;18) (~ 20%); 8q24/MYC (~ 10%)

 

Can DLBCL harbor a MYC translocation

●        YES!

●        Tend to have higher Ki67, and have BCL2 protein expression

 

Most frequent mutation in DLBCL, ABC?

●        BCL6 > MYC

 

Most frequent mutation in DLBCL, GCB?

●        BCL2 > BCL6

 

What mutational changes are associated with poor outcomes?       

●        bcl-6, bcl-2, p53, c-myc, and Ki-67 expression

 

What is the Choi algorithm?

●        Choi et al described an algorithm using markers which closely approximated gene expression profiling with a concordance rate of 93%

 

Note: GCET = a GC marker, FOXP1 = non GC marker

3 common chromosomal translocations in DLBCL NOS

●        3q27/BCL6 (∼ 30%)

●        t(14;18)/BCL2  (∼ 20%)

●        8q24/MYC(∼ 10%)

○        MYC translocations impart poorer prognosis

○        Double-hit lymphoma imparts very poor prognosis (separate category)

 

Top Differential Diagnoses for DLBCL NOS

●        Burkitt lymphoma

●        High-grade B-cell lymphoma: NOS or double-hit lymphoma

●        Follicular lymphoma (grade 3B)

●        Plasmablastic lymphoma

 

What is the prognosis of DLBCL?

●        5-year survival is 65% in RCHOP era

 

What are clinical features associated with bad prognosis in DLBCL?

●        Bulky disease >10cm

●        Male

●        Vitamin D deficiency

●        Low BMI

●        Elevated free light chains

●        IgM monoclonal protein

●        Low lymphocyte/monocyte count

●        Concordant BM involvement

What is the IPI for DLBC?

APLES

●        Age > 60

●        Performance status >1

●        LDH > ULN

●        Extra-nodal sites >1

●        Stage III or IV

 

Do the morphological variants impact outcome in DLBCL?

●        Not reproducibly

 

Does immunophenotype impact outcome in DLBCL

●        GCB does better than ABC

●        De novo CD5+ has prognostic importance (high risk)

●        MYC + BCL2+ protein expression may be worse

●        Note: CD30+ does better!

 

What genetic mutations are associated with worse survival in DLBCL?

●        MYC

●        BCL2

●        9p21 deletion

●        trisomy 3

 

What is the most common rearrangement in ABC versus GCB?

●        GCB: BCL2 rearrangement

●        ABC: BCL6 rearrangement

 

What is the most common copy number alteration in ABC?

·       BCL2 gains

 

What % of DLBCL NOS, Immunoblastic present in stage IV?

●        At least 1/3 of cases

Is BM involvement by DLBCL NOS, immunoblastic variant more or less frequent than low-grade B-cell lymphomas?

●        BM involvement = less frequent than low-grade B-cell lymphomas

●        Involvement in 10-20% of cases

 

Clinical features of DLBCL NOS, immunoblastic variant

●        Frequent B symptoms (fever, night sweats, or weight loss)

●        Stage IV in ∼ 1/3 of cases

●        Bone marrow involvement in 10-20% of patients

 

Standard therapy for DLBCL NOS?

●        R-CHOP regimen

○        Rituximab + cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, Oncovin/vincristine, and prednisone

 

DDx for DLBCL NOS, immunoblastic variant?

●        DLBCL, centroblastic variant

●        DLBCL, anaplastic variant

●        Plasmablastic lymphoma

●        Primary cutaneous DLBCL, leg type

●        ALK(+) large B-cell lymphoma

●        High grade B cell lymphoma (previously called: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features between DLBCL and Burkitt lymphoma)

 

What are the differential diagnoses of large-cell neoplasms with a prominent sinusoidal pattern of nodal involvement? From Jaffe

●        Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

○        Sinusoidal DLBCL, CD30+

○        Microvillous DLBCL

○        ALK+ large B-cell lymphoma

○        DLBCL, NOS (uncommon)

●        ALCL, ALK+

●        ALCL, ALK-

●        Histiocytic neoplasm or tumor like conditions

○        LCH

○        Rosai-Dorfman disease

○        Histiocytic sarcoma (uncommon)

●        Metastatic non-hematolymphoid malignancies( e.g melanoma, germ-cell tumors)

 

What are the major DDx of DLBCL with CD5 expression?

●        Mantle cell lymphoma, blastoid or pleomorphic variant

●        Paraimmunoblastic variant of CLL

●        DLBCL arising in CLL (Richters syndrome)

●        Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma

●        Splenic DLBCL

●        De novo CD5+ DLBCL

 

T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma

T-cell/histiocyterich large B-cell lymphoma (THRLBCL) is an aggressive B-cell lymphoma with < 10% large neoplastic B cells, scattered in a diffuse background rich in T cells and histiocytes, and with a virtual absence of small B cells. A subset of cases show marked clinical, immunophenotypic, and molecular overlap with nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma (NLPHL).

 

What is T-cell/Histiocyte-rich Large B-cell Lymphoma?

 

●        Large B-cell lymphoma characterized by scattered large malignant B cells → representing < 10% of total cell population

●        The remainder of cellular infiltrate consists of → T cells and histiocytes

THRLBCL Prognosis?

 

●        Poor

●        Usually aggressive and often refractory to chemotherapy

THRLBCL, Extranodal sites of involvement?

 

●        Liver, spleen, and bone marrow often involved

THRLBCL Histologic findings?

 

●        Diffuse pattern of infiltration (by definition, NOT nodular)

●        Large B cell lymphoma cells (<10% of the population) have variable cytologic features:

○        Can resemble centroblasts or immunoblasts, or HRS-like cells

○        CD20 (+) confirms they are B cells (usually strong)

●        Reactive cells → small T lymphocytes and histiocytes:

○        Histiocyte number can be variable

●        No granulocytes or plasma cells

 

 

THRLBCL, Infiltration pattern?

 

●        Diffuse

 

Large lymphoma cells have variable cytologic features including (what can they look like)?

 

●        Centroblasts

●        Immunoblasts

●        HRS-like cells

Reactive cells are composed of what 2 types?

 

  1. Small T lymphocytes
  2. Histiocytes

 

●        Note: No small B cells

○        If the inflammatory infiltrate surrounding the large atypical cells is composed of CD20(+) small mature B cells, you need to rethink the Dx (e.g. NLPHL)

○        Similarly, if the infiltration pattern is nodular, consider NLPHL

●        Histiocyte number can be variable


Large lymphoma cells are B cells with what immunophenotype?

 

●        Positive for CD20, CD79a, Pax-5, and other pan-B-cell markers

●        CD45 positive

●        Bcl-6 usually positive; CD10 variable

●        CD30 & CD15

○        CD30 often negative → but can be positive in subset

○        CD15 negative

●        Negative for T-cell antigens

B cells are CD30 pos or neg?

 

●        CD30 often negative but can be positive in subset

Immunophenotype by IHC for reactive T cells in THRLBCL?

 

●        T cells CD3(+), CD5(+)

●        T cells often show cytotoxic immunophenotype

○        CD8(+), TIA-1(+), granzyme B(-)

●        Histiocytes CD68(+)

●        A follicular dendritic cell stain (CD21 or CD23) will show lack of nodular architecture.

THRLBCL top Differential Diagnoses?

 

●        Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (rare neoplastic cells in background inflammatory cells)

●        Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma (main differential)

●        Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, NOS (large B cell lymphoma)

●        Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (large CD30+ cell lymphoma)

 

Note: Cases fairly identical to THRLBCL can occur as transformation of NLPHL

 

*Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma/high grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangement

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma / high-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements (DLBCL/HGBCL-MYC/BCL2) is an aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma with structural chromosomal aberrations with breakpoints at both MYC and BCL2 loci.

 

What is the old term used in WHO4R?

●        High grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangement (double/dual hit lymphoma)

●        high-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC, BCL2, and BCL6 rearrangements

 

What 3 types of HGBL are included in WHO5?

●        DLBCL/HGBL with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements

●        HGBL, NOS

●        HGBL with 11q aberrations

 

What are the subtypes in this category?

●        DLBCL/HGBCL-MYC/BCL2 without BCL6 rearrangement

●        DLBCL/HGBCL-MYC/BCL2 with BCL6 rearrangement

●        DLBCL/HGBCL-MYC/BCL2 (with or without BCL6 rearrangement) with TdT expression

 

What is the morphologic pattern of this entity?

●        Diffuse pattern: starry-sky appearance common

●        Many apoptotic cells and mitotic cells

●        May exhibit a spectrum of morphologic patterns resembling DLBCL, BL-like, LBL/leukemia like

 

What is the immunophenotypic feature?

●        CD10+, BCL6+, CD38br, MYC+, BCL2+

●        Pan B markers +

●        Lack surface Ig

●        Negative TdT

 

Should FL 3b and B-ALL with MYC and BCL2 be included or excluded?

●        Exclude

●        HGBL may be associated with underlying FL

ALK-pos large B-cell lymphoma

Anaplastic lymphoma kinasepositive large B-cell lymphoma (ALK+ LBCL) is a diffuse, monomorphic neoplasm of large B cells with a plasmablastic immunophenotype and ALK expression due to ALK rearrangement.

 

ALK(+) Large B-Cell Lymphoma definition?

 

●        B-cell lymphoma with a diffuse pattern composed of immunoblasts or plasmablasts that express ALK and carry ALK gene abnormalities

 

ALK+LBCL was called what in WHO 2008?

 

●        ALK+ Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma

●        Diffuse has been replaced by large in 2016 WHO

 

ALK gene is located on what chromosome?       

 

●        Chromosome 2p23

Is ALK+LBCL common or rare?   

 

●        Rare; ∼ 184 cases reported

●        (Rare as hens teeth)

Key transforming event in ALK+LBCL?   

 

●        ALK gene abnormalities at chromosome 2p23

●        Result in formation of fusion genes and ALK overexpression

Most common site of involvement by ALK+LBCL?             

 

●        Lymph nodes are most commonly involved and biopsied (~ 75%)

What % of ALK+LBCL patients have stage III or IV disease?            

 

●        60-70% of patients

ALK+LBCL clinical course & survival?     

 

●        Aggressive clinical course and poor survival

●        5-year overall survival is ∼ 25%

ALK+LBCL Microscopic LN features?

             

●        Partial or diffuse effacement of lymph node architecture

●        Lymphoma cells infiltrate sinusoids in many cases

●        Monomorphic, large immunoblast-like cells or plasma blast like cells (plasmacytoid differentiation)

 



ALK+LBCL characteristic immunophenotype by IHC?             

 

●        ALK strongly positive

●        Plasma cell markers!

●        EMA[QZ3] (+), CD138(+), VS38c[QZ4] (+), BLIMP1[QZ5] (+), XBP1[QZ6] (+)

●        Cytoplasmic IgA[QZ7] (+) in > 95% of cases

●        CD30 (+) in 15%, EBER(-)

●        Pan-B- and pan-T-cell markers negative

 

What is BLIMP1?

 

●        B lymphocyte-induced maturation protein-1 (Blimp-1)

●        A transcriptional repressor of the IFNbeta promoter

●        In the B cell lineage, Blimp-1 is required for:

○        Development of immunoglobulin-secreting cells

○        Maintenance of long-lived plasma cells (LLPCs)

●        Direct targets of Blimp-1 and the transcriptional cascades Blimp-1 initiates to trigger plasmacytic differentiation

●        Also plays a role in T cell homeostasis and development

3 fusion genes associated with ALK+LBCL?         

 

●        1) Clathrin heavy-chain gene (CLTC)-ALK t(2;17)

●        2) Nucleophosmin (NPM)-ALK t(2;5)

●        3) SEC31A-ALK - cryptic insertion of ALK into 4q22-24

●        All result in overexpression of ALK protein

ALK+LBCL most common ALK gene abnormality?             

 

●        Most common: CLTC-ALK t(2;17)

What is ALK?    

 

●        Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)

●        aka ALK tyrosine kinase receptor or CD246 Enzyme encoded by the ALK gene

3 ways the ALK gene can be oncogenic?

 

●        1) By forming a fusion gene with any of several other genes

●        2) By gaining additional gene copies

●        3) Through mutations of the actual DNA code for the ALK gene

ALK+LBCL Top Differential Diagnoses?  

 

Think of B cell lymphomas with plasmacytic differentiation and ALK+ neoplasms

 

●        Plasmablastic lymphoma (many overlap: immunoblastic/plasmablastic/CD138/38+/20-; PBL CD30+EBER+HIV+)

●        DLBCL immunoblastic variant

●        Plasmacytoma/plasma cell myeloma

●        ALK(+) anaplastic large cell lymphoma

 

Large B-cell Lymphoma with IRF4 mutation

Large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) with IRF4 rearrangement (LBCL-IRF4-R) is a de novo mature B-cell lymphoma with a follicular and/or diffuse growth pattern, defined by strong expression of IRF4 (MUM1), usually due to an IG::IRF4 translocation.


What is Large B-cell Lymphoma with IRF4 mutation?

●        Uncommon subtype of Large B cell lymphoma that can have variable histo topography

○        Entirely diffuse, follicular and diffuse, or entirely follicular

○        Characterized by strong expression of IRF4/MUM1, usually with IRF4 mutation


Who gets Large B-cell Lymphoma with IRF4 mutation?

●        Children/young adults

●        Age range 4-79 years

●        Median age 12

●        M-F


What is the localization of Large B-cell Lymphoma with IRF4 mutation?

●        Predominantly Waldeyer ring or Head and neck LN

●        Stage I-II localized disease common


How common is Large B-cell Lymphoma with IRF4 mutation?

●        0.05% of DLBCL

 

What is the cellular morphology of Large B-cell Lymphoma with IRF4 mutation?

 

●        Medium-sized to large cells

●        Chromatin is more open than typically seen in centrocytes - small basophilic nucleoli

●        Mitotic figures are infrequent

●        Starry-sky pattern is absent

What is the growth pattern of Large B-cell Lymphoma with IRF4 mutation?

●         1. Follicular

○        Large a back-to-back follicles

○        Absent or attenuated mantle zones

●        2. Follicular and diffuse

●        3. Diffuse

●        Difference from pediatric-type FL - the follicles lack serpiginous configuration and starry sky

What is the immunophenotype of Large B-cell Lymphoma with IRF4 mutation?

●        Mature B-cells

○        CD20, CD79a, Pax5

●        IRF4/MUM1 strong

●        BCL6+

●        BCL2 & CD10 in 2/3rds

●        Ki67 high

●        PRDM1/BLIMP1 negative

 

What is the mutation in Large B-cell Lymphoma with IRF4 mutation?

●        Cryptic rearrangement of → IRF4 with IGH in most cases: t(6;14)

●        Rarely with light chains

●        May also have BCL6 rearrangement, but lack BCL2 or MYC rearrangement


What is the prognosis of Large B-cell Lymphoma with IRF4 mutation?
 

●        Favourable after immunochemotherapy

 

High-grade B-cell lymphoma with 11q

What is Burkitt-like Lymphoma with 11q aberration?         

 

●        Morphologically & mostly phenotypically similar to Burkitts

●        Lacks MYC rearrangement

●        Has 11q alteration

●        Ie It looks just like BL, but lacks the characteristic molecular lesion, and has a different genetic abnormality


What is the 11q aberration in Burkitt-like?         

 

●        11q alteration characterized by:

○        Proximal gains (blue)

○        Telomeric losses (red)

●        Specifically - interstitial gains and losses in distal 11q23/24

 


What is the morphology of Burkitt-like Lymphoma with 11q aberration?         

 

●        Similar to BL

○        High mitotic index

○        Starry sky pattern

●        Certain degree of cytological pleomorphism

●        Occasional follicular pattern

●        Frequent nodal presentation


What is the clinical course of Burkitt-like Lymphoma with 11q aberration?         

 

●        Similar to BL

●        Only a limited number of reported cases

 

What are lymphomas associated with MYC abnormalities?

 

●        BL (90-100%)

●        HGBL-DH (100%)

●        HGBL-NOS (30-50%)

●        Plasmablastic lymphoma (50%)

●        Myeloma

●        De Novo DLBCL 5-10% (not double hit lymphoma)

●        Rare :

○        Transformed CLL and MCL

○        TdT+ precursor B-cell lymphomas leukemias with double hit!

 

Lymphomatoid granulomatosis

Lymphomatoid granulomatosis (LYG) is an EBV-associated angiocentric and angiodestructive B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder involving extranodal sites, composed of EBV-positive atypical large B cells usually admixed with a large number of reactive T cells. It occurs in patients lacking evidence of inborn or acquired immune deficiency/dysregulation other than immunosenescence.

 

What is Lymphomatoid Granulomatosis?

             

●        Extranodal, predominantly pulmonary, angiocentric &/or angiodestructive EBV(+) B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder

○        Neoplastic B-cells are EBV(+)

○        Many admixed T cells, histiocytes, ± plasma cells

●        The lesion has a spectrum of histological grade and clinical aggressiveness, which is related to the proportion of large B cells.

[QZ8] 

[QZ9] 

Etiology of LYG?            

 

●        Underlying immunosuppression in a subset of patients

●        HIV infection

●        High dose chemo

 

What drives lymphomatoid granulomatosis?

●        EBV!     

 

What can predispose patients to Lymphomatoid granulomatosis?

 

  • Congenital and acquired causes
    • Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
    • HIV infection
    • High-dose chemotherapy
    • Post solid organ transplant immunosuppression

 

Is LYG more common in the elderly or young?  

 

●        Most frequent in young adults (~ 30-40 years)

●        More common in men

LYG most frequent site of involvement? Other sites?

 

●        Pulmonary involvement in 90%

○        Multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules (most frequent) -> differ with DLBCL in lung -> usually solitary nodule

●        Other sites:
- Brain (CNS ~ 30%)
- Kidneys ~30%
- Liver ~30%
- Skin ~ 40-50%
- Upper GI

●        RARE: LN and spleen     

 

What are the clinical features of Lymphomatoid granulomatosis?

 

●        Respiratory tract Sx

○        Cough, dyspnea, chest pain

●        Constitutional Sx

○        Fever, malaise, weight loss

○        Neurological Sx

○        Arthralgias

 

What are the macroscopic features of Lymphomatoid granulomatosis?

●        1. Pulmonary nodules of varying size

○        Bilateral in mid/lower lungs

○        May have central necrosis/cavitation

●        2. Skin lesion - diverse

○        Nodular, plaques, maculopapular             

What are the microscopic features of Lymphomatoid granulomatosis?

●        Angiocentric, nodular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate

●        Small lymphocytes, histiocytes, plasma cells, and variable number of large lymphoid cells

●        Lymphocytic "vasculitis" with transmural invasion

○         ± Necrosis

○        Lymphocytic = no granulocytes

●        Variable # of EBV+ cells showing atypia (Hodgkin cell-like) in background

●        Skin lesions:

○        prominent granulomatous reaction

 

(MUST distinguish from NK/T-cell lymphoma which has an angiodestructive growth pattern too)      

 



What histologic finding in LYG correlates with prognosis?

 

●        Number of large EBV(+) large B cells correlates with prognosis

LYG grading based on number of?

 

●        EBV(+) large B cells

●        Extent of necrosis

 

What is the grading of LyG?

 

●        Gr 1:
- Polymorphous infiltrate without cytological atypia
- Large transformed cells are rare
- Focal necrosis only
- <5 per HPF of EBER+ cells

●        Gr 2:
- Occasional large cells/immunoblasts in polymphorous background
- Small clusters of these large cells with CD20+
- Necrosis common
- EBER shows 5-20 per HPF on average (up to 50 focally)

●        Gr 3:
- Inflammatory background
- Large atypical B cells CD20+ forming large aggregates
- Hodgkin-like cells often present
- Extensive necrosis
- EBER >50 cells per HPF, with some confluent sheet spossible

Note: A uniform population of large atypical EBV+ cells should be classified as EBV+ DLBCL, NOS     

What are the 3 LYG grades and their treatment?             

 

●        Grades 1 and 2 of uncertain malignant potential

○        Some cases may regress spontaneously or respond to interferon-α 2b therapy

●        Grade 3 considered subtype of DLBCL

○        LYG grade 3 should be distinguished from grade 1 and grade 2 for treating purposes

○        Grade 3 LYG is treated as DLBCL

 

Effective treatment for grade 1 and 2 LYG

 

●        Interferon alpha 2 B

Effective treatment for grade 3 LYG

 

●        As for DLBCL (R-CHOP)

Immunophenotype for large cells seen in LYG?

 

●        EBV+ larger cells cells:
- CD45+, CD20+, CD30+, CD15neg
- LMP1 pos in larger cells, EBV+

●        - Monoclonal IgH Rearrangement

●        Background lymphocytes are CD3+ T cells, with CD4>CD8  

●        Relates to proportion of EBV+ B cells relative to background

IHC findings in LYG?

 

●        Positive for pan-B-cell markers

○        CD19, CD20, CD22, CD79-a, pax-5

●        CD45/LCA(+), CD30(+/-)

●        EBV-LMP1(+/-), CD15(-)

●        Rare cytoplasmic monotypic Ig light chain in large B cells

●        Smaller cells are reactive T cells: CD3(+), CD4 > CD8

●        Histiocytes positive for CD68, CD163

●        Plasma cells express polytypic Ig

What are the small cells seen in LYG?

 

●        Smaller reactive cells are T cells: CD4 > CD8

Are monoclonal IGH rearrangements seen in LYG cases?

 

●        Yes

●        40% grade 2

●        70% grade 3

LYG Top Differential Diagnoses?            

 

●        Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener granulomatosis)

●        Classic Hodgkin lymphoma

●        Peripheral T-cell lymphoma

●        Extranodal NK-/T-cell lymphoma

●        DLBCL, not otherwise specified

●        Fungal or mycobacterial infections

●        Necrotizing sarcoidosis

 

EBV-pos diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

What are the EBV-associated B-cell Lymphoproliferative Disorders? (8)

 

  1. Burkitt lymphoma
  2. Classical Hodgkin lymphoma
  3. Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorders
  4. Lymphomas associated with HIV infection
  5. Primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the central nervous system
  6. EBV(+) diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, NOS
  7. EBV+ mucocutaneous ulcer
  8. HHV8(+) primary effusion lymphoma
  9. Plasmablastic lymphoma
  10. Lymphomatoid granulomatosis
  11. Primary Effusion Lymphoma

What are the EBV-associated T-/NK-cell Lymphoproliferative Disorders? (3)

 

  1. Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, NOS
    1. Ie. Nodal PTCL, EBV+
  2. Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma
  3. Extranodal T-/NK-cell lymphoma, nasal type
  4. Aggressive NK Cell Leukemia
  5. EBV+ Lymphoproliferative disorders of Childhood
    1. Systemic EBV+ T cell lymphoma of Childhood
    2. Chronic Active EBV of T and NK-cell type, systemic form
    3. Hydroa vacciniforme-like lymphoproliferative disorder (Cutaneous CAEBV)
    4. Severe mosquito bite allergy (Cutaneous CAEBV)

Define EBV+ Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma, NOS

 

●        DLBCL infected by EBV occurring in:

○        Patients without history of immunodeficiency or lymphoma

○        No age cutoff in current (2016) WHO classification (> 50 years old in 2008)

○        These tumors exhibit a broad morphologic spectrum from polymorphous and Hodgkin-like lesions to monotonous DLBCL

○        Do not fall into other EBV-pos entities: LYG, EBV+ mucocutaneous ulcer, etc.

EBV(+) DLBCL, NOS Median age?

 

●        70 years (range: 45-92 years)

Are patients with EBV(+) DLBCL,NOS sick or healthy prior to diagnosis?

 

●        Affected patients are relatively healthy prior to diagnosis

●        Patients have no evidence of immunodeficiency

In EBV(+) DLBCL, NOS,  do patients have lymphadenopathy? 

 

●        Extranodal mass ± lymphadenopathy in ~ 70%

●        Only lymphadenopathy in ~ 30%

EBV(+) DLBCL, NOS  median survival?

 

●        2 years

●        In Asia, EBV(+) DLBCL has a poorer prognosis than EBV(-) DLBCL

EBV(+) DLBCL, NOS - 2 morphologic subtypes?  

 

●        Polymorphous and monomorphous (large cell lymphoma)

●        Represent morphologic spectrum

●        No clinical or prognostic relevance

EBV(+) DLBCL, NOS Microscopic Pathology?

 

●        Effaces architecture of extranodal site &/or lymph node

●        Sheets of necrosis; often with geographic pattern

●        These tumors exhibit a broad morphologic spectrum from polymorphous and Hodgkin-like lesions to monotonous DLBCL

 

 

For EBV(+) DLBCL-E, what IHC marker is associated with poorer prognosis in Western countries

 

●        CD30 expression

EBV(+) DLBCL has a better, or worse prognosis than EBV(-) DLBCL in the USA and Europe?

 

●        In Asia, EBV(+) DLBCL has a poorer prognosis than EBV(-) DLBCL

●        EBV(+) DLBCL is not associated with poorer prognosis in

○        United States and Europe or young patients

2 subtypes of EBV(+) DLBCL,NOS?

 

●        Polymorphous and large cell lymphoma (monomorphous)

●        Represent a morphologic spectrum

●        No clinical or prognostic relevance

EBV(+) DLBCL, NOS positive IHC stains?

 

●        CD20(+), CD22(+), CD79α(+), pax-5(+)

●        IRF-4/MUM1(+), CD30(+/-)

●        Ki67 with high proliferation index

EBV(+) DLBCL, NOS --> Ki-67 (MIB1) shows?      

 

●        High proliferation index

EBV(+) DLBCL, NOS →  Lymphoma cells have EBV type ____ ? latency pattern

 

●        Type III latency pattern

EBV(+) DLBCL, NOS Top Differential Diagnoses?

 

●        DLBCL, not otherwise specified

●        Plasmablastic lymphoma

●        Classical Hodgkin lymphoma

In EBV(+) DLBCL, NOS, what cutoff for EBER positivity is commonly used?

 

●        EBER(+):

○        No defined cutoff

○        Many studies use 20%

●        EBER highlights more cells than LMP1

EBV(+) DLBCL, NOS - poor prognostic factors?

 

●        Age >45

○        Particularly Age >70

●        Monomorphic pattern

○        TCHR LBL-like pattern do better

●        CD30+, EBNA2+ may do worse

●        B-Symptoms

 

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with chronic inflammation

What is DLBCL associated with chronic inflammation?

 

●        Lymphoid neoplasm occurring in the setting of → long-standing chronic inflammation

●        Association with EBV

●        Most cases involve body cavities or narrow spaces

 

What is the prototypical Lymphoma of DLBCL associated with chronic inflammation? Are there any others that are outlined in the WHO?

 

●        1) Pyothorax-associated lymphoma (PAL) is the prototypical form

○        > 90% of cases of DLBCL-CI

○        Develops in the pleural cavity of patients with longstanding pyothorax.

●        2) Fibrin-associated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

○        An unusual form of DLBCL with chronic inflammation

○        Not mass-forming and does not directly produce symptoms

○        Discovered incidentally on histological examination of surgical pathology specimens excised for various pathologies other than lymphoma

○        Indolent

○        The cells are found in clusters or individually in fibrin clot without a stromal background

○        Occur in otherwise immunocompetent patients

 

What is Pyothorax-associated lymphoma (PAL)

 

●        Large B-cell lymphoma

●        Occurs in context of longstanding chronic inflammation from pyothorax

○        Long latency period from pyothorax until PA

 

Name 4 B cell lymphomas occurring in fluids

 

●        (1) Primary effusion lymphoma (PEL) or (2) pyothorax associated lymphomas (PAL).

○        These are usually EBV+ but occur in specific clinicopathologic settings such as HIV infection for PEL or in patients who have a long history of pyothorax (PAL)

●        (3) Fibrin-associated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

○        These lymphomas have been now reported in a variety of settings including cardiac prostheses, atrial myxoma, metallic implants, cysts, and pseudocyst

○        These are usually EBV+

●        (4) Breast implant associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL)

○        This CD30+ T-cell lymphoma occurs in the setting of seroma fluid around a silicone breast implant and is EBV-negative.

 

Where do most cases of DLBCL-CI occur?

 

●        In body cavities or narrow spaces

Causes of pyothorax in patients who develop PAL

 

●        Surgical artificial pneumothorax → to treat pulmonary tuberculosis

What is the etiology of DLBCL-CI

 

  1. Chronic Inflammation:
    1. Chronic pyothorax precedes PAL type of DLBCL-CI
  2. Infectious Agents:
    1. EBV is present in most cases of DLBCL-CI
  3. Other:
    1. Metallic implants in bones/joints, surgical mesh implant, longstanding hydrocele
    2. Chronic osteomyelitis; splenic false cyst, atrial myxoma

Explain the possible roles of chronic inflammation in pathogenesis of PAL

 

●        Generation of reactive oxygen species

●        Local immunosuppression

●        EBV(+) B cells secrete various cytokines (e.g., IL-10)

●        Interleukin-6 is possible autocrine growth factor

PAL appears to arise from what cells?

 

●        Post-germinal center B cells

●        Lymphoma cells often have crippling IGH mutations

Patients with PAL present with what symptoms?

 

●        Localized symptoms

○        Chest/back pain, tumor/swelling of chest wall

●        B symptoms, cough, dyspnea, hemoptysis

What is the relationship between onset of pyothorax until PAL?

 

●        Chronic pyothorax precedes PAL type of DLBCL-CI

●        Very long latency period from onset of pyothorax until PAL

○        19-67 years; median 43 years

EBV is present in most cases of DLBCL-CI and has what type of latency pattern?  

 

●        EBV(+) in type III latency pattern in most cases

●        Latency III pattern → indicates an immune suppressed environment

 

 

 


 



 

What are the general microscopic features of DLBCL-CI?

 

●        Centroblastic, immunoblastic, or plasmablastic

●        Diffuse growth pattern composed of sheets of large cells

●        ± massive necrosis; ± angiocentric growth pattern

●        High mitotic rate common

●        Large cells can exhibit centroblastic or immunoblastic features

●        ± plasmacytoid differentiation

●        Rare cases exhibit anaplastic features

Does DLBCL-CI have a GC or non-GC phenotype?

 

●        Non-germinal center B-cell immunophenotype

●        IRF-4/MUM1(+)

●        CD10(-), Bcl-6(-)

Infectious agent associated with DLBCL-CI?

 

●        EBV(+), HHV8(-)

 

DLBCL-CI immunophenotype?

 

●        Non-germinal center B-cell immunophenotype

●        CD20(+), CD79a(+), pax-5(+), IRF-4/MUM1(+)

●        CD10(-), Bcl-6(-) LMP1(+), EBER(+), HHV8(-)

●        Cases with plasmacytoid differentiation can be CD138(+), monotypic Ig(+/-)

Top Differential Diagnoses for PAL?

 

●        Fibrin-associated EBV(+) large B-cell lymphoma

●        Primary effusion lymphoma

●        Systemic lymphomas involving body cavity lining

○        Eg. Breast implant associated ALCL

●        EBV(+) DLBCL of elderly

 

Fibrin-associated large B-cell lymphoma

pending

Fluid overload-associated large B-cell lymphoma

pending

Plasmablastic lymphoma

What is Plasmablastic Lymphoma?

             

●        Diffuse neoplasm of large neoplastic cells with immunoblastic or plasmablastic cytologic features

●        Immunophenotype overlaps with neoplastic plasma cells

○        CD38(+), CD138(+), CD20(-)

●        Aggressive clinical course

●        Poor prognosis

Plasmablastic lymphoma was initially described as a rare variant of?

 

●        DLBCL involving oral cavity

●        15 of 16 patients were immunodeficient as a result of HIV infection

Plasmablastic lymphoma occurs in what patient group?

 

●        Immunodeficient patients

○        HIV most commonly

●        Subset occurs in immunocompetent


Plasmablastic lymphoma infectious associations?

 

●        EBV positive

●        Strongly associated with *HIV infection*

●        Has been reported in patients with immunodeficiency due to other causes

○        Example: Post-transplantation

Plasmablastic lymphoma frequently originates in what site?        

 

●        Mucosa of oral cavity

●        Non-oral cases also occur

Is Plasmablastic lymphoma a nodal or extranodal disease?            

 

●        Predominantly extranodal disease → oral mucosa most commonly

●        Nodal disease in 10%

Plasmablastic lymphoma microscopic features?

 

●        Large neoplastic cells with variable degree of immunoblastic or plasmablastic features

●        Immunoblastic morphology in oral cavity of HIV positive patient

●        "Starry sky" pattern frequent

●        High mitotic and apoptotic rate

 



Plasmablastic lymphoma immunophenotype? 

 

●        Pan-B-cell antigens: Weak or absent CD20 (-)

○        If strong B-cell markers, it is not called plasmablastic lymphoma (it would be DLBCL)

●        Plasma cell markers (+) [CD38(+), CD138(+)

●        EBER(+), HHV8(-)

●        CD56 + in 25% (expression of CD56 should raise suspicion for underlying plasma cell myeloma)

●        Monoclonal IgH gene rearrangements

●        High proliferation index (Ki-67)

●        MYc (+)

Plasmablastic lymphoma Pan-B-cell antigens are (-) or (+)?  

 

●        Weak or absent (-)

●        CD20 (-)

Plasmablastic lymphoma Plasma cell markers are (-) or (+)?  

 

●        Positive (+)

●        CD38(+), CD138(+)

Plasmablastic lymphoma EBER, HHV8 results?  

 

●        EBER(+), HHV8(-)

Plasmablastic lymphoma: Monoclonal IgH gene rearrangements present or absent?      

 

●        Present

●        Monoclonal IgH gene rearrangements

Plasmablastic lymphoma: Ki-67 result?

 

●        High proliferation index (Ki-67)

Plasmablastic lymphoma Top Differential Diagnoses?             

 

●        Large B-cell lymphoma, immunoblastic variant

●        Plasmablastic plasma cell myeloma

●        Multicentric Castleman disease, HHV8 positive

●        ALK(+) large B-cell lymphoma

●        Melanoma
