Quick mental algorithm

Plasmablastic morphology + CD138/MUM1+ + CD20/PAX5−

→ HHV8+ → PEL
→ ALK+ → ALK+ LBCL
→ EBER+ → strongly consider PBL
→ EBER− → PBL vs plasmablastic myeloma → look for myeloma-defining clinical features

 

Primary large B-cell lymphoma of immune-privileged sites

What is Primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of CNS (DLBCL-CNS)?         

 

●        DLBCL confined to CNS (brain, spinal cord, leptomeninges, but not DURA!) &/or intraocular location

○        Immunocompromised patients excluded from this category

○        Intraocular lymphomas included as part of WHO classification

●        Primary vitreoretinal lymphoma

○        Lymphoma confined to intraocular region; usually DLBCL

○        a.k.a. primary intraocular lymphoma

What patient group is excluded from a diagnosis of DLBCL-CNS?

 

●        Immunocompromised patients excluded from this category

2 possibilities for Origin of Lymphoma-Initiating Cells in DLBCL-CNS?

 

  1. Benign systemic B cells entering CNS under physiologic conditions
  2. Dissemination of systemic lymphoma cells
    1. Extra-CNS disease eliminated by immune response
    2. Lymphoma cells survive in immune-privileged microenvironment of CNS

Clinical Issues for DLBCL-CNS?

 

●        Neuropsychiatric signs and symptoms

●        Raised intracranial pressure

●        Intraocular involvement:

○        Blurred vision and floaters

Imaging findings for DLBCL-CNS?

 

●        Single or multiple bilateral, symmetrical, periventricular lesions

●        Homogeneous contrast enhancement

Microscopic features of DLBCL-CNS?

 

●        Diffuse pattern; may be patchy

●        Single-cell apoptosis and geographic necrosis

●        Large cells; usually centroblastic

●        Often perivascular &/or angioinvasive (image)

●        Intermixed reactive lymphocytes, histiocytes and astrocytes

 



Microscopic features of Corticosteroid effects in DLBCL-CNS?

 

●        Extensive necrosis, sheets of macrophages

DLBCL-CNS Immunophenotype

 

●        B-cell antigens (+)

○        CD19, CD20, CD22, CD79a, pax-5

●        CD45/LCA(+)

●        Bcl-6(+), Bcl-2(+)

●        IRF-4/MUM1(+)

●        Usually CD10 negative

●        CD10(+) in 10-20% of cases (More likely ABC)

○        Query CNS involvement by systemic DLBCL if CD10 is positive

●        Proliferation index (Ki-67) usually high (> 50%)

●        Myeloid-associated antigens (-)

●        T-cell antigens (-)



Molecular findings in DLBCL-CNS?          

 

●        Monoclonal IGH rearrangements

●        Bi-allelic loss of CDKN2A/p16 in ∼ 60-90%

●        BCL6 (3q27) dysregulated in 20-50%

●        6q deletions common

●        Mutations of MYD88 in ∼ 80% and CD79B in ∼ 60%

●        Copy number changes of chromosome 9p24.1

○        Locus of PD-L1 and PD-L2

DLBCL-CNS Top Differential Diagnoses

 

●        DLBCL of brain associated with HIV infection

●        Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma

●        High-grade astrocytoma

●        Poorly differentiated carcinoma

Role of Flow Cytometry in DLBCL-CNS

 

May demonstrate

●        Ig light chain restriction

●        ± aberrant immunophenotype

●        Particularly helpful to confirm diagnosis in

○        Ocular specimen

○        CSF

 

What are the lymphomas at increased risk for CNS involvement?

 

●        DLBCL

○        CD5+ DLBCL

○        Intravascular large B cell lymphoma

○        IgM secreting DLBCL

○        Double expressor DLBCL if ABC subtype

○        DLBCL involving breast, testis, uterus, epidural , kidney/adrenal

●        HGBL with MYC and BCL2 and or BCL6 rearrangement

●        MCL, blastoid variant or Ki67>= 30%

●        PTCL, NOS

●        AITL

●        ALK+ ALCL

 

Primary cutaneous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, leg type

What is Primary Cutaneous Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma, Leg Type?  

 

●        Primary cutaneous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma composed predominantly or exclusively of large transformed B cells (immunoblasts)


PCDLBCL-LT, What mutation is seen in 70% of cases?             

 

●        Activating mutation of MYD88 L265P in ∼ 70% of cases

●        Note most non GCB B cell lymphomas are MYD88 positive

 

 

What is MYD88?

 

●        Myeloid differentiation primary response 88 (MYD88)

○        MYD88 gene provides instructions for making a protein involved in signaling within immune cells.

○        MYD88 protein acts as an adapter

■        Connecting proteins that receive signals from outside the cell → to the proteins that relay signals inside the cell.

○        In particular, MYD88 transfers signals from certain proteins called Toll-like receptors and interleukin-1 (IL-1) receptors, which are important for an early immune response to foreign invaders such as bacteria.

○        In response to signals from these receptors, the MYD88 adapter protein → stimulates signaling molecules that turn on a group of interacting proteins known as nuclear factor-kappa-B (NF-kB).

○        Nuclear factor-kappa-B regulates the activity of multiple genes

■        Including genes that control the body's immune responses and inflammatory reactions.

PCDLBCL-LT composes what % of primary cutaneous B-cell lymphomas?

 

●        20%

Does PCDLBCL, Leg Type only occur in the leg?

 

●        Most cases arise in skin of lower leg

●        ~ 85% of all cases

What % of PCDLBCL-LT do NOT arise in the skin of lower leg? What are the other common locations?

 

●        15% of cases arise in skin of other sites

●        Trunk, arms, head and neck

 

Does PCDLBCL-LT present as a single lesion?

 

●        Single or multiple lesions at time of presentation

PCDLBCL-LT 5 yr survival rate?

 

●        Relapse is common; 50% 5-year survival

Rx for PCDLBCL-LT?

 

●        Treated with systemic R-CHOP

What mutation correlates with an adverse prognosis?        

 

●        MYD88 L265P-activating mutation correlates with adverse prognosis

PCDLBCL-LT characteristic microscopy findings?

 

●        Diffuse pattern of involvement in dermis

●        Monotonous sheets of large immunoblasts or centroblasts

○        No centrocytes (or small B cells) present

●        Few small reactive T cells in background

●        No epidermotropism

PCDLBCL-LT immunophenotype?

 

●        Pan-B-cell antigens(+), Bcl-2(+), Bcl-6(+)

●        MUM1(+), FOXP1(+), IgM(+), CD10(-)

●        Non-GCB

In PCDLBCL-LT, FISH may show rearrangements of what genes?    

 

●        MYC, BCL6, or IGH genes in ∼ 10-20% of cases

PCDLBCL-LT Top Differential Diagnoses?            

 

●        PCDLBCL, not otherwise specified

●        Primary cutaneous follicle center lymphoma (PCFCL) with increased large cells

●        Systemic DLBCL involving skin

●        Plasmablastic lymphoma involving skin

●        Epstein-Barr Virus (+) DLBCL

●        Monomorphic post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder

 

Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma

What is Intravascular Large B-cell Lymphoma? 

 

●        Rare large B-cell lymphoma characterized by → selective intravascular growth

●        Preferential intravascular growth is REQUIRED for diagnosing IVLBCL

○        Extranodal, involves small blood vessels

○        Concomitant and minimal extravascular location of neoplastic cells, usually surrounding involved vessels, can be seen

 

Is IVLBCL associated with LAD? 

 

●        No, Absence of marked lymphadenopathy

●        Splenomegaly may be present

IVLBCL sites of involvement?

 

●        Any extranodal site can be involved

2 major clinical variants of IVLBCL

 

●        Western

○        Central nervous system and skin manifestations predominate

○        Symptoms are related to organs involved

●        Asian

○        Hemophagocytic syndrome (HLH)

○        Bone marrow infiltration, pancytopenia

○        Central nervous system and skin involvement are uncommon

●        These variants show much overlap

IVLBCL  2 predominant clinical manifestations?

 

●        Predominant neurologic and dermatologic manifestations (Western countries)

 



IVLBCL patients from Asia (mainly Japan) preferentially show what clinical feature (Asian variant)

 

●        Hemophagocytic syndrome (HLH)

Typical IHC/immunophenotype findings for IVLBCL

 

●        Pan-B-cell markers (+)

●        Bcl-2(+), MUM1/IRF-4(+)

●        CD5(+) ∼ 30%, other T-cell markers (-)

●        CD10(+) ∼ 10%, Bcl-6(+) ∼ 25%

●        Ki-67 high

 



IVLBCL may show aberrant expression of what T cell marker?            

 

●        CD5

●        30%

IVLBCL Microscopic Pathology findings?             

 

●        Lymphoma cells are mainly located in → lumina of small vessels

●        Sinusoidal involvement of → liver, spleen, and bone marrow

●        Lymphoma cells are large

○        Vesicular chromatin, nucleoli, and frequent mitoses

 

 



IVLBCL Top Differential Diagnoses?

 

●        Peripheral T- or NK-cell lymphomas with intravascular pattern

●        Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma

●        T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia

●        Aggressive NK-cell leukemia/lymphoma

●        Splenic B-cell marginal zone lymphoma

●        Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Mechanisms responsible for selective growth of IVLBCL cells within blood vessel lumina → 2 possible explanations?  

 

●        1) Chemokine-chemokine receptor interactions

○        e.g., CXCL9 (expressed in endothelium) and CXCR3 (expressed in IVLBCL)

●        2) Decreased expression of adhesion molecules on surface of IVLBCL cells

e.g., CD29 and CD54

Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma

Where does PMBCL arise?

·       Anterior-superior mediastinum

·       Extension to the lung, pleura, or pericardium

·       Frequent reginal LN involvement, most commonly the supraclavicular LN

·       BM uncommon

 

What are the clinical features of PMBCL?

·       Cough

·       Dyspnea

·       Superior vena cava syndrom

·       Most stage I or II

·       LDL elevated in 80%

 

Which age/sex group is PMBCL presented in?

·       Predominantly in young adults, 30s

·       Female predominance, M:F 1:2

 

Which hematolymphoid tumor can PMBCL present with?

·       PMBCL can present before, with, or at relapse of NSCHL

 

What GEP can show in PMBCL?

·       Gene expression profiling of PMBCL is significantly overlapping with NSCHL, and markedly distinct from other aggressive BCL

 

What are the molecular hallmarks of PMBCL?

·       NF-kB

·       JAK/STAT signalling pathways

·       Most frequent gene alterations

o   Too many, do not commit to memorize

o   9p24, 16p13 common

o   BCL2, BCL6, MYC-r rare

 

What are the histological features of PMBCL?

·       Diffuse infiltration of neoplastic lymphoid cells, distributed in clusters or sheets, in a fibrotic background (compartmentalizing alveolar fibrosis)

 

What are the morphological features of PMBCL neoplastic cells?

·       Usually medium-sized to large, with abundant pale cytoplasm and round or ovoid nuclei with small nucleoli

·       Other cells: immunoblasts with cohesive proliferation, pleomorphic cells ranging in size with vesicular nuclei, scattered cells resembling HRS cells, paucicellular infiltrate in dense sclerotic stroma, admixed reactive lymphocytes, histiocytes, granulocytes

 

Immunophenotype of PMBCL

·       POSITIVE: CD45, B markers  CD19 CD22 CD20 CD79a, CD30 (weak variable), MUM1, variable BCL2 and BCL6, CD10 <30%

·       NEGATIVE: Immunoglobulin (common) and EBV (can be positive in exceptional cases but does not absolutely exclude the diagnosis)

·       Biomarkers with high specificity and sensitivity >70% for PMBCL - CD23, MAL, CD200, PDL1, PDL2

·       NF-kB, TNF, JAK/STAT pathway activation  c-REL, TRAF1, TNFAIP2, phosphorylated STAT6

 

Differential diagnosis of PMBCL

·       DLBCL (nodal involvement common)

·       Classic Hodgkin lymphoma (admixed inflammatory cells, dense sclerosis [in NSHL], RS cells with prominent nucleoli, CD30+ [strong, uniform], CD20 -/+, CD45-)

·       B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between DLBCL and HL (IHC expression of both B-cell and HL markers)(Grey zone lymphoma)

Mediastinal grey zone lymphoma

What is B-Cell Lymphoma, Unclassifiable, Intermediate between Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma and Classic Hodgkin Lymphoma   

 

●        Lymphoma with morphologic and immunophenotypic features of both → DLBCL and CHL

●        B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between → DLBCL and CHL

○        a.k.a. *gray zone lymphoma*


Clinical presentation of B-Cell Lymphoma, Unclassifiable, Intermediate between Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma and Classic Hodgkin Lymphoma

 

●        Can present at mediastinal or non mediastinal sites

○        Mediastinum:

■        Younger patients and slight female predominance

○        Non mediastinum:

■        Older patients and more often men

How does the clinical course of B-Cell Lymphoma, Unclassifiable, Intermediate between Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma and Classic Hodgkin Lymphoma compare to CHL? 

 

●        More aggressive clinical course than either CHL and PMBL

○        No consensus regarding therapy

Microscopic features of B-Cell Lymphoma, Unclassifiable, Intermediate between Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma and Classic Hodgkin Lymphoma compare to CHL?

   

●        Overlapping histologic features that make classification difficult

○        Can exhibit sheets of large cells resembling DLBCL

○        Can have scattered RS+H-like cells resembling CHL

 

 

 


Immunophenotype for B-Cell Lymphoma, Unclassifiable, Intermediate between Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma and Classic Hodgkin Lymphoma compared to CHL?

   

●        Immunophenotype is discordant with morphologic findings

○        Strong and uniform CD30(+) in all cases

●        CHL-like morphology

○        B-cell antigens (+), CD45/LCA(+), CD15(-)

●        DLBCL-like morphology

○        CD15(+/-), CD45/LCA(-/+)


Top Differential Diagnoses for B-Cell Lymphoma, Unclassifiable, Intermediate between Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma and Classic Hodgkin Lymphoma compared to CHL?

   

●        Nodular sclerosis or mixed cellularity CHL

●        Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma

●        DLBCL at non mediastinal sites

When Morphology Resembles Classic Hodgkin Lymphoma

Which immunophenotypic features support DLBCL/CHL (Gray Zone) rather than true CHL?

Markers suggesting DLBCL/CHL:

·       Strong, uniform B-cell markers:

·       CD20 (bright)

·       CD79a

·       PAX5 (strong, not weak)

·       OCT2, BOB1 (preserved)

·       CD15 negative

·       Often CD30 positive (but with strong B-cell program)

Concept:

·       CHL-like morphology + strong B-cell transcription program = Gray Zone Lymphoma


When Morphology Resembles Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma

Which immunophenotypic features support DLBCL/CHL (Gray Zone) rather than true DLBCL?

Markers suggesting DLBCL/CHL:

·       CD15 positive

·       CD30 strong and uniform

·       Loss or weak expression of B-cell markers (CD20 dim/negative, PAX5 weak)

·       EBV positive (in a subset)

·       Reduced or absent OCT2 / BOB1

Concept:

·       DLBCL-like morphology + Hodgkin-type phenotype = Gray Zone Lymphoma

Mediastinal Gray-zone lymphoma

Q. What is the definition of Mediastinal Gray zone Lymphoma?

·       Mediastinal gray zone lymphoma (MGZL) is a B-cell lymphoma with overlapping features between primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (PMBL) and classic Hodgkin lymphoma (CHL), especially nodular sclerosis CHL (NSCHL).

 

Q. What is the previous term in WHO 2017?

·       B-cell-lymphoma, unclassifiable with features intermediate between DLBCL and classic Hodgkin lymphoma

 

Q. How does MGZL present?

·       Presents as large anterior mediastinal mass

·       Bulky (> 10 cm) in 30-40% of patients

·       Superior vena cava syndrome in 15-20% of patients

·       Supraclavicular lymph nodes can be involved

 

Q. What is the age range of MGZL?

·       20-40 years of age (range: 13-70 years)

·       More aggressive clinical course than either CHL or PMBL

 

Q. What are the microscopic features of MGZL?

·       Can exhibit sheets of large cells resembling diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)

·       Can have scattered RS+H-like cells

·       Many neoplasms show spectrum with DLBCL-like and CHL-like areas

 

Q. What are the ancillary tests to diagnose MGZL?

·       Immunophenotype is discordant with morphologic findings

·       Strong and uniform CD30(+) in almost all cases

·       CHL-like morphology

o   B-cell antigens (+), CD45/LCA(+), CD15(-)

·       DLBCL-like morphology

o   CD15(+/-), CD45/LCA(-/+)

 

Q. What are the differential diagnoses of MGZL?

·       Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma

·       Nodular sclerosis CHL

·       EBV(+) DLBCL

·       DLBCL-NOS

 

Q. Diagnostic Checklist

·       Tumor cell rich

·       RS+H-like cells are often CD20(+), CD15(-)

·       In cases that morphologically resemble DLBCL

o   CD15(+), EBV(+), &/or CD20(-) suggest MGZL

 

Mediastinal Grey Zone Lymphoma new

Q. What is the definition of MGZL?

B-cell neoplasm arising in mediastinum with clinicopathologic, immunophenotypic, and molecular features that overlap with both DLBCL and CHL

 

Q. What is extramediastinal MGZL?

These neoplasms have some morphologic resemblance to MGZL; these neoplasms may be closely related to DLBCL, not otherwise specified (NOS)

 

Q. What is the typical age of MGZL?

20-40 years

 

Q. MGZL presents in male or female?

Predominantly male

 

Q. What are the presentations of MGZL?

Anterior mediastinal mass

·       Supraclavicular lymph nodes can be involved

·       Often direct extension into lungs

·       Superior vena cava syndrome in 15-20% of patients

 

Q. What are the histologic features of MGZL?

·       Areas of confluent sheets of pleomorphic large tumor cells resembling DLBCL

·       Other areas can show scattered large cells, resembling Reed-Sternberg and Hodgkin (RS+H) cells in CHL

·       Variable inflammatory infiltrate in background

o   Typically much less than observed in cases of CHL

·       Mild stromal fibrosis and focal necrosis

o   Necrosis is usually not associated with neutrophils (unlike CHL)

·       Nonnecrotizing granulomas and histiocytes

 

Q. What are the cytologic features of MGZL?

·       Broad spectrum of cytologic features, including

·       Centroblasts, immunoblasts, &/or RS+H-like cells

·       Cells resembling lacunar cells and mummified cells (apoptotic large cells) are common

 

Q. What is the immunohistochemistry profile of MGZL?

·       Mixed immunophenotype with

o   Expression of common markers of CHL

§  CD30(+) (all cases) &/or CD15(+) (in 50-75% cases)

§  pax-5 (+) and IRF4/MUM1(+)

o   Expression of markers usually absent in CHL

§  CD45/LCA(+), CD20(+) (uniformly strong), and CD79a(+)

§  OCT2(+), BOB1(+)

 

Q. T/F. Most cases of MGZL carry monoclonal IGH rearrangement.

T.

 

Q. The most frequent mutated genes in MGZL are

SOCS1 (45%), B2M (45%), TNFAIP3 (35%), GNA13 (35%), NFKIB (30%)

 

Q. Diff dx of MGZL (5)?

1.       Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma

2.       Nodular sclerosis classic Hodgkin lymphoma

3.       EBV+ diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

4.       DLBCL, NOS

5.       ALK+ ALCL

6.       ALK- ALCL

7.       Composite lymphoma

8.       Carcinoma, sarcoma, and melanoma

 

*High-grade B-cell lymphoma, NOS

What is High-Grade B-Cell Lymphoma         

 

Category introduced in 2016 WHO classification

 

●        1st introduction of category of HGBL

●        2 types are specified

○        1) Not otherwise specified (NOS)

○        2) Associated with MYC and BCL2 &/or BCL6 rearrangements (Also known as double- (or triple-) hit lymphoma)


2 types of High-Grade B-Cell Lymphoma         

 

●        1) Not otherwise specified (NOS)

●        2) Associated with MYC and BCL2 &/or BCL6 rearrangements (a.k.a. double- (or triple-) hit lymphoma)


High-Grade B-Cell Lymphoma patients present with?         

 

●        Lymphadenopathy &/or extranodal masses; high stage in > 50%

Does High-Grade B-Cell Lymphoma have an indolent or aggressive clinical course?         

 

●        Aggressive clinical course for most patients


Prognosis for High-Grade B-Cell Lymphoma?         

 

●        Poor

●        Patients respond poorly to standard diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) therapy (R-CHOP)

Microscopic features of High-Grade B-Cell Lymphoma?         

 

●        Histologically aggressive BCL with features that include

○        Diffuse pattern; starry-sky appearance is common (apoptotic bodies)

○        High mitotic rate; many apoptotic cells

●        Tumors exhibit morphologic spectrum and may look like:

○        DLBCL [with double hit]

○        Burkitt lymphoma [but Bcl-2 (+)]

○        "Gray zone" with intermediate and large-sized cells


High-Grade B-Cell Lymphoma immunophenotype?   

 

●        Pan-B-cell antigens (+), Ki-67 high, CD30 (+/-), CD5(-)

●        Double-hit lymphomas: CD10(+), Bcl-2(+), Bcl-6(+)


Is MYC expression common in High-Grade B-Cell Lymphoma?

 

●        MYC is often expressed

○        Most common and bright in double-hit lymphoma

○        ∼ 50% of cases of HGBL-NOS

●        MYC rearrangement occurs in

○        ∼ 30% of HGBL-NOS

○        100% of double-hit lymphomas


What karyotype abnormality is common in High-Grade B-Cell Lymphoma?

   

●        Complex karyotype is common

●        Gene expression profile intermediate between DLBCL and Burkitt lymphoma or similar to Burkitt lymphoma


High-Grade B-Cell Lymphoma top DDx?    

 

Think of other high grade, proliferative B cell neoplasms

 

●        DLBCL-NOS

●        Burkitt lymphoma

●        Lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma

●        Mantle cell lymphoma, blastoid variant

 

WHO algorithm for classifying Aggressive B-cell Lymphomas (Morphology, IHC, FISH)

 

 

·       Blastoid morphology means that the case looks like a lymphoblastic lymphoma;

·       DLBCL+ morphology means that the case is a B-cell lymphoma with the morphological features of a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), NOS.

·       DLBCL/BL+ morphology means that the case has morphological features of both DLBCL and Burkitt lymphoma (BL), with a relatively monotonous appearance with or without a starry-sky pattern

Please note that while some cases of BL have a somewhat atypical morphological appearance that might suggest DLBCL/BL, finding a typical Burkitt lymphoma phenotype (CD10+, BCL2-) and an isolated IGH/MYC translocation cannot be used by themselves to make a definitive diagnosis of BL in a case with a DLBCL/BL morphologic appearance if the morphologic or other features are considered to be too atypical.

Algorithm for classification of aggressive B-cell lymphomas in WHO-HAEM5 in the light of MYC, BCL2 and BCL6 rearrangement and complex 11q gain/loss patterns. HGBL high grade B-cell lymphoma, R rearrangement, G germline configuration.

*Burkitt lymphoma

What is Burkitt Lymphoma (BL)?   

 

●        A highly aggressive B cell NHL that has very short doubling time


BL doubling time?         

 

●        25 hours, ie 1 day!


WHO "gold standard" for BL diagnosis?         

 

●        WHO states that there is no "gold standard" for diagnosis

What features are considered typical of BL?         

 

●        Extranodal sites of involvement

●        Monomorphic, intermediate-sized (not large) cells (roughly equal to the width of endothelial cell or histiocyte nucleus)

●        Basophilic cytoplasm, cytoplasmic vacuoles and numerous mitoses

●        Chromosomal translocations involving MYC, eg t(8;14)

 


What sites if involvement are considered typical of BL?

        

●        Extranodal sites of involvement

●        In Western hemisphere, BL presents as abdominal mass

●        BL may also present in leukemic phase


Typical BL cytologic features?  

      

●        Monomorphic, intermediate-sized cells with basophilic cytoplasm, cytoplasmic vacuoles and numerous mitoses (starry sky appearance)


 

Chromosomal translocations in BL typically involve what gene?         

 

●        MYC

What sort of gene is Myc (c-Myc) ?   

 

●        A regulator gene that codes for a transcription factor

●        The protein encoded by this gene is a multifunctional, nuclear phosphoprotein that plays a role in → cell cycle progression, apoptosis and cellular transformation


How do translocations involving MYC cause cancer?         

 

●        Constitutive expression leads to the unregulated expression of the MYC gene (transcription factor involved in cell proliferation), which results in the formation of cancer


Myc is located on chromosome __?         

 

●        Chromosome 8q24.2


3 clinicopathologic variants of BL         

 

  1. Endemic
  2. Sporadic
  3. Immunodeficiency-associated


Where does endemic BL occur?         

 

●        Equatorial Africa

Endemic BL is associated with what infection?         

 

●        EBV in almost all cases

●        ? Plasmodium falciparum is a driver as well!


What clinical BL variant is seen in western countries? What is the patient type?         

 

●        Sporadic BL occurs in the West in immunocompetent patients

●        Abdo mass - ileo cecal region

●        25% EBV



Immunodeficiency-associated BL occurs in what patient group?         

 

●        HIV/AIDS

●        aka AIDS-associated BL in patients infected with HIV

●        LN/Bone marrow involvement

●        45% Burkitt


BL median age in adult group?         

 

●        30 years


Typical BL presentation in the west?         

 

●        An abdominal mass

●        May also present as acute leukemia

●        Other possible sites

○        Breasts (bilateral) - BL expresses PRL receptor

○        Ovaries, kidneys

Microscopic Pathology features of BL?         

 

●        Monomorphic proliferation of medium-sized transformed B lymphocytes

●        Round nuclei, clumped chromatin, basophilic, vacuolated cytoplasm

●        Multiple small nucleoli

●        Numerous mitoses & macrophages with phagocytosed debris ("starry sky" pattern)


BL characteristic IHC?         

 

●        B cells with germinal center phenotype

●        IgM(+), CD10(+), Bcl-6(+)

●        TdT(-), Bcl-2(-)

What translocation is characteristic of BL? Most typical and variant translocations?         

 

●        t(8;14)

●        Partners:

○        IGH (85-90%)

○        IGK or IGL = chr 2 and 22 respectively (10-15%)

 




●        Think: "Burk-8 lymphoma"

●        MYC translocation is characteristic of BL but can be seen in other NHL

Is BL a high or low grade lymphoma?         

 

●        High


Is BL karyotype complex or simple?         

 

●        BL karyotype is usually simple, unlike other high-grade lymphomas

Typical Gene expression profiling for BL?         

 

●        Expressed at high levels: MYC and target genes

●        Expressed at low levels: NF-κB target genes and major histocompatibility complex class I genes

Gene expression profiling for BL: Expressed at high levels?         

 

●        MYC and target genes


Gene expression profiling for BL: Expressed at low levels?

 

●        NF-κB target genes and major histocompatibility complex class I genes

Name 3 mutations common in sporadic BL  

    

●        TCF3 mutations

●        ID3 mutations

●        CCND3 mutations

BL top DDx?        

Ie What is the DDx for high grade lymphoma?

 

●        Burkitt lymphoma

●        High-grade B-cell lymphoma (WHO 2016)

●        Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, NOS

●        Lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma

●        Mantle cell lymphoma, blastoid variant

 

KSHV/HHV8-associated B-cell LPD

Primary effusion lymphoma

What is Primary Effusion Lymphoma?  

 

●        Primary effusion lymphoma (PEL) is human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)-associated large B-cell lymphoma

●        Most often involving body cavities

●        No tumor mass

 

Which body cavities are most often involved by PEL?             

 

●        Pleural, pericardial, or peritoneal cavity

2 forms of PEL  

 

●        Classic and extracavitary/solid

 

HHV-8(+) lymphomas indistinguishable from PEL rarely present as solid tumor mass, These are designated?     

 

●        Extracavitary or solid variant of PEL

●        ie There are 2 forms of PEL: classic (involving a body cavity) and extracavitary/solid

What virus is essential for PEL diagnosis?          

 

●        HHV-8 virus (a.k.a. Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus)

●        EBV is virtually constant in setting of HIV infection

 

What is HHV-8 virus

 

●        γ herpes double-stranded DNA lymphotropic virus

●        Transmitted by body fluids, especially saliva

●        Encodes number of homologues of cellular genes involved in cell proliferation and apoptosis

●        HHV-8 evades host cytotoxic T-cell immunosurveillance by infecting → B cells

●        Lifelong and latent infection

●        5-20% seroprevalence bordering → Mediterranean Sea

●        < 5% seroprevalence in North America, Northern Europe, and Asia

 

Is there IHC for HHV8?

 

●        Yes

●        LANA1

 

HHV-8 is associated with what malignancies - name 3?         

 

●        PEL

●        Kaposi sarcoma

●        Multicentric Castleman disease (MCD)

●        MCD-associated plasmablastic/large B-cell lymphoma

What is the etiology of PEL?      

 

●        HHV-8 virus is essential for diagnosis

What patients are affected by PEL?       

 

●        Severely immunosuppressed (usually HIV infection)

How do the 2 forms of PEL present?     

 

●        Classic form of PEL

○        Lymphoma cells grow in pleural, peritoneal, &/or pericardial effusions

○        Intracavitary mass in ∼ 25% of patients

●        Extracavitary or solid variant of PEL

○        Patients present with extracavitary mass

Microscopic features of the classic form of PEL?             

 

●        Classic form of PEL is seen in cytologic preparations of effusion

●        Large cells with round to irregular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm

 



Microscopic features of the extracavitary/solid variant of PEL ?

 

●        Extracavitary/solid variant of PEL involves tissue specimens

●        Diffuse pattern; starry sky common; high mitotic activity

Key findings of Ancillary Tests in PEL?   

 

●        HHV-8(+) is essential for diagnosis (LANA1)

●        Plasma cell-associated markers (+); pan-B cell (-)

●        No rearrangements of MYC, BCL2, BCL6, CCND1

●        TP53 and RAS genes are rarely mutated

●        Gene expression profile

●        Features of plasma cells and EBV-transformed lymphocytes

Immunophenotype of PEL         

 

HHV-8(+) is essential for diagnosis

 

Classic form of PEL

●        Plasma cell-associated markers (+)

○        CD138, CD38, IRF-4/MUM1

●        Pan-B-cell markers (-)

○        Neg for: CD19, CD20, CD79a, pax-5

○        CD10(-), CD15(-), Bcl-6(-), LMP1(-), FMC7

●        Specific T cell markers negative

○        CD3(-), CD2(-)

○        Aberrant expression of T-cell antigens

■        CD45RO (∼ 90%), CD7 (∼ 30%), CD4 (∼ 20%)

●        CD38, EMA

●        CD45/LCA(+), CD71(+),

●        HLA-DR(+); CD23(+) in ∼ 20%

●        CD30(+/-), surface Ig(-), cytoplasmic Ig(+/-)

●        Notch (+) in most cases

Can PEL have rearrangements of MYC and BCL2?             

 

●        No rearrangements of MYC, BCL2, BCL6, CCND1

What 2 genes are rarely mutated in PEL?           

 

●        TP53 and RAS genes are rarely mutated

●        Gene expression profile

○        Features of plasma cells and EBV-transformed lymphocytes

Top Differential Diagnoses for PEL?

 

●        Anaplastic plasma cell myeloma

●        Large B-cell lymphoma arising in HHV8-associated multicentric Castleman disease

●        HHV8/EBV+ germinotropic lymphoproliferative disorder

●        Plasmablastic lymphoma

●        Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma associated with chronic inflammation

KSHV/HHV8-associated LPD (MCD, DLBCL, GLPD)

What three disorders are classified under HHV8-associated LPD in WHO 2016

 

  1. Multicentric Castlemans Disease (MCD)
  2. HHV8+ DLBCL, NOS
  3. HHV8-positive germinotropic lymphoproliferative disorder (GLPD)

 

Note: Primary effusion lymphoma (PEL) is a specific category of HHV-8-associated large B-cell lymphoma in WHO 2016

 

What are the 2 general types of Castleman's disease?

 

Castleman's disease, an atypical lymphoproliferative disorder, can be classified into 2 types:

1) Hyaline-vascular type

2) Plasma cell types

●        Classification is according to the histologic features of the affected lymph nodes.

●        The plasma cell type is frequently associated with systemic manifestations and is often refractory to systemic therapy including corticosteroids and chemotherapy, particularly in multicentric form.

 

What is thought to be the key to the pathogenesis of Castlemans Disease?

 

●        Caused by excessive production of cytokines, in particular IL6

●        Dysregulated overproduction of interleukin-6 (IL-6) from affected lymph nodes is thought to be responsible for the systemic manifestations of this disease.

 

What is Multicentric Castlemans Disease?

 

●        Clinicopathological entity

●        Encompasses a group of systemic polyclonal lymphoproliferative disorders with proliferation of morphologically benign lymphocytes, plasma cells, and vessels

●        In patients with HIV, MCD is almost always HHV8-related

○        In the absence of HIV, MCD is HHV8-related in as many as 50% of cases, and usually occurs in HHV8-endemic areas

 

What is the clinical presentation of Multicentric Castlemans Disease?

 

●        Generalized LAD

●        Splenomegaly

●        Constitutional Symptoms

 

What are the microscopic features of Multicentric Castlemans Disease?

 

●        Abnormal follicles

○        Involuted germinal centres

○        Hyalinized

●        Prominent mantle zones intruding into GC

○        Prominent rings of concentric mantle zone cells

■        AKA onion skinning

●        Plasmablasts in mantle zones, GCs and interfollicular plasma cell hyperplasia

 

 

 

What is the immunophenotype of Multicentric Castlemans Disease?

 

●        B cell antigens +/-

●        cIgM Lambda +

●        IRF4 +

●        CD138-

 

Plasma cells in multicentric Castlemans disease are lambda-restricted, does this mean that they are monoclonal?

 

●        NO!

●        Molecular studies have shown that they are polyclonal!

 

What is the prognosis of Multicentric Castlemans Disease?

 

●        Poor, but improved with new therapies!

●        Interference with IL-6 signal transduction may constitute a new therapeutic strategy for this disease.

●        Eg. Siltuximab (an Anti-Interleukin-6 Monoclonal Antibody)

 

What is HHV-8(+) DLBCL, NOS? 

 

●        2016: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)(+) large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) arising in multicentric Castleman disease (MCD)

●        Although similar lymphomas with HHV8-positivity have been shown without MCD!

 

What was HHV-8(+) Large B-Cell Lymphoma called in WHO 2008?

 

●        "Plasmablastic Lymphoma Arising in HHV8+ Multicentric Castleman disease (PBL-MCD)"

●        HHV-8(+) Large B-Cell Lymphoma was previously (WHO 2008) called PBL arising in MCD

Why is the term "plasmablastic" used for this lymphoma?      

 

●        Cells morphologically resemble plasma cells and have abundant cytoplasmic immunoglobulin

●        However it corresponds to a naive, IgM-producing plasma cell without Ig somatic hypermutation

HHV-8 infects persons via?        

 

●        Body fluids, particularly saliva

Is HHV-8 infection transient or lifelong?

 

●        Latent infection in B lymphocytes is lifelong

What is HHV-8 

 

●        Double-stranded DNA virus

●        Latent infection in B lymphocytes is lifelong

●        High HHV-8 seroprevalence in parts of Africa, South American, and Mediterranean basin

●        Uncommon (< 5%) in North America

Describe the pathogenesis of DLBCL arising in MCD             

 

●        HHV-8 initially infects plasmablasts in mantle zones of follicles

●        HHV-8(+) plasmablasts expand to form aggregates (a.k.a. microlymphomas)

●        HHV-8(+) aggregates progress/expand into histologically overt LBCL

●        Most patients have profound immunosuppression

Plasmablasts in HHV-8(+) Large B-Cell Lymphoma express what Ig?           

 

●        IgM Lambda

In HHV-8(+) Large B-Cell Lymphoma HHV8 infects what cells?

 

●        HHV8 initially infects singly scattered plasmablasts in mantle zones of follicles


HHV8(+) plasmablasts expand to form so-called ______________ lymphomas?

●        HHV8(+) "microlymphomas" expand into histologically overt Lymphoma

Does HHV-8(+) Large B-Cell Lymphoma occur in immunocompetent or immunosuppressed patients?

             

●        Immunosuppressed

●        Most patients with PBL-MCD have profound immunosuppression

HHV-8(+) Large B-Cell Lymphoma sites of disease involvement?   

 

●        Lymph nodes, spleen

HHV-8(+) Large B-Cell Lymphoma Leukemic involvement occurs at what disease phase (early or late)?   

 

●        Leukemic involvement as part of a terminal phase

HHV-8(+) Large B-Cell Lymphoma prognosis?    

 

●        Poor; survival often < 1 year

HHV-8(+) Large B-Cell Lymphoma predominant histological finding?     

 

●        Plasmablastic lymphoma:

○        Sheets of large cells diffusely replacing LN

○        Plasmablasts, immunoblasts or centroblasts

○        Mitotic figures common

 



HHV-8(+) Large B-Cell Lymphoma immunophenotype?    

 

●        HHV8(+), IgM(+), λ(+)

●        CD45/LCA(+/-), CD20(-/+), CD79a(-), EBV(-)

●        Monoclonal IgH rearrangements on PCR

PBL-MCD Top DDx?       

 

●        Primary effusion lymphoma (PEL)
Extracavitary PEL
HHV8(+) germinotropic lymphoproliferative disorder
HHV-8+ LBCL, NOS

Plasma cell neoplasms with associated paraneoplastic syndrome

 [QZ1]In lymphoid neoplasms, such as lymphomas and leukemias, CDKN2A deletions contribute significantly to disease progression by disabling cell cycle control and apoptosis mechanisms.

1.       p16 Function in Lymphoid Neoplasms: p16 normally acts as a brake on cell division. It inhibits CDK4 and CDK6, preventing cells from advancing from the G1 to the S phase in the cell cycle. In lymphoid cells, the deletion of CDKN2A, leading to p16 loss, allows these cells to divide uncontrollably. This uncontrolled cell division is a key driver of lymphoid tumor growth.

2.       p14 Role in Lymphoid Neoplasms: p14 works by stabilizing p53, a protein that signals damaged cells to undergo apoptosis (programmed cell death). Without p14, p53s function is compromised, allowing lymphoid cells with DNA damage to avoid apoptosis and continue dividing. This is particularly dangerous in lymphoid neoplasms, where unchecked proliferation of abnormal cells can quickly escalate.

 

 

 

 

 

 [QZ2]Cyclin Dependent Kinase Inhibitor 2A

 [QZ3]Uses of EMA Immunostain

·        Tumor Identification: EMA staining is widely used to help identify and classify tumors, as it is typically positive in epithelial-origin tumors (carcinomas) and negative in most non-epithelial tumors. It can be useful in distinguishing:

·        Carcinomas: EMA is generally positive in carcinomas (e.g., breast, ovarian, and lung adenocarcinomas).

·        Mesothelioma vs. Carcinoma: EMA is usually positive in both, but membranous EMA staining supports a diagnosis of carcinoma, whereas cytoplasmic or weak EMA staining may suggest mesothelioma.

·        Lymphomas vs. Carcinomas: EMA is usually negative in lymphomas but can be positive in some types of Hodgkin lymphoma and plasma cell neoplasms.

·        Soft Tissue and Other Tumors: EMA can also be positive in some non-epithelial tumors, including:

·        Meningiomas: EMA helps in the identification of meningiomas as they often express this marker.

·        Plasma Cell Tumors: EMA is commonly positive in multiple myeloma and other plasma cell neoplasms.

·        Some Sarcomas: Certain sarcomas, like synovial sarcoma, may show EMA positivity.

 [QZ4]What It Detects: VS38c highlights the ER in cells that produce a lot of protein, like plasma cells.

Why It's Used:

 

·        Plasma Cell Cancers: Helps diagnose multiple myeloma and plasmacytomas by identifying plasma cells.

·        Other Tumors: Useful for some lymphomas and tumors with high ER activity.

Staining Pattern: VS38c shows up in the cell cytoplasm, where the ER is located.

 [QZ5]What It Detects: BLIMP1 is a protein found in cells transforming into plasma cells, which are responsible for antibody production.

Why Its Used:

 

·        Plasma Cell Cancers: BLIMP1 helps diagnose conditions like multiple myeloma by identifying plasma cells.

·        Autoimmune and Immune Disorders: Changes in BLIMP1 are linked to some autoimmune diseases and immune cell functions.

Staining Pattern: BLIMP1 shows up in the nucleus of plasma cells, where it regulates genes for antibody production.

 [QZ6]What It Detects: XBP1 is primarily found in cells with high protein production demands, like plasma cells and other secretory cells.

Why Its Used:

 

·        Plasma Cell Disorders: XBP1 is used to study multiple myeloma and other plasma cell cancers, where it plays a role in antibody production.

·        Cell Stress Responses: Important in conditions involving cell stress and diseases related to protein misfolding, as it helps cells adapt to stress by managing protein synthesis.

Staining Pattern: XBP1 shows up in the nucleus when active, helping control genes related to protein folding and secretion.

 [QZ7]Where It's Found: Mostly in plasma cells in tissues where IgA is produced, like mucosal areas.

Why It's Useful:

 

·        IgA Nephropathy: Shows up as IgA deposits in kidney cells, helping confirm this diagnosis.

·        Skin Conditions: Certain skin diseases, like dermatitis herpetiformis, show IgA deposits in specific skin layers.

·        IgA Myeloma: In this plasma cell cancer, cytoplasmic IgA staining identifies the IgA type of myeloma.

 [QZ8]NK/T-cell lymphoma was previously referred to as angiocentric lymphoma. It shows angiocentric growth with invasion and destruction of vessel walls as illustrated here. The elastic lamina of small arteries is disrupted and there is deposition of fibrinoid material in the walls and lumen. The vascular damage is postulated to be caused by EBV-induced chemokines.

Destruction of blood vessels results in coagulative necrosis and ulceration of the involved tissues. In advanced stages, the lesions may coalesce producing highly disfiguring facial lesions that ultimately prove lethal.

 [QZ9]Morphology: The lymphomatoid granulomatosis lesions are characterized by angiocentric and angioinvasive lymphoid infiltrates with fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls and widespread necrosis of the surrounding parenchyma (as shown here). Large centrally necrotic nodules are common. There is karyorrhectic debris but no neutrophils (unlike the necrotizing lesions of Wegener's granulomatosis).

The infiltrate is polymorphous and consists of small lymphocytes (mostly reactive T-cells), histiocytes, immunoblasts, and EBV-positive large atypical lymphoid cells. The number of EBV-positive cells varies within and among nodules and forms the basis of grading of LG. Cases with diffuse sheets of EBV-positive cells without an angiocentric T-cell infiltrate should be classified as EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Plasma cells are not a prominent component. There are no neutrophils, eosinophils, multinucleated giant cells, or granulomas.

The morphology of LG lesions in the brain, kidneys, and liver is similar to those seen in the lungs with angiocentric and angiodestructive growth pattern. In brain, it can form lymphohistiocytic nodules with necrotic centers (but no well-formed granulomas) and cause brain infarcts.

The skin lesions consist of subcutaneous or dermal nodules (most common) or plaques (about 15% of cases). The lymphoid infiltrate is perivascular and periadnexal in distribution resembling lichen sclerosus et atrophicus. The infiltrate is located in the dermis and may extend into the subcutis. Granulomas are not seen. EBV-positive cells are more difficult to demonstrate than in the lungs.
